acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
The Kurhula 3:3 Female arrived as part of a twin litter, born around August 2023 to the Ntsumi 3:3 Female and sired by the Nweti Male, a dominant and exceptionally relaxed male who held a vast territory across the southeastern reaches of Londolozi for the better part of a decade.

She and her twin sister, the Mgiba 3:3 Female, are among the Nweti Male’s most recent offspring, and with him believed to have passed in early 2025, they now represent one of the clearest threads of his legacy on this land.

The Kurhula 3:3 Female has been seen periodically along the eastern portion of Londolozi’s southern boundary as she navigates the early stages of independence. Where her sister has moved further south toward the Sabi River, Kurhula has remained closer to the ground she was raised on — beginning the process of establishing herself in a landscape that, for a young female, is both familiar and fiercely contested.

She is still finding her feet. That, in itself, is worth watching.

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: The last surviving cub of a litter of three, he is on the cusp of independence.
acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt_alt: With growing size, confidence, and a strong lineage behind him, he is beginning the classic nomadic journey of a young male leopard.
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
Recently independent, he has been named after the prominent waterhole in the southeast, Shingi Dam.

Heritage & Lineage

Born in January 2024 to the Nkoveni 2:2 Female and sired by the Maxim’s Male, the Nkoveni Young Male represents the merging of two powerful leopard lineages. His mother is one of Londolozi’s most prolific and well-known females, descended from the Mashaba Female and Marthly Male of the Sunsetbend bloodline. His father, the Maxim’s Male, is currently the dominant male across much of the southern Sabi Sands and is known for his impressive size, power, and success.

He was born into a litter of three—two sisters and himself. Tragically, both of his sisters were lost to the Kambula Pride in separate incidents, leaving him as the sole survivor of the litter. This is the first time the Nkoveni Female has successfully raised a male cub to this age, making his development particularly significant.

Developmental Stage & Independence

Now approximately 18 months old, the Nkoveni Young Male is at the brink of full independence. While he continues to share kills with his mother on occasion, his behaviour increasingly reflects the hallmarks of an emerging solitary male: prolonged solo forays, bold exploration, and frequent tree-climbing displays.

He has become notably dominant around food, often denying his mother access to kills she has made. This behaviour is more typical of established adult males and highlights his accelerating maturity. On multiple occasions, he has hoisted kills into trees, growled his mother away, and shown reluctance to share—behaviour that is not typically expected from a cub still under maternal care. His physical development has kept pace: he now rivals his mother in size and is rapidly growing in muscle and confidence.

The coming months will likely see him pushed further afield, and the extent to which his father, the Maxim’s Male, tolerates his presence will heavily influence the timing and direction of this next phase.

Physical Characteristics

3:3 spot pattern
Muscular frame for his age, with a developing thick neck and broad chest
Golden coat with rich rosettes that reflect his father’s impressive genetics
Expressive amber eyes, slightly softer features compared to other males of similar age

Behavioural Notes

The Nkoveni Young Male displays a growing self-assurance nurtured by the security of his mother’s territory and her attentive guidance. While he was once the least confident of his litter, he has evolved into a bold and dominant young leopard.

He has repeatedly been observed asserting control over kills, hoisting and guarding them even from his mother and, in one remarkable instance, standing his ground against the Maxim’s Male. Though the larger male eventually redirected his attention to the Nkoveni Female, the young male’s audacity signalled a readiness to challenge dominance far earlier than expected.

Still, his inexperience remains evident. He retreats into trees at the approach of hyenas and exhibits a learning curve in refining hunting and defensive strategies. Despite this, his play, curiosity, and physical boldness are unmistakable signs of his emergence as a force in the making.

Territorial Outlook

Like all young males, the Nkoveni Young Male will soon embark on a nomadic phase. He will likely spend the next year or two wandering the reserve and beyond, avoiding dominant males while developing the skills and strength needed to one day compete for a territory of his own.

Initially, his movements are expected to orbit the outer reaches of his mother’s territory, particularly near productive hunting areas like Shingilana Dam. The timing of his final departure will depend on food availability, his confidence, and most significantly, the tolerance of his father, the Maxim’s Male.

Significance and Legacy

The Nkoveni Young Male is an important emerging figure in the continuing story of the Sunsetbend lineage. He represents both the resilience of his mother—who survived the loss of two cubs and a brutal encounter with lions—and the genetic strength of his dominant father. He is poised to take his place as a future force in the Londolozi leopard landscape, provided he can navigate the complex and often perilous nomadic chapter ahead.

In his journey, we see echoes of those who came before him: the survival instincts of the Nkoveni Female, the dominance of the Maxim’s Male, and the mysterious and ancient rhythm that guides all young male leopards as they step out into the wild to find their future.

If his recent behaviour is anything to go by, he will not go quietly, he is a leopard with presence, power, and a future worth watching closely.

users_spotted.user_description: California native, travel junkie, animal lover...... have traveled to Africa over a dozen times to fulfill my passion for observing animals in their natural environment. Londolozi has become my favorite place to stay, with almost yearly visits since 2019.

I came here for the 1st time with my husband in Feb 2010, 2nd stop on a Vic Falls-Londolozi-Cape Town trip. I'd wanted to come here for years, as my ambition was to see a leopard in the wild. We looked at the cost, thought "ouch!" then - well it is just a one-off! On our 1st game drive  we saw Vomba, so mission achieved. Then the next morning we saw Camp Pan mating with Nottens! Within 24 hours of arriving we were completely smitten, and knew we not only had to come back, but come back the next year. So began a highly expensive addiction, and my trip 3 weeks ago was my 9th consecutive year and I celebrated my 100th game drive!
First visited Londolozi in June 2011.  My profile picture up close with the Nkuwa female during our 2023 visit. We returned again in 2025.  Can't wait to come back again!
South African living in Canada for the past +25 years, lover of the African bush!
Passionate about wildlife conservation and Big Cats!   Travel, family, reading, hiking, skiing, safaris!

Love nature, watching animals and going on safari. Been lots of times on safari to different African countries. Londolozi is one of my favourite places. I am always looking forward to my next trip to Londolozi!

Bob and I live in the San Francisco Bay Area where we enjoy boating, hiking, photography and travel. After many trips to Eastern and Southern Africa, we are pleased to call Londolozi our 'African home!'
Have been coming to Londolozi since 1987!

I am a published author and wildlife and travel writer, specializing is African safaris.  I have always had a deep affinity with all living creatures, even while growing up in urban Amsterdam. Going on safari has enhanced that innate connection into a lifelong passion.
Self proclaimed Leopardographer.

Born in New York and settled down in Hong Kong for the past 20 years after living in London and Tokyo.  I "found" Londolozi in 2009 and have been a regular visitor since.  Over that time I have gained a passion for the bush and the photographic opportunities it provides.  Thanks to the tutelage of the Londolozi rangers and Creative hub I am getting my photography to an acceptable level.

Passionate Londolozi Guests! Avid wildlife photographers. Supporters and advocates for the Good Work Foundation through the All Heart Fund in the USA. Restaurateurs and wine & spirits retailers in Sarasota, Florida at Michael’s On East (www.bestfood.com)

Nick grew up in Johannesburg with a deep love for the outdoors. After finishing high school, he spent a formative gap year in the Zimbabwean bushveld — an experience that cemented his passion for wildlife and conservation. Although he went on to study and build a career in corporate real estate, the pull of the wilderness never faded. Now an experienced member of the Londolozi guiding team, Nick finds the greatest joy in tracking leopards and immersing himself in the intricate world of birding. He has developed a strong passion for wildlife photography, always looking to capture authentic moments in the wild.

I am a published writer of three non fiction books, including My Life With Leopards, the Graham Cooke Story, which was set at Londolozi in the early 1990s. I am a seasoned safari traveller, contributing publications of safari lodges and destinations to various magazines and a keen safari photographer.

For the past 35 years I've been amazed and inspired by wildlife from all corners of the world. Following a career in the City of London I now dedicate my time to wildlife photographer and commitment to wildlife conservation. When not travelling I volunteer for Conservation Organisations based in London. Social Media - www.janeaddey.co.uk & @addeyphotos.

I live in Canada. My first visit was June 2023 and I stayed at Tree Camp for 1 week. 
I returned in June 2024 for another week. June 2025 I have reserved 10 days at Tree Camp. Londolozi has changed me. I am on a non-stop thrill during visits. The animals, the food, the service, nothing is too much to ask for during your stay. The Healing House services are spectacular! Londolozi is a truly magical place. It makes one feel alive! That is me with the amazing John Varty in my profile photo.

I am passionate about travel, photography, Africa(its people and wildlife), my family, especially my grandchildren! Going to Africa for the first time in 2010 changed my life and made me want to do wildlife expeditions! Since then I have traveled to all the continents mostly focusing on photographing wildlife! Londolozi has become one of my favorite places of all and I look forward to returning as many more times as possible! It has stolen my heart and I am humbled by the beauty of all the amazing creatures I have seen there.
If I’m not running, I’m hanging with Jo Ann loving retired life and planning our next trip!

I live in the US but I am from Argentina. Africa has conquered my heart! Kenya, Botswana, Zimbabwe, and now South Africa. Following the concept of wildness from Craig Foster... So much to learn from traditional cultures throughout the world!
I was a physicist in my professional life. I treasure the everlasting connections with many of my former students...

acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
Recently independent, she has been named after the Shangaan word tinxiya, meaning eyebrows. This is in relation to her particularly long eyebrow lashes when she was young ,and now the prominent eyebrow ridge she has inherited from her father.

Heritage & Lineage

Born in March 2024 to the Three Rivers 2:2 Female and sired by the Maxim’s Male, the Three Rivers Young Female represents the next generation in a legendary bloodline. Her mother, descended from the Piva Male and Xidulu Female, is known for her resilience and success despite early orphaning. Her father, the Maxim’s Male, is arguably one of the largest and most dominant male leopards in the Sabi Sand Reserve. The young female bears a striking resemblance to him, both in her robust build and in the confident, assured way she carries herself.

Though she was born into a litter of two, only she has survived; her sibling lost early.

Territorial Development

Still partially dependent on her mother, the Three Rivers Young Female is entering the exploratory phase of adolescence. She is frequently seen alongside her mother at kills, yet sightings also show her venturing into surrounding areas with increasing independence. It is anticipated that she will soon be fully independent and forced to establish a territory of her own.

Her future territorial prospects remain uncertain. Her mother’s territory, positioned in the southeastern sector of Londolozi, lies at the convergence of several other female territories, such as the Nkoveni, Xinkhova, Ximungwe, and Ndzanzeni Females. This makes for a highly contested environment. While it is possible that the Three Rivers Female may cede part of her territory to her daughter (a common maternal behaviour), external pressures may drive the young female to seek space further afield, possibly across the Sand River into a less densely populated region.

Physical Characteristics
  • Compact, muscular frame
  • Eyes reminiscent of her mother with the broad facial structure of her father
  • Confident posture, often observed climbing and scanning her surroundings from elevated positions
Development and Behaviour

Displaying a balance of playfulness and growing maturity, the Three Rivers Young Female is often seen climbing trees, stalking small prey, and practising critical survival skills. Her relationship with her mother has begun to shift, with less grooming, more tolerance, indicating the early stages of separation. While she continues to benefit from her mother’s skills and presence, the signs of emerging independence are clear.

Notably, she was recently seen with both her mother and the Maxim’s Male, an unusual sighting given the typically solitary nature of leopards and the male’s tendency to remain aloof. In a rare moment, she was observed playfully interacting with the male, suggesting an extraordinary degree of tolerance on his part. These interactions offer a unique glimpse into her social development and the bonds that may have helped safeguard her early life.

Current Status

Now around 17 months old, the Three Rivers Young Female is approaching the threshold of independence. Her presence still overlaps heavily with her mother’s, but she is slowly carving out her own narrative. The next few months will likely see her establishing a more defined range and refining her hunting and territorial skills. As she matures, the resilience and adaptability she inherits from her lineage will be crucial in determining her success.

Significance and Legacy

The Three Rivers Young Female represents the continuing arc of one of Londolozi’s most iconic lineages. Her mother, the Three Rivers Female, was herself orphaned at a young age but managed to establish territory and successfully raise cubs. Her father is a powerful force across the reserve. Now, as their daughter nears independence, she carries forward not only their genetic strength but also the hopes of continuing a story that began with the legendary Mother Leopard over four decades ago.

users_spotted.user_description: South African living in Canada for the past +25 years, lover of the African bush!

Love nature, watching animals and going on safari. Been lots of times on safari to different African countries. Londolozi is one of my favourite places. I am always looking forward to my next trip to Londolozi!

Bob and I live in the San Francisco Bay Area where we enjoy boating, hiking, photography and travel. After many trips to Eastern and Southern Africa, we are pleased to call Londolozi our 'African home!'
Passionate about wildlife conservation and Big Cats!   Travel, family, reading, hiking, skiing, safaris!

I am a published author and wildlife and travel writer, specializing is African safaris.  I have always had a deep affinity with all living creatures, even while growing up in urban Amsterdam. Going on safari has enhanced that innate connection into a lifelong passion.

Born in New York and settled down in Hong Kong for the past 20 years after living in London and Tokyo.  I "found" Londolozi in 2009 and have been a regular visitor since.  Over that time I have gained a passion for the bush and the photographic opportunities it provides.  Thanks to the tutelage of the Londolozi rangers and Creative hub I am getting my photography to an acceptable level.

I came here for the 1st time with my husband in Feb 2010, 2nd stop on a Vic Falls-Londolozi-Cape Town trip. I'd wanted to come here for years, as my ambition was to see a leopard in the wild. We looked at the cost, thought "ouch!" then - well it is just a one-off! On our 1st game drive  we saw Vomba, so mission achieved. Then the next morning we saw Camp Pan mating with Nottens! Within 24 hours of arriving we were completely smitten, and knew we not only had to come back, but come back the next year. So began a highly expensive addiction, and my trip 3 weeks ago was my 9th consecutive year and I celebrated my 100th game drive!

I am a published writer of three non fiction books, including My Life With Leopards, the Graham Cooke Story, which was set at Londolozi in the early 1990s. I am a seasoned safari traveller, contributing publications of safari lodges and destinations to various magazines and a keen safari photographer.

California native, travel junkie, animal lover...... have traveled to Africa over a dozen times to fulfill my passion for observing animals in their natural environment. Londolozi has become my favorite place to stay, with almost yearly visits since 2019.

Growing up in the small coastal town of Mtunzini, Matt's childhood was shaped by endless hours spent exploring the forests, beaches and wetlands that sparked a lifelong passion for wildlife. After completing a BSc degree, he worked in construction and landscaping before the opportunity to join Londolozi changed the course of his career. Today, as a ranger and wildlife photographer, he has the privilege of spending every day immersed in the wilderness that first inspired him as a child.

I am passionate about travel, photography, Africa(its people and wildlife), my family, especially my grandchildren! Going to Africa for the first time in 2010 changed my life and made me want to do wildlife expeditions! Since then I have traveled to all the continents mostly focusing on photographing wildlife! Londolozi has become one of my favorite places of all and I look forward to returning as many more times as possible! It has stolen my heart and I am humbled by the beauty of all the amazing creatures I have seen there.
If I’m not running, I’m hanging with Jo Ann loving retired life and planning our next trip!

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: An elusive and intriguing newcomer with an unknown past. Likely originating from the Kruger National Park, he is currently unnamed.
acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt_alt: Currently being seen in the southeastern parts, he is not firmly territorial and is seeking out a potential territory.
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
Heritage & Origins

Little is known about the 3:2 Male’s background. First seen on Mala Mala and subsequently across several reserves in the Sabi Sand system, his increasing presence in Londolozi suggests a westward dispersal typical of young males from the Kruger National Park. With no known maternal or paternal lineage in this area, he appears to be a truly wild, independent arrival, unmarked by prior habituation or familial ties to existing leopards on the reserve.

His spot pattern of 3:2 gives him his temporary identifier, and distinctive physical traits include:

  • Striking amber eyes
  • A noticeable nick in his right ear
  • Hairless scarring around the right eye

Behavioural Notes & Habituation

Initially highly skittish, the 3:2 Male has begun to show signs of becoming more relaxed around vehicles. However, he still displays typical behaviours of an unhabituated leopard: favouring dense thickets, dry riverbeds, and making himself scarce except when found on a kill. These rare sightings, often at hoisted kills, have given guides and trackers a fleeting glimpse into his secretive nature.

Despite this elusive behaviour, he has begun vocalising and scent-marking in various areas of southeastern Londolozi—an early sign that he may be exploring territorial intent. This, combined with reports of him feeding near the Sand River and remaining in the same area for several days, indicates a potential interest in establishing a foothold.

Current Status

  • Age: Unknown, but likely in early adulthood (estimated 4–6 years)
  • First sighted: 2024, on Mala Mala
  • Recent range: Southeastern Londolozi and neighbouring reserves
  • Habituation: Still semi-skittish but improving
  • Behaviour: Scent-marking, patrolling, feeding on kills in prominent trees

Territorial Outlook

The 3:2 Male’s appearance comes at a pivotal time. With the confirmed disappearance of the Senegal Bush Male and the absence of the Nweti Male, southeastern Londolozi holds a gap in dominant male presence. Nearby females like the Xinkhova Female are reaching reproductive maturity and are likely in search of stable male territory holders.

Whether the 3:2 Male will be able to establish himself remains uncertain. He may face pressure from other emerging or established males, such as the Maxim’s Male, Hlambela Male, or even the Flat Rock Male and Ntomi Male. As such, his future in this region will depend heavily on his ability to defend a territory and attract mating opportunities in the face of stiff competition.

Significance & Future Potential

Every new arrival reshapes the tapestry of Londolozi’s leopard population. Just as the Maxim’s Male once arrived unknown and now features prominently in the genetics of the next generation, the 3:2 Male may one day hold similar influence. His arrival marks the beginning of a story still in its early pages.

With ongoing collaboration between Londolozi and neighbouring reserves, a formal name may soon be given to this mysterious male. For now, the 3:2 Male remains a figure of quiet intrigue—a powerful symbol of the ever-shifting dynamics that define life in the wild.

We watch. We wait. And perhaps, we welcome.

acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
Heritage & Lineage

The Hlambela Male is the son of the Boulders Female and the Ravenscourt Male, both respected individuals within the greater Sabi Sands. He was given the name Hlambela, which means “he who swims” in Shangaan, inspired by his remarkable early hunting attempts that saw him wading through water in pursuit of White-faced Whistling Ducks.

Territorial Movement & Dominance

Initially, more skittish around vehicles, the Hlambela Male has undergone a notable behavioural shift in recent months. As he has grown in confidence, he has begun regularly patrolling a wide swath of territory that spans across the western sections of Marthly and stretches beyond Londolozi’s northern boundary.

With the presumed death of the Senegal Bush Male and the eastward shift of the ageing Flat Rock Male, space has opened in the north, creating a power vacuum. The Hlambela Male has moved quickly to exploit this opportunity. Increasing pressure on the Tortoise Pan Male suggests that he may be carving out a stronghold in what was once highly contested land. His consistent scent-marking, regular presence, and bold patrols indicate that he may be establishing himself as a dominant male in the region.

Physical Characteristics

  • Broad-chested, muscular build
  • Rich golden coat with dense rosettes
  • Facial structure strongly reminiscent of the Ravenscourt Male

Behavioural Notes

The Hlambela Male is known for his extensive and purposeful movements. He is frequently encountered patrolling along the Marthly riverbeds and western boundary lines. His ability to cover long distances in short periods suggests a leopard with ambition—and the physical capability to enforce it.

Early on, he displayed some nervousness around vehicles, but in recent months, he has become increasingly tolerant of vehicle presence, offering superb sightings. His comfort in diverse terrain, including riverine thickets and open grassland, speaks to his adaptability. This bodes well for his future as a territorial male, particularly in the dynamic and often unpredictable northern reaches of Londolozi.

His current size and presence suggest that he is commanding attention among his rivals and establishing himself in the hierarchy of northern male leopards. With neighbouring males like the Tortoise Pan Male, Thamba Male, and possibly even the returning Ntomi Male in the broader region, the Hlambela Male’s ability to maintain and defend a core territory will be tested in the near future.

Current Status

Age: Born July 2018 (7 years old)
Territory: Western Marthly and beyond the northern boundary; beginning to push eastward
Rivals: Tortoise Pan Male, Thamba Male, possible overlap with Maxim’s Male in the river corridor
Behaviour: Assertive, expanding range, increasingly relaxed around vehicles

Significance and Outlook

As the northern leopard dynamics continue to evolve, the Hlambela Male stands out as one of the most promising rising males. His strong lineage, physical stature, and expanding territorial presence make him a compelling figure in Londolozi’s current male hierarchy.

With time, he may become the dominant male across Marthly and the surrounding regions, filling a power vacuum left by the disappearance of older leopards. His increasing tolerance for vehicle presence also means that he will likely feature more prominently in guest sightings and photographic records in the months ahead.

The future of the Hlambela Male is still unfolding, but all signs suggest that he is not just passing through—he is here to stay.

acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
Named with reference to her being denned near to a pan call Jacana pan which is close to Little Bush Camp.

Heritage & Lineage
Born in March 2021 to the Kigelia Female and the White Dam Male. Part of a successful litter of two females, with her sister the Tsatsuma Female establishing territory further east. Represents a new generation exploring previously underutilized territories.

Territory
Currently establishing herself in an unconventional area for leopards:

Southwestern grasslands
Area from Vertical Dam to Cheetah Pools third clearing
Open territory largely unoccupied by other female leopards
Well-populated with prey species despite open terrain

Physical Characteristics

2:2 spot pattern
Distinctive orange eyes
Pink nose

Reproductive History
Not yet reproduced – still establishing territory

Current Status
Newly independent female pioneering territory in the southwestern grasslands, an area traditionally considered unusual for leopards but offering abundant hunting opportunities due to high prey density and limited competition from other females.

Behavioural Notes
She shows varying levels of comfort with vehicles, occasionally displaying shy behaviour by seeking cover, likely due to less frequent vehicle exposure in her chosen territory. Her adaptation to open grasslands demonstrates remarkable habitat selection flexibility, challenging traditional leopard habitat preference assumptions.

Currently showing promising hunting capabilities in open terrain, though still developing the confidence typical of established territorial females. Her comfort in such exposed areas suggests the potential for unique hunting strategies to develop.

Historical Significance
This represents an interesting case study of leopard adaptability, choosing to establish territory in an area traditionally considered marginal for leopards. Her success could potentially open up a new understanding of leopard habitat utilization at Londolozi. Her presence in the southwestern grasslands helps maintain predator balance in an area historically less frequented by leopards.

users_spotted.user_description:
As a young boy growing up on an agricultural farm in Zimbabwe, Sean spent every opportunity entertaining himself outdoors, camping in the local nature reserve and learning about all facets of the natural world.  

After completing a Bachelor of Science degree in Environmental Science in Cape Town, Sean was free to follow his nature ambitions and return to his bush-loving childhood dreams, which led him to Londolozi.

Going into semi-retirement on the guiding front in 2020 saw Sean settle into a far more permanent role in the LCH, focusing his efforts on producing media content for the Londolozi online space.

California native, travel junkie, animal lover...... have traveled to Africa over a dozen times to fulfill my passion for observing animals in their natural environment. Londolozi has become my favorite place to stay, with almost yearly visits since 2019.

Bob and I live in the San Francisco Bay Area where we enjoy boating, hiking, photography and travel. After many trips to Eastern and Southern Africa, we are pleased to call Londolozi our 'African home!'

I came here for the 1st time with my husband in Feb 2010, 2nd stop on a Vic Falls-Londolozi-Cape Town trip. I'd wanted to come here for years, as my ambition was to see a leopard in the wild. We looked at the cost, thought "ouch!" then - well it is just a one-off! On our 1st game drive  we saw Vomba, so mission achieved. Then the next morning we saw Camp Pan mating with Nottens! Within 24 hours of arriving we were completely smitten, and knew we not only had to come back, but come back the next year. So began a highly expensive addiction, and my trip 3 weeks ago was my 9th consecutive year and I celebrated my 100th game drive!

Love nature, watching animals and going on safari. Been lots of times on safari to different African countries. Londolozi is one of my favourite places. I am always looking forward to my next trip to Londolozi!

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: Born 2021, mirrors father Nweti's presence. Young force showing remarkable confidence while navigating nomadic phase in southern territories
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
Named after the area where he first established presence

Heritage & Lineage
Born to the Ntsumi Female and Nweti Male, inheriting his father’s impressive stature and relaxed demeanour. Part of an initial litter of two, though his female sibling did not survive.
Territory Evolution

Early Life: South of Londolozi’s boundary

Current Phase:

Exploring southwestern Londolozi
Operating within father’s broader territory
Particularly active around:

Southern grasslands
Drainage systems
The area around Piva Pan

Physical Characteristics

4:4 spot pattern
Striking resemblance to his father
Notably large size for his age
Already showing impressive physical development at three years

Behavioural Notes
Demonstrates remarkable characteristics:

Shows unusual confidence around other predators (shared warthog kill with hyena)
Displays impressive strength (documented dragging warthog 800m)
Maintains calm demeanor in challenging situations
Follows father’s movements for safety

Current Status
Currently navigating the nomadic phase while staying within the relative safety of his father’s territory. Shows growing confidence in interactions with other predators while developing hunting and survival skills.

Historical Significance
Represents interesting aspects of male leopard development:

Demonstrates father-son territory dynamics
Shows early independence adaptation
Currently contributing to southern territory dynamics

His presence in the southern territories and growing confidence suggest potential for future territorial establishment, though high male density may influence his eventual dispersal.

users_spotted.user_description: After a few years of working in the world of economic consulting, Kate’s love of adventure, wilderness and sense of curiosity led her to move away from the city and join the Londolozi guiding team.  It was amidst her years of studying politics, philosophy and economics that her love of exploring and understanding different wilderness areas in South Africa compounded through trips with friends and family. Kate has been fortunate to travel to many different corners of the world but she’ll argue that nothing quite beats being surrounded by nature watching an African sunrise or sunset, especially at Londolozi!

California native, travel junkie, animal lover...... have traveled to Africa over a dozen times to fulfill my passion for observing animals in their natural environment. Londolozi has become my favorite place to stay, with almost yearly visits since 2019.

Growing up in the small coastal town of Mtunzini, Matt's childhood was shaped by endless hours spent exploring the forests, beaches and wetlands that sparked a lifelong passion for wildlife. After completing a BSc degree, he worked in construction and landscaping before the opportunity to join Londolozi changed the course of his career. Today, as a ranger and wildlife photographer, he has the privilege of spending every day immersed in the wilderness that first inspired him as a child.

Bob and I live in the San Francisco Bay Area where we enjoy boating, hiking, photography and travel. After many trips to Eastern and Southern Africa, we are pleased to call Londolozi our 'African home!'
Passionate about wildlife conservation and Big Cats!   Travel, family, reading, hiking, skiing, safaris!

Nick grew up in Johannesburg with a deep love for the outdoors. After finishing high school, he spent a formative gap year in the Zimbabwean bushveld — an experience that cemented his passion for wildlife and conservation. Although he went on to study and build a career in corporate real estate, the pull of the wilderness never faded. Now an experienced member of the Londolozi guiding team, Nick finds the greatest joy in tracking leopards and immersing himself in the intricate world of birding. He has developed a strong passion for wildlife photography, always looking to capture authentic moments in the wild.

I live in the US but I am from Argentina. Africa has conquered my heart! Kenya, Botswana, Zimbabwe, and now South Africa. Following the concept of wildness from Craig Foster... So much to learn from traditional cultures throughout the world!
I was a physicist in my professional life. I treasure the everlasting connections with many of my former students...

Having joined the Londolozi team, he is now fulfilling his childhood dream of living and working in the African bush.

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: Born 2019 in Ngala, ventured far south. Young nomad showing adaptability and patience while seeking territory amid northern dynamics.
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
Named after the Shangaan word for Gardenia tree

Heritage & Lineage
Born in March/April 2019 to the Xitsalala Female and Tamboti Male at Ngala in the Timbavati Reserve. Born in a litter of two, with his sister also reaching independence though her current status remains unknown.

Territory Evolution

Early Life (2019-2021): Ngala, Timbavati Reserve

Young, developing male physique

Represents interesting aspects of leopard dispersal:

Demonstrates long-distance male dispersal capabilities

Exemplifies patience in territory acquisition

users_spotted.user_description: Nick grew up in Johannesburg with a deep love for the outdoors. After finishing high school, he spent a formative gap year in the Zimbabwean bushveld — an experience that cemented his passion for wildlife and conservation. Although he went on to study and build a career in corporate real estate, the pull of the wilderness never faded. Now an experienced member of the Londolozi guiding team, Nick finds the greatest joy in tracking leopards and immersing himself in the intricate world of birding. He has developed a strong passion for wildlife photography, always looking to capture authentic moments in the wild.

I am a published author and wildlife and travel writer, specializing is African safaris.  I have always had a deep affinity with all living creatures, even while growing up in urban Amsterdam. Going on safari has enhanced that innate connection into a lifelong passion.

Bob and I live in the San Francisco Bay Area where we enjoy boating, hiking, photography and travel. After many trips to Eastern and Southern Africa, we are pleased to call Londolozi our 'African home!'

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: Born 2019, nomadic explorer named for curious eyes. Early human exposure created remarkably relaxed demeanor despite nomadic challenges.
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
Named for the Shangaan word ‘kangela’ meaning to look with curious eyes

Heritage & Lineage
Born in December 2019 to the Schotia Female and the Nyeleti Male on Singita property. His early exposure to humans near Singita Ebony Lodge shaped his remarkably relaxed nature. Born as part of a litter of two, though his sibling was lost at a few months of age.

Territory Evolution

Early Life (2019-2021): Around Singita Ebony Lodge
Independence (June 2021): Began nomadic phase
Exploration Phase (2023): First appeared on Londolozi’s western sections
Later Phase (2023-2024): Explored northern territories, particularly Marthly

Current Status: Dispersed from Sabi Sands (mid-2024)

Physical Characteristics

Distinctive spot pattern with black dots inside rosettes
Elongated, elegant build
Dark facial features around the eyes
Notable battle scars along spine from territorial conflicts
Not particularly large but graceful in form

Behavioural Notes
Demonstrated several notable characteristics:

Exceptionally relaxed around vehicles
Showed unusual tolerance of other young males (shared tree with Ntomi Male)
Maintained a curious nature throughout the nomadic phase

Historical Significance
Represents interesting aspects of leopard behaviour:

Demonstrates impact of early human exposure
Shows unusual social tolerance for a male leopard

Though his time at Londolozi was relatively brief, his story provides valuable insights into the challenges and adaptations of nomadic male leopards, particularly in their exploration of potential territories.

Growing up in the small coastal town of Mtunzini, Matt's childhood was shaped by endless hours spent exploring the forests, beaches and wetlands that sparked a lifelong passion for wildlife. After completing a BSc degree, he worked in construction and landscaping before the opportunity to join Londolozi changed the course of his career. Today, as a ranger and wildlife photographer, he has the privilege of spending every day immersed in the wilderness that first inspired him as a child.

Love nature, watching animals and going on safari. Been lots of times on safari to different African countries. Londolozi is one of my favourite places. I am always looking forward to my next trip to Londolozi!

Keagan has always had a connection with wildlife, having been lucky enough to visit Londolozi as a child. After growing up in Johannesburg, he attended boarding school in the KwaZulu Natal Midlands where weekends were spent exploring the reserve and appreciating his surroundings. Having joined the Londolozi team, he is now fulfilling his childhood dream of living and working in the African bush.
Self proclaimed Leopardographer.

acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
Named after the Shangaan word for a playful hide-and-seek game played with mothers

Heritage & Lineage
Born in March/April 2022 to the Xinzele Female and presumably the Flat Rock Male. Born into a litter of two, though her male sibling did not survive beyond May 2022. Represents the continuation of the northern Marthly lineage.

Territory
Currently establishing herself in the southern portions of her mother’s territory, focusing on:

Central Marthly
Manyelethi Riverbed
Areas around the Leadwood forest
Rocky outcrops and boulder systems

Physical Characteristics

4:3 spot pattern
Growing confidence in her movements
Particularly adept at tree climbing and boulder navigation

Reproductive History
Not yet of reproductive age

Current Status
Successfully navigating the transition to independence, showing increasing confidence in exploring her territory solo. Demonstrates excellent hunting potential during a fortuitous time of year with abundant young prey species available.

Behavioural Notes
Lives up to her name with a notably playful nature, particularly in her interactions with her mother during their time together. Shows remarkable comfort around vehicles despite being raised near the northern boundary where sightings were initially limited. Demonstrates growing hunting skills, particularly focused on the seasonal abundance of young prey.

Her successful transition to independence has been aided by the timing, coinciding with the arrival of impala lambs, warthog piglets, and wildebeest calves. Currently developing her hunting technique, still relying more on speed and opportunistic pursuits rather than the patient stealth that will come with age.

Historical Significance
Represents the successful continuation of the Xinzele Female’s lineage in the northern territories. Her survival as a sole cub and successful journey to independence demonstrates the increasing stability of leopard populations in the northern sections of Londolozi. Her growing presence in central Marthly provides exciting potential for consistent viewing in this scenic part of the reserve.

users_spotted.user_description:
As a young boy growing up on an agricultural farm in Zimbabwe, Sean spent every opportunity entertaining himself outdoors, camping in the local nature reserve and learning about all facets of the natural world.  

After completing a Bachelor of Science degree in Environmental Science in Cape Town, Sean was free to follow his nature ambitions and return to his bush-loving childhood dreams, which led him to Londolozi.

Going into semi-retirement on the guiding front in 2020 saw Sean settle into a far more permanent role in the LCH, focusing his efforts on producing media content for the Londolozi online space.

California native, travel junkie, animal lover...... have traveled to Africa over a dozen times to fulfill my passion for observing animals in their natural environment. Londolozi has become my favorite place to stay, with almost yearly visits since 2019.

Nick grew up in Johannesburg with a deep love for the outdoors. After finishing high school, he spent a formative gap year in the Zimbabwean bushveld — an experience that cemented his passion for wildlife and conservation. Although he went on to study and build a career in corporate real estate, the pull of the wilderness never faded. Now an experienced member of the Londolozi guiding team, Nick finds the greatest joy in tracking leopards and immersing himself in the intricate world of birding. He has developed a strong passion for wildlife photography, always looking to capture authentic moments in the wild.

Bob and I live in the San Francisco Bay Area where we enjoy boating, hiking, photography and travel. After many trips to Eastern and Southern Africa, we are pleased to call Londolozi our 'African home!'
First visited Londolozi in June 2011.  My profile picture up close with the Nkuwa female during our 2023 visit. We returned again in 2025.  Can't wait to come back again!

Lucie and I are retired and have turned our energies to photography and videography, of which wildlife is by far the favorite subject.  We have been to Africa every 2-3 years over the last 35 years.  We have been to several camps in each of South Africa, Botswana, Kenya, Tanzania, Namibia, Uganda and Rwanda but Londolozi and Tiger Canyon are our go-to favorite places.  We are unabashedly predator-centric and aviary-sated.  And we are so thankful that the Varty family built this community-driven concept and has taught us all the meaning of "ubuntu".

Born in New York and settled down in Hong Kong for the past 20 years after living in London and Tokyo.  I "found" Londolozi in 2009 and have been a regular visitor since.  Over that time I have gained a passion for the bush and the photographic opportunities it provides.  Thanks to the tutelage of the Londolozi rangers and Creative hub I am getting my photography to an acceptable level.

acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
Named for the Shangaan word ‘nsuku’ meaning gold, referencing his striking golden coat.

Heritage & Lineage

Born in July 2021 to the Three Rivers Female and Maxim’s Male, inheriting their distinctive golden coats. Born in a litter of two at Mala Mala Rattray’s Camp, though his sister was lost at approximately five months of age.

Territory Evolution

Early Phase (2021-2022): Within mother’s southeastern territory
Early Independence (2022): Pushed to independence at 17 months
Current Phase (2024-2025):

Establishing a presence across all of Londolozi
Seen near causeway, all the way into central areas south of camps
Operating within father’s (Maxim’s Male) territory

Physical Characteristics

2:3 spot pattern
Distinctive rich golden coat inherited from both parents
Already larger than most adult males despite young age
Impressive size development at only 2.5 years

Behavioural Notes

Shows interesting developmental patterns:

Initially extremely relaxed and inquisitive
Became more skittish after early independence
Shows growing confidence in territory establishment
Capable of taking substantial prey
Prefers dense vegetation and riverine areas
Shows unusual precociousness in mating behaviour

Current Status
Currently navigating the critical transition between the nomadic phase and potential territory establishment. Growing in both size and confidence, showing increasing presence in central Londolozi while maintaining a careful relationship with his father’s territory.

Historical Significance
Represents interesting aspects of male leopard development:

Demonstrates the impact of early independence
Shows unusual mating success at a young age (Nkoveni Female at 2 years)
Provides insights into father-son territorial dynamics
Currently influencing dynamics with established females
Growing into potential future dominant male

His ongoing development provides valuable insights into male leopard maturation and territory establishment, particularly within the context of an existing paternal presence.

users_spotted.user_description:
As a young boy growing up on an agricultural farm in Zimbabwe, Sean spent every opportunity entertaining himself outdoors, camping in the local nature reserve and learning about all facets of the natural world.  

After completing a Bachelor of Science degree in Environmental Science in Cape Town, Sean was free to follow his nature ambitions and return to his bush-loving childhood dreams, which led him to Londolozi.

Going into semi-retirement on the guiding front in 2020 saw Sean settle into a far more permanent role in the LCH, focusing his efforts on producing media content for the Londolozi online space.

After a few years of working in the world of economic consulting, Kate’s love of adventure, wilderness and sense of curiosity led her to move away from the city and join the Londolozi guiding team.  It was amidst her years of studying politics, philosophy and economics that her love of exploring and understanding different wilderness areas in South Africa compounded through trips with friends and family. Kate has been fortunate to travel to many different corners of the world but she’ll argue that nothing quite beats being surrounded by nature watching an African sunrise or sunset, especially at Londolozi!

Nick grew up in Johannesburg with a deep love for the outdoors. After finishing high school, he spent a formative gap year in the Zimbabwean bushveld — an experience that cemented his passion for wildlife and conservation. Although he went on to study and build a career in corporate real estate, the pull of the wilderness never faded. Now an experienced member of the Londolozi guiding team, Nick finds the greatest joy in tracking leopards and immersing himself in the intricate world of birding. He has developed a strong passion for wildlife photography, always looking to capture authentic moments in the wild.

Bob and I live in the San Francisco Bay Area where we enjoy boating, hiking, photography and travel. After many trips to Eastern and Southern Africa, we are pleased to call Londolozi our 'African home!'

I came here for the 1st time with my husband in Feb 2010, 2nd stop on a Vic Falls-Londolozi-Cape Town trip. I'd wanted to come here for years, as my ambition was to see a leopard in the wild. We looked at the cost, thought "ouch!" then - well it is just a one-off! On our 1st game drive  we saw Vomba, so mission achieved. Then the next morning we saw Camp Pan mating with Nottens! Within 24 hours of arriving we were completely smitten, and knew we not only had to come back, but come back the next year. So began a highly expensive addiction, and my trip 3 weeks ago was my 9th consecutive year and I celebrated my 100th game drive!

Keagan has always had a connection with wildlife, having been lucky enough to visit Londolozi as a child. After growing up in Johannesburg, he attended boarding school in the KwaZulu Natal Midlands where weekends were spent exploring the reserve and appreciating his surroundings. Keagan further went on to study Engineering at the University of Cape Town, during which each holiday was spent with either family or friends in the Lowveld, solidifying his dream of becoming a ranger. Having joined the Londolozi team, he is now fulfilling his childhood dream of living and working in the African bush.

Growing up in the small coastal town of Mtunzini, Matt's childhood was shaped by endless hours spent exploring the forests, beaches and wetlands that sparked a lifelong passion for wildlife. After completing a BSc degree, he worked in construction and landscaping before the opportunity to join Londolozi changed the course of his career. Today, as a ranger and wildlife photographer, he has the privilege of spending every day immersed in the wilderness that first inspired him as a child.

Love nature, watching animals and going on safari. Been lots of times on safari to different African countries. Londolozi is one of my favourite places. I am always looking forward to my next trip to Londolozi!

California native, travel junkie, animal lover...... have traveled to Africa over a dozen times to fulfill my passion for observing animals in their natural environment. Londolozi has become my favorite place to stay, with almost yearly visits since 2019.

Born in New York and settled down in Hong Kong for the past 20 years after living in London and Tokyo.  I "found" Londolozi in 2009 and have been a regular visitor since.  Over that time I have gained a passion for the bush and the photographic opportunities it provides.  Thanks to the tutelage of the Londolozi rangers and Creative hub I am getting my photography to an acceptable level.

Lucie and I are retired and have turned our energies to photography and videography, of which wildlife is by far the favorite subject.  We have been to Africa every 2-3 years over the last 35 years.  We have been to several camps in each of South Africa, Botswana, Kenya, Tanzania, Namibia, Uganda and Rwanda but Londolozi and Tiger Canyon are our go-to favorite places.  We are unabashedly predator-centric and aviary-sated.  And we are so thankful that the Varty family built this community-driven concept and has taught us all the meaning of "ubuntu".

Passionate Londolozi Guests! Avid wildlife photographers. Supporters and advocates for the Good Work Foundation through the All Heart Fund in the USA. Restaurateurs and wine & spirits retailers in Sarasota, Florida at Michael’s On East (www.bestfood.com)

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: Initially fairly skittish, but seems to be relaxing a bit now.
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
Born in northern Mala Mala into a litter of three. They all made it to at least six months before the female cub was lost, all that was found was her tail in a rhino midden. Both male cubs reached independence in 2019 and the other male is now known as the Ngoboswan Male.
The Eyrefield Male’s movements have been erratic recently and we are not sure where he will settle.

He came to blows with the Senegal Bush Male and was then seen in the company of the Ximungwe Female in early October 2022.

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: A small leopard that was forced into early independence and struggled to establish territory. Moved around eating anything it could.
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
Being forced into early independence as his mother was killed when he was less than a year old. He then went through an incredibly challenging time fending for himself and basically had to resort to eating anything he could. As a result of the nutritional stress, his growth was stunted and at the age of six, he is still a small unthreatening leopard than sadly may never secure his own territory.

He was seen catching and eating catfish from a small pool of water, monitor lizards, and tortoises in mid-2020 near the Londolozi Camps. He was not seen from then until April 2022.

He has grown a little larger but is still small and unlikely to be able to challenge for territory with the current dominant males in the area as it stands.

acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
Named after the Shangaan word for freckle, referencing his distinctive eye-marking

Heritage & Lineage
Born in February 2021 to the Ximungwe Female and presumably the Senegal Bush Male. He is the only cub from his mother’s second litter, representing the continuation of the Sunsetbend lineage. His mother’s second successful offspring after the Mahlahla Male.

Territory Evolution
Pre-independence phase (2021-2022):

Initially denned in Three-streaked Donga
Primarily within the mother’s central territory

Nomadic phase (2023-early 2024):

Ranging between the western boundary and central areas
Frequently seen around the airstrip and western sections
Exploring deeper into southwestern grasslands

Current Phase (2024-Present): Shifted westwards following his father the Senegal Bush Male and has subsequently inherited his territory after his passing.

Shows increasing confidence in territory expansion

Physical Characteristics

3:3 spot pattern
Distinctive freckle in the left iris (birthmark)
Growing into an impressive size

Behavioural Notes
Demonstrates remarkable development in hunting skills:

Successfully hunting increasingly large prey (wildebeest calf)
Displays ambitious hunting behaviour (attempting hippo calf)
Growing confidence in territory exploration

Current Status
Currently navigating the critical transition between dependence and full independence:

Showing increasing confidence in territory exploration
Now faces pressure from territorial males such as Maxim’s and Thamba.
Will likely sire cubs with the Nkuwa Female, Nhlanguleni Female and possibly the Xinzele Female.

Historical Significance
Represents an important case study in male leopard development:

Well-documented growth from dependency to independence
Provides insights into hunting skill development
Demonstrates successful maternal care from Ximungwe Female
Shows the typical pattern of gradual independence

His story is particularly valuable as a documented example of male leopard development from birth through independence.

Thanks to the tutelage of the Londolozi rangers and Creative hub I am getting my photography to an acceptable level.

Passionate Londolozi Guests! Avid wildlife photographers. Supporters and advocates for the Good Work Foundation through the All Heart Fund in the USA. Restaurateurs and wine & spirits retailers in Sarasota, Florida at Michael’s On East (www.bestfood.com)
South African living in Canada for the past +25 years, lover of the African bush!

As a young boy growing up on an agricultural farm in Zimbabwe, Sean spent every opportunity entertaining himself outdoors, camping in the local nature reserve and learning about all facets of the natural world.  

After completing a Bachelor of Science degree in Environmental Science in Cape Town, Sean was free to follow his nature ambitions and return to his bush-loving childhood dreams, which led him to Londolozi.

Going into semi-retirement on the guiding front in 2020 saw Sean settle into a far more permanent role in the LCH, focusing his efforts on producing media content for the Londolozi online space.

Growing up in the small coastal town of Mtunzini, Matt's childhood was shaped by endless hours spent exploring the forests, beaches and wetlands that sparked a lifelong passion for wildlife. After completing a BSc degree, he worked in construction and landscaping before the opportunity to join Londolozi changed the course of his career. Today, as a ranger and wildlife photographer, he has the privilege of spending every day immersed in the wilderness that first inspired him as a child.

I came here for the 1st time with my husband in Feb 2010, 2nd stop on a Vic Falls-Londolozi-Cape Town trip. I'd wanted to come here for years, as my ambition was to see a leopard in the wild. We looked at the cost, thought "ouch!" then - well it is just a one-off! On our 1st game drive  we saw Vomba, so mission achieved. Then the next morning we saw Camp Pan mating with Nottens! Within 24 hours of arriving we were completely smitten, and knew we not only had to come back, but come back the next year. So began a highly expensive addiction, and my trip 3 weeks ago was my 9th consecutive year and I celebrated my 100th game drive!

For the past 35 years I've been amazed and inspired by wildlife from all corners of the world. Following a career in the City of London I now dedicate my time to wildlife photographer and commitment to wildlife conservation. When not travelling I volunteer for Conservation Organisations based in London. Social Media - www.janeaddey.co.uk & @addeyphotos.

Bob and I live in the San Francisco Bay Area where we enjoy boating, hiking, photography and travel. After many trips to Eastern and Southern Africa, we are pleased to call Londolozi our 'African home!'

Love nature, watching animals and going on safari. Been lots of times on safari to different African countries. Londolozi is one of my favourite places. I am always looking forward to my next trip to Londolozi!
Self proclaimed Leopardographer.

Garrett has always had an incredible love for the wilderness and found his way to Londolozi straight after University. After spending time as a Londolozi Camp Manager, the incredible stories of daily sightings from his ranger counterparts and guests alike pushed him to become a Londolozi Guide, where he enjoyed 3 years in the field sharing Londolozi with thousands of guests. After a brief sabbatical travelling through Southern Africa and working in Tanzania, Garrett returned to the Londolozi Family as Sales Manager sharing Londolozi with as many people as possible.

Megan grew up at Londolozi, where her love for nature blossomed. With a degree in Visual Studies and Social Media Marketing, her journey came full circle when she joined the dynamic Londolozi Creative Hub, where her love for nature and visuals finds its perfect home. 

Guided by an unwavering love for photography, videography, and the captivating realm of visuals, Megan hopes to impart a unique and vibrant essence to each of the creative projects she takes on.
Full-time Manhattanites raising a city kid; happily improved by our experience staying at Founder's Camp this Summer.

Lucie and I are retired and have turned our energies to photography and videography, of which wildlife is by far the favorite subject.  We have been to Africa every 2-3 years over the last 35 years.  We have been to several camps in each of South Africa, Botswana, Kenya, Tanzania, Namibia, Uganda and Rwanda but Londolozi and Tiger Canyon are our go-to favorite places.  We are unabashedly predator-centric and aviary-sated.  And we are so thankful that the Varty family built this community-driven concept and has taught us all the meaning of "ubuntu".

Nick grew up in Johannesburg with a deep love for the outdoors. After finishing high school, he spent a formative gap year in the Zimbabwean bushveld — an experience that cemented his passion for wildlife and conservation. Although he went on to study and build a career in corporate real estate, the pull of the wilderness never faded. Now an experienced member of the Londolozi guiding team, Nick finds the greatest joy in tracking leopards and immersing himself in the intricate world of birding. He has developed a strong passion for wildlife photography, always looking to capture authentic moments in the wild.

After a few years of working in the world of economic consulting, Kate’s love of adventure, wilderness and sense of curiosity led her to move away from the city and join the Londolozi guiding team.  It was amidst her years of studying politics, philosophy and economics that her love of exploring and understanding different wilderness areas in South Africa compounded through trips with friends and family. Kate has been fortunate to travel to many different corners of the world but she’ll argue that nothing quite beats being surrounded by nature watching an African sunrise or sunset, especially at Londolozi!

Coming to Africa has kick-started a life of wildlife based travel for me. My first adventure was to Kenya, Tanzania and Rwanda. That trip would become one of the things that define who I am. I was bitten hard with the Africa travel bug as they say. The rest is so called history (still in the making of course), and over the years I have come to know South Africa as a second home.

Keagan has always had a connection with wildlife, having been lucky enough to visit Londolozi as a child. After growing up in Johannesburg, he attended boarding school in the KwaZulu Natal Midlands where weekends were spent exploring the reserve and appreciating his surroundings. Keagan further went on to study Engineering at the University of Cape Town, during which each holiday was spent with either family or friends in the Lowveld, solidifying his dream of becoming a ranger. Having joined the Londolozi team, he is now fulfilling his childhood dream of living and working in the African bush.

California native, travel junkie, animal lover...... have traveled to Africa over a dozen times to fulfill my passion for observing animals in their natural environment. Londolozi has become my favorite place to stay, with almost yearly visits since 2019.
First visited Londolozi in June 2011.  My profile picture up close with the Nkuwa female during our 2023 visit. We returned again in 2025.  Can't wait to come back again!

Wildlife Photography Enthusiast

acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
Named after a small drainage line near the Sand River where she spent much of her early life

Heritage & Lineage
Born in February 2021 to the Nkoveni Female and the Maxim’s Male, alongside her sister the Xinkhova Female. Part of the prestigious Sunsetbend lineage, she represents the continuing strength of her mother’s bloodline.

Territory
Has established herself primarily in Mala Mala, along her mother’s eastern boundary. Initially spent considerable time in the drainage systems and dense thickets around Stone Drift, but has since shifted her territorial focus eastward, making sightings on Londolozi increasingly rare.

Physical Characteristics

3:2 spot pattern
Notably larger than her sister

Reproductive History
Currently raising her first litter:

November/December 2023: First litter of cubs (denned in Mala Mala)

Current Status
Successfully established as a territorial female in Mala Mala and now experiencing her first venture into motherhood. Her choice to establish territory along her mother’s eastern boundary demonstrates the typical pattern of female leopards often settling near their natal range.

Behavioural Notes
Showed confidence from an early age, often appearing more assured than her sister. During their dependent years, she and her sister were frequently seen sharing kills even after reaching independence, an unusual behaviour that demonstrated their strong sibling bond. Her successful transition to independence and quick establishment of territory speaks to her capabilities as a young leopard.

Historical Significance
Represents another successful branch of the Nkoveni Female’s lineage, though primarily beyond Londolozi’s borders. Her quick transition to motherhood and successful territory establishment suggests she will play a significant role in maintaining the strength of the Sunsetbend lineage in the greater Sabi Sands area, even if primarily viewed on neighbouring properties.

acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
Named after Xinkhova road, with ‘xinkhova‘ being the Shangaan word for owl

Heritage & Lineage
Born in February 2021 to the Nkoveni Female and the Maxim’s Male, part of a litter of two females with her sister, the Stone Drift Female. Represents the continuing strength of the Sunsetbend lineage. Their birth marked another successful litter for the prolific Nkoveni Female.

Territory
She is currently establishing herself in a strategically important area around the Londolozi airstrip and east of camps, particularly in the territory formerly held by her deceased half-sister, the Plaque Rock Female. Her emerging territory includes:

Areas along the Sand River
Open crests dotted with marula trees
Regions around the airstrip
Areas previously part of Plaque Rock Female’s territory

Physical Characteristics

2:2 spot pattern
Slightly smaller than her sister Stone Drift Female
Strong resemblance to her mother

Reproductive History
Not yet reproduced – approaching reproductive age and showing signs of territorial establishment

Current Status
At approximately three years old, she is actively establishing territory in prime real estate near the Londolozi camps. She is currently navigating complex territorial dynamics with established females, including the Three Rivers Female, and managing competition from other young females seeking territory.

Behavioural Notes
Demonstrates remarkable confidence for her age, regularly seen scent-marking and patrolling potential territory. Shows excellent climbing abilities and comfort in trees, particularly important in the relatively open terrain she frequents. Initially more present around the airstrip, she has shown adaptability in response to territorial pressure, exploring various areas before potentially settling in the former territory of her deceased half-sister.

Historical Significance
This represents an important continuation of the Nkoveni Female’s lineage and potentially the next generation of dominant females at Londolozi. Her establishment in the former Plaque Rock Female’s territory would maintain a family presence in this prime area, while her comfort around vehicles suggests potential for excellent viewing opportunities in coming years. Her journey provides fascinating insights into how young female leopards navigate territorial establishment in a landscape dense with established leopards.

She is currently establishing herself in a strategically important area around the Londolozi airstrip and east of camps, particularly in the territory formerly held by her deceased half-sister, the Plaque Rock Female. Her emerging territory includes:

Areas along the Sand River
Open crests dotted with marula trees
Regions around the airstrip
Areas previously part of Plaque Rock Female’s territory

Physical Characteristics

2:2 spot pattern
Slightly smaller than her sister Stone Drift Female
Strong resemblance to her mother

Reproductive History
Not yet reproduced – approaching reproductive age and showing signs of territorial establishment

Current Status
At approximately three years old, she is actively establishing territory in prime real estate near the Londolozi camps. She is currently navigating complex territorial dynamics with established females, including the Three Rivers Female, and managing competition from other young females seeking territory.

Behavioural Notes
Demonstrates remarkable confidence for her age, regularly seen scent-marking and patrolling potential territory. Shows excellent climbing abilities and comfort in trees, particularly important in the relatively open terrain she frequents. Initially more present around the airstrip, she has shown adaptability in response to territorial pressure, exploring various areas before potentially settling in the former territory of her deceased half-sister.

Historical Significance
This represents an important continuation of the Nkoveni Female’s lineage and potentially the next generation of dominant females at Londolozi. Her establishment in the former Plaque Rock Female’s territory would maintain a family presence in this prime area, while her comfort around vehicles suggests potential for excellent viewing opportunities in coming years. Her journey provides fascinating insights into how young female leopards navigate territorial establishment in a landscape dense with established leopards.

users_spotted.user_description:
As a young boy growing up on an agricultural farm in Zimbabwe, Sean spent every opportunity entertaining himself outdoors, camping in the local nature reserve and learning about all facets of the natural world.  

After completing a Bachelor of Science degree in Environmental Science in Cape Town, Sean was free to follow his nature ambitions and return to his bush-loving childhood dreams, which led him to Londolozi.

Going into semi-retirement on the guiding front in 2020 saw Sean settle into a far more permanent role in the LCH, focusing his efforts on producing media content for the Londolozi online space.

Tristan is a Zimbabwean born journalist. He grew up moving farms in his home country and moved to South Africa to attend Rhodes University. With a passion for wildlife, it was a natural progression that he gravitated to Londolozi. He worked in the creative team bringing content to our online audience.

I came here for the 1st time with my husband in Feb 2010, 2nd stop on a Vic Falls-Londolozi-Cape Town trip. I'd wanted to come here for years, as my ambition was to see a leopard in the wild. We looked at the cost, thought "ouch!" then - well it is just a one-off! On our 1st game drive  we saw Vomba, so mission achieved. Then the next morning we saw Camp Pan mating with Nottens! Within 24 hours of arriving we were completely smitten, and knew we not only had to come back, but come back the next year. So began a highly expensive addiction, and my trip 3 weeks ago was my 9th consecutive year and I celebrated my 100th game drive!

For the past 35 years I've been amazed and inspired by wildlife from all corners of the world. Following a career in the City of London I now dedicate my time to wildlife photographer and commitment to wildlife conservation. When not travelling I volunteer for Conservation Organisations based in London. Social Media - www.janeaddey.co.uk & @addeyphotos.

Bob and I live in the San Francisco Bay Area where we enjoy boating, hiking, photography and travel. After many trips to Eastern and Southern Africa, we are pleased to call Londolozi our 'African home!'

Love nature, watching animals and going on safari. Been lots of times on safari to different African countries. Londolozi is one of my favourite places. I am always looking forward to my next trip to Londolozi!

Megan grew up at Londolozi, where her love for nature blossomed. With a degree in Visual Studies and Social Media Marketing, her journey came full circle when she joined the dynamic Londolozi Creative Hub, where her love for nature and visuals finds its perfect home. 

Guided by an unwavering love for photography, videography, and the captivating realm of visuals, Megan hopes to impart a unique and vibrant essence to each of the creative projects she takes on.

Lucie and I are retired and have turned our energies to photography and videography, of which wildlife is by far the favorite subject.  We have been to Africa every 2-3 years over the last 35 years.  We have been to several camps in each of South Africa, Botswana, Kenya, Tanzania, Namibia, Uganda and Rwanda but Londolozi and Tiger Canyon are our go-to favorite places.  We are unabashedly predator-centric and aviary-sated.  And we are so thankful that the Varty family built this community-driven concept and has taught us all the meaning of "ubuntu".

Nick grew up in Johannesburg with a deep love for the outdoors. After finishing high school, he spent a formative gap year in the Zimbabwean bushveld — an experience that cemented his passion for wildlife and conservation. Although he went on to study and build a career in corporate real estate, the pull of the wilderness never faded. Now an experienced member of the Londolozi guiding team, Nick finds the greatest joy in tracking leopards and immersing himself in the intricate world of birding. He has developed a strong passion for wildlife photography, always looking to capture authentic moments in the wild.

I'm a free lance Home Economist working mostly on Masterchef a BBC cookery show. I live in England with my husband and two black Labradors. We have three grown up sons, one grandson and  granddaughter . We have visited Londolozi four times and are making a fifth visit in early June and we cant wait!!

Coming to Africa has kick-started a life of wildlife based travel for me. My first adventure was to Kenya, Tanzania and Rwanda. That trip would become one of the things that define who I am. I was bitten hard with the Africa travel bug as they say. The rest is so called history (still in the making of course), and over the years I have come to know South Africa as a second home.

Growing up in the small coastal town of Mtunzini, Matt's childhood was shaped by endless hours spent exploring the forests, beaches and wetlands that sparked a lifelong passion for wildlife. After completing a BSc degree, he worked in construction and landscaping before the opportunity to join Londolozi changed the course of his career. Today, as a ranger and wildlife photographer, he has the privilege of spending every day immersed in the wilderness that first inspired him as a child.

Born in New York and settled down in Hong Kong for the past 20 years after living in London and Tokyo.  I "found" Londolozi in 2009 and have been a regular visitor since.  Over that time I have gained a passion for the bush and the photographic opportunities it provides.  Thanks to the tutelage of the Londolozi rangers and Creative hub I am getting my photography to an acceptable level.

Passionate Londolozi Guests! Avid wildlife photographers. Supporters and advocates for the Good Work Foundation through the All Heart Fund in the USA. Restaurateurs and wine & spirits retailers in Sarasota, Florida at Michael’s On East (www.bestfood.com)
South African living in Canada for the past +25 years, lover of the African bush!

I am a published author and wildlife and travel writer, specializing is African safaris.  I have always had a deep affinity with all living creatures, even while growing up in urban Amsterdam. Going on safari has enhanced that innate connection into a lifelong passion.
Passionate about wildlife conservation and Big Cats!   Travel, family, reading, hiking, skiing, safaris!

Keagan has always had a connection with wildlife, having been lucky enough to visit Londolozi as a child. After growing up in Johannesburg, he attended boarding school in the KwaZulu Natal Midlands where weekends were spent exploring the reserve and appreciating his surroundings. Keagan further went on to study Engineering at the University of Cape Town, during which each holiday was spent with either family or friends in the Lowveld, solidifying his dream of becoming a ranger. Having joined the Londolozi team, he is now fulfilling his childhood dream of living and working in the African bush.

I live in Canada. My first visit was June 2023 and I stayed at Tree Camp for 1 week. 
I returned in June 2024 for another week. June 2025 I have reserved 10 days at Tree Camp. Londolozi has changed me. I am on a non-stop thrill during visits. The animals, the food, the service, nothing is too much to ask for during your stay. The Healing House services are spectacular! Londolozi is a truly magical place. It makes one feel alive! That is me with the amazing John Varty in my profile photo.
First visited Londolozi in June 2011.  My profile picture up close with the Nkuwa female during our 2023 visit. We returned again in 2025.  Can't wait to come back again!

I am a published writer of three non fiction books, including My Life With Leopards, the Graham Cooke Story, which was set at Londolozi in the early 1990s. I am a seasoned safari traveller, contributing publications of safari lodges and destinations to various magazines and a keen safari photographer.

California native, travel junkie, animal lover...... have traveled to Africa over a dozen times to fulfill my passion for observing animals in their natural environment. Londolozi has become my favorite place to stay, with almost yearly visits since 2019.

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: This female was born in the Sabi Sabi camps and became territorial in central Shaws, after inheriting a piece of her mother's territory.
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
This female was born in the Sabi Sabi camps and became territorial in central Shaws, after inheriting a piece of her mother’s territory. Slowly but surely she shifted her territory further north to now be seen on the southeastern side of Dudley and is shifting further and further east in Charleston.

She has recently just raised her first cub to independence at just over a year old, now known as the Golonyi Female who was born in January 2021. Having had two unsuccessful litters prior to that.

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: Large Male leopard that originated in the Kruger National Park, spent time in the north.
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
Reports and Photographic evidence indicate that the Hukumuri Male originated in the Kruger National Park, in the Crocodile Bridge area.

He initially moved north to Ngala, which is a dispersal of 130km!

He then turned back south and started being seen on Londolozi in early-mid 2019. He was a contender for the northern parts of Marthly, until an altercation with either the Anderson Male, Flat Rock Male or Hosana Male left him blind in one eye in 2019.

He managed to hold his own but shifted further west towards the western fenceline of the Sabi Sands Wildtuin.

Richie is Londolozi's Director of Technology and Sustainability and the founder of the Londolozi blog. Over the past decade he has built Londolozi's online ecosystem into a platform for advocacy of the restoration and rewilding of the natural world. Today he applies that same thinking to the land itself, helping lead the Save the Sand initiative to restore the Sand River catchment that gives Londolozi its lifeblood.
