acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: Born 2020 during lockdown to Piccadilly Female. Once skittish, now confident mother denning her first litter in Marthly's rocky terrain.
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
Named after the local Shangaan word for African Fish Eagle, referencing the Ngungwe road in her territory

Heritage & Lineage

Born in April 2020 to the Piccadilly Female and presumably sired by the Flat Rock Male, she represents the continuation of the Sunsetbend lineage. She was her mother’s first successfully raised offspring.

Territory

Currently established in central Marthly, particularly around the Manyelethi riverbed. Her territory encompasses a diverse landscape including:

Lush Sand River banks
Marula-scattered crests
Dense Combretum thickets
Granite outcrops and boulder-strewn hillsides
Ancient Manyelethi riverbed

Physical Characteristics

3:3 spot pattern
Characteristic golden coat of the Sunsetbend lineage
Growing into a powerful adult frame

Reproductive History

Currently raising her first litter:

December 2023: First litter denned at Marthly Pools Koppies- she is very wary of vehicles around the den and is prone to moving cubs to a new den soon after.

Current Status

Successfully established as a territorial female and now a first-time mother. Has shown a remarkable transformation from a skittish young leopard to a confident adult, regularly providing spectacular viewing opportunities in her territory.

Behavioural Notes

Her development has been particularly interesting because she was born during the COVID-19 lockdown period, which initially limited her exposure to vehicles. Despite this challenging start, she has evolved into a self-assured adult, displaying excellent hunting skills and territorial behaviour. Her choice of den site in the rocky outcrops of Marthly Pools demonstrates sound maternal instincts.

Historical Significance

This represents an interesting case study in leopard habituation, showing how even an initially skittish leopard can develop comfort around vehicles through patient viewing practices. As the daughter of the Piccadilly Female, she maintains the prestigious Sunsetbend lineage in the central portions of Marthly, and her recent transition to motherhood marks an important continuation of this bloodline.

This represents an interesting case study in leopard habituation, showing how even an initially skittish leopard can develop comfort around vehicles through patient viewing practices. As the daughter of the Piccadilly Female, she maintains the prestigious Sunsetbend lineage in the central portions of Marthly, and her recent transition to motherhood marks an important continuation of this bloodline.

users_spotted.user_description: California native, travel junkie, animal lover...... have traveled to Africa over a dozen times to fulfill my passion for observing animals in their natural environment. Londolozi has become my favorite place to stay, with almost yearly visits since 2019.

Love nature, watching animals and going on safari. Been lots of times on safari to different African countries. Londolozi is one of my favourite places. I am always looking forward to my next trip to Londolozi!

Lucie and I are retired and have turned our energies to photography and videography, of which wildlife is by far the favorite subject.  We have been to Africa every 2-3 years over the last 35 years.  We have been to several camps in each of South Africa, Botswana, Kenya, Tanzania, Namibia, Uganda and Rwanda but Londolozi and Tiger Canyon are our go-to favorite places.  We are unabashedly predator-centric and aviary-sated.  And we are so thankful that the Varty family built this community-driven concept and has taught us all the meaning of "ubuntu".

Nick grew up in Johannesburg with a deep love for the outdoors. After finishing high school, he spent a formative gap year in the Zimbabwean bushveld — an experience that cemented his passion for wildlife and conservation. Although he went on to study and build a career in corporate real estate, the pull of the wilderness never faded. Now an experienced member of the Londolozi guiding team, Nick finds the greatest joy in tracking leopards and immersing himself in the intricate world of birding. He has developed a strong passion for wildlife photography, always looking to capture authentic moments in the wild.

Bob and I live in the San Francisco Bay Area where we enjoy boating, hiking, photography and travel. After many trips to Eastern and Southern Africa, we are pleased to call Londolozi our 'African home!'
Passionate about wildlife conservation and Big Cats!   Travel, family, reading, hiking, skiing, safaris!

I am a published author and wildlife and travel writer, specializing is African safaris.  I have always had a deep affinity with all living creatures, even while growing up in urban Amsterdam. Going on safari has enhanced that innate connection into a lifelong passion.

I live in Canada. My first visit was June 2023 and I stayed at Tree Camp for 1 week. 
I returned in June 2024 for another week. June 2025 I have reserved 10 days at Tree Camp. Londolozi has changed me. I am on a non-stop thrill during visits. The animals, the food, the service, nothing is too much to ask for during your stay. The Healing House services are spectacular! Londolozi is a truly magical place. It makes one feel alive! That is me with the amazing John Varty in my profile photo.

I am a published writer of three non fiction books, including My Life With Leopards, the Graham Cooke Story, which was set at Londolozi in the early 1990s. I am a seasoned safari traveller, contributing publications of safari lodges and destinations to various magazines and a keen safari photographer.

Born in New York and settled down in Hong Kong for the past 20 years after living in London and Tokyo.  I "found" Londolozi in 2009 and have been a regular visitor since.  Over that time I have gained a passion for the bush and the photographic opportunities it provides.  Thanks to the tutelage of the Londolozi rangers and Creative hub I am getting my photography to an acceptable level.

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt_alt: First-time mother, this once-elusive leopard has transformed from a pandemic-born cub into a confident territorial female commanding Marthly

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: Forced into early independence at 11 months. Despite her small size, she's proven resilient, currently raising a cub in SE Londolozi.
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
Named after the confluence of the Three Major Rivers on Mala Mala.

Heritage & Lineage

Born in May 2016 to the Xidulu Female and sired by the Piva Male, part of the Sunsetbend lineage. Her early life was marked by tragedy when her mother was killed by the Avoca male lions when she was just 11 months old. Her male sibling disappeared shortly afterwards.

Territory

Currently maintains territory in southeastern Londolozi, characterized by beautiful tamboti thickets, marshes, and open grasslands. Her territory has evolved through recent conflicts, particularly with the Nkoveni Female, leading to some territorial adjustments. She’s known to utilize the area from the Sand River south to the Maxabene riverbed.

Physical Characteristics

2:2 spot pattern
Notably small frame for an adult female
Athletic build despite her size
Distinctive pink nose and narrow muzzle

Reproductive History

Has shown remarkable resilience in her reproductive efforts:

Successful Offspring:

July 2021: Nsuku Male (raised to independence, sibling lost at 4 months)
March 2024: Currently raising one cub (sibling lost)

Notable Attempts:

July 2021: Two cubs denned in Mala Mala. One lost at 4 months old. The remaining cub survived- Nsuku Male
April 2023: Seen with suckle-marks, litter lost.
November 2023: Litter lost
March 2024: Two cubs denned in Mala Mala. Young Female still alive.

Current Status

Currently raising a single three-month-old cub after losing its sibling. Despite recent territorial conflicts with the Nkoveni Female that resulted in severe injuries, she has shown remarkable recovery and continues to demonstrate excellent maternal care.

Behavioural Notes

Despite her small size, she’s proven to be an exceptionally capable hunter, often taking down prey significantly larger than herself. She displays remarkable resilience, having recovered from severe injuries sustained in territorial disputes, particularly the dramatic 2023 conflict with the Nkoveni Female.
Her territory presents unique challenges, including the regular presence of the Kambula Pride and Ndzhenga Males, territorial pressure from the Nkoveni Female and Xinkhova Female, and the presence of nomadic males. Despite these challenges, she continues to adapt and thrive.

Historical Significance

The Three Rivers Female represents one of Londolozi’s most remarkable survival stories. Forced into independence at an unusually young age, she has defied expectations to become a successful territorial female. Her resilience in the face of numerous challenges – from early orphaning to territorial conflicts and the challenges of raising cubs – makes her one of Londolozi’s most inspiring leopard stories.

users_spotted.user_description: I came here for the 1st time with my husband in Feb 2010, 2nd stop on a Vic Falls-Londolozi-Cape Town trip. I'd wanted to come here for years, as my ambition was to see a leopard in the wild. We looked at the cost, thought "ouch!" then - well it is just a one-off! On our 1st game drive  we saw Vomba, so mission achieved. Then the next morning we saw Camp Pan mating with Nottens! Within 24 hours of arriving we were completely smitten, and knew we not only had to come back, but come back the next year. So began a highly expensive addiction, and my trip 3 weeks ago was my 9th consecutive year and I celebrated my 100th game drive!

Garrett has always had an incredible love for the wilderness and found his way to Londolozi straight after University. After spending time as a Londolozi Camp Manager, the incredible stories of daily sightings from his ranger counterparts and guests alike pushed him to become a Londolozi Guide, where he enjoyed 3 years in the field sharing Londolozi with thousands of guests. After a brief sabbatical travelling through Southern Africa and working in Tanzania, Garrett returned to the Londolozi Family as Sales Manager sharing Londolozi with as many people as possible.

Bob and I live in the San Francisco Bay Area where we enjoy boating, hiking, photography and travel. After many trips to Eastern and Southern Africa, we are pleased to call Londolozi our 'African home!'

Born in New York and settled down in Hong Kong for the past 20 years after living in London and Tokyo.  I "found" Londolozi in 2009 and have been a regular visitor since.  Over that time I have gained a passion for the bush and the photographic opportunities it provides.  Thanks to the tutelage of the Londolozi rangers and Creative hub I am getting my photography to an acceptable level.

Growing up in the small coastal town of Mtunzini, Matt's childhood was shaped by endless hours spent exploring the forests, beaches and wetlands that sparked a lifelong passion for wildlife. After completing a BSc degree, he worked in construction and landscaping before the opportunity to join Londolozi changed the course of his career. Today, as a ranger and wildlife photographer, he has the privilege of spending every day immersed in the wilderness that first inspired him as a child.

For the past 35 years I've been amazed and inspired by wildlife from all corners of the world. Following a career in the City of London I now dedicate my time to wildlife photographer and commitment to wildlife conservation. When not travelling I volunteer for Conservation Organisations based in London. Social Media - www.janeaddey.co.uk & @addeyphotos.

Megan grew up at Londolozi, where her love for nature blossomed. With a degree in Visual Studies and Social Media Marketing, her journey came full circle when she joined the dynamic Londolozi Creative Hub, where her love for nature and visuals finds its perfect home. 

Guided by an unwavering love for photography, videography, and the captivating realm of visuals, Megan hopes to impart a unique and vibrant essence to each of the creative projects she takes on.

Lucie and I are retired and have turned our energies to photography and videography, of which wildlife is by far the favorite subject.  We have been to Africa every 2-3 years over the last 35 years.  We have been to several camps in each of South Africa, Botswana, Kenya, Tanzania, Namibia, Uganda and Rwanda but Londolozi and Tiger Canyon are our go-to favorite places.  We are unabashedly predator-centric and aviary-sated.  And we are so thankful that the Varty family built this community-driven concept and has taught us all the meaning of "ubuntu".

I am a lifelong animal lover, especially cats!  I got to fulfill my dream of going on an African safari for my 52nd birthday (it was supposed to be for my 50th but Covid interfered!).  I fell in LOVE with Londolozi, the people, and the country.  I am counting the days until I can return!!

After a few years of working in the world of economic consulting, Kate’s love of adventure, wilderness and sense of curiosity led her to move away from the city and join the Londolozi guiding team.  It was amidst her years of studying politics, philosophy and economics that her love of exploring and understanding different wilderness areas in South Africa compounded through trips with friends and family. Kate has been fortunate to travel to many different corners of the world but she’ll argue that nothing quite beats being surrounded by nature watching an African sunrise or sunset, especially at Londolozi!

Now an experienced member of the Londolozi guiding team, Nick finds the greatest joy in tracking leopards and immersing himself in the intricate world of birding. He has developed a strong passion for wildlife photography, always looking to capture authentic moments in the wild.

Coming to Africa has kick-started a life of wildlife based travel for me. My first adventure was to Kenya, Tanzania and Rwanda. That trip would become one of the things that define who I am. I was bitten hard with the Africa travel bug as they say. The rest is so called history (still in the making of course), and over the years I have come to know South Africa as a second home.
I fell in love with S. Africa in 2014 and returned again in 2018.  My next visit will be May, 2019.  My husband and I can’t get enough.  His hobby is photography and I am a professional artist.
Alan and I have been ambassadors for many years, this is our favorite place on earth ?

Wildlife Photography Enthusiast
@wildcattraveler on IG

acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
Heritage & Lineage

Born in the Sabi Sands to an unrelaxed female, his early years were marked by minimal exposure to vehicles – a factor that would significantly influence his later behaviour. His sister shared his cautious nature, highlighting the strong influence of their mother’s temperament on their development.

Territory Evolution

His territory establishment followed an unconventional path:

Initial Phase: Arrived in Londolozi’s southwestern grasslands
Establishment: Successfully took over the territory from ageing Makhotini Male
Current Domain: Controls vast stretches of southwestern grasslands
Recent Dynamics: Experiencing pressure from Maxims Male’s expansion and Nweti Male’s territorial shift

Physical Characteristics

3:4 spot pattern
Carries himself with characteristic wariness
Shows battle scars from territorial conflicts

Behavioural Notes

The Mawelawela Male’s journey from aggressive outsider to established territorial male represents one of Londolozi’s most remarkable stories of leopard adaptation. His early encounters with vehicles were characterized by defensive displays – charging, snarling, and retreating into thick vegetation. Yet through consistent, patient viewing, a gradual transformation began to unfold. While he never developed the relaxed nature of some males, his tolerance grew enough to allow for meaningful observations of his remarkable hunting prowess.

It is in his hunting behaviour that his true ingenuity shines. Where most leopards rely on ambush tactics in dense vegetation, the Mawelawela Male has mastered the art of open terrain hunting. His speciality lies in taking down prey that would intimidate many leopards – zebra foals and even giraffe calves fall prey to his strength and cunning. He moves like a ghost through the grasslands, using scattered drainage lines and ancient fig trees as staging posts for his hunts. His extensive territory, far larger than those of more conventional habitat specialists, requires careful management through regular long-distance patrols.

Current Status

Now in his tenth year, the Mawelawela Male faces the challenges that come with maintaining such vast territory. Recent pressure from the expanding Maxims Male and the shifting Nweti Male tests his resilience, yet he continues to adapt. His mating success with multiple females, including the Mashaba Golonyi and Jacana Females, suggests his unconventional territory choice hasn’t hindered his reproductive prospects. If anything, his mastery of the grasslands has carved out a unique niche, allowing him to thrive where other leopards might struggle.

Historical Significance

The Mawelawela Male’s legacy extends beyond his immediate impact on Londolozi’s leopard population. His success challenges fundamental assumptions about leopard habitat requirements and behavioural patterns. By establishing and maintaining territory in what was traditionally considered a marginal habitat, he demonstrates the remarkable adaptability of his species. His journey from aggressive outsider to successful territorial male offers hope for other challenging individuals, showing that with time and space, even the most difficult leopards can find their place in the ecosystem. Through his unique hunting specializations and territorial strategies, he has redefined what’s possible for a leopard in the open grasslands of Londolozi.

His story particularly resonates as an example of successful adaptation to unconventional territory, proving that leopards can thrive in what was previously considered marginal habitat. At approximately ten years old, he now faces the typical challenge of maintaining territory against younger males, while his potential offspring in the area adds another layer of complexity to the territorial dynamics.

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: Born 2014, dominant force in southern Londolozi. Notable for jaguar-like rosettes and exceptional hunting prowess, particularly of warthogs
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
Named after the road in the western sector where he was first viewed

Heritage & Lineage
Born in December 2014 to the Hlaba’nkunzi Female and Nyelethi Male in the western sector. His exposure to vehicles from a young age contributed to his remarkably relaxed nature around game drive vehicles.

Territory Evolution
His territory has developed in distinct phases:

Initial Phase (2017): First seen after independence from western territories
Exploration Phase (2018): Expanded from Gert’s Pan to Open Areas
Establishment Phase (2019): Secured territory on Sabi Sabi
Current Domain: Controls vast territory including:

Large sections of southern Londolozi- Southeastern Dudley
Extensive areas beyond the southern boundary
Territory reaching as far north as the Vlei

Physical Characteristics

4:2 spot pattern
Distinctive jaguar-like rosettes with spots inside
Notably large and tall frame
Tuft of hair on neck
Impressive overall size

Presumed Offspring
Successfully sired multiple offspring:

Nottens Male (with Ntsumi Female)
Potential father to multiple cubs in his extensive territory
Recently seen mating with both Mashaba and Ndzanzeni Females simultaneously

Behavioural Notes
Demonstrates exceptional hunting abilities:

Particularly skilled at hunting warthogs
Shows remarkable patience and strategy in pursuit
Displays excellent problem-solving abilities
Maintains calm demeanor around vehicles
Shows strategic thinking in territory management
Demonstrates unusual tolerance of other leopards, as seen in multiple-female mating event

Historical Significance
Represents an important presence in southern territories:

Successfully established vast territory
Shows remarkable adaptability between open grasslands and thick vegetation
Provides continued leopard presence in less frequently viewed areas
Passes on superior genes through successful offspring
Demonstrates unusual social flexibility for a male leopard

His presence in the southern territories has brought consistent leopard viewing to an area traditionally more challenging for leopard sightings, while his remarkable hunting abilities and unusual social behaviours provide new insights into leopard capabilities.

Eventually moved south, establishing a territory on Sabi Sabi, but as of late 2019, he was been seen more and more in southeastern Dudley. Now becoming the dominant male in the southeastern reaches of Dudley coming as far north as the Vlei.

He is a large, tall, and long male who has an incredible coat with rosettes that have spots in them that resemble those of a jaguar.

users_spotted.user_description: California native, travel junkie, animal lover...... have traveled to Africa over a dozen times to fulfill my passion for observing animals in their natural environment. Londolozi has become my favorite place to stay, with almost yearly visits since 2019.

I came here for the 1st time with my husband in Feb 2010, 2nd stop on a Vic Falls-Londolozi-Cape Town trip. I'd wanted to come here for years, as my ambition was to see a leopard in the wild. We looked at the cost, thought "ouch!" then - well it is just a one-off! On our 1st game drive  we saw Vomba, so mission achieved. Then the next morning we saw Camp Pan mating with Nottens! Within 24 hours of arriving we were completely smitten, and knew we not only had to come back, but come back the next year. So began a highly expensive addiction, and my trip 3 weeks ago was my 9th consecutive year and I celebrated my 100th game drive!

For the past 35 years I've been amazed and inspired by wildlife from all corners of the world. Following a career in the City of London I now dedicate my time to wildlife photographer and commitment to wildlife conservation. When not travelling I volunteer for Conservation Organisations based in London. Social Media - www.janeaddey.co.uk & @addeyphotos.

Bob and I live in the San Francisco Bay Area where we enjoy boating, hiking, photography and travel. After many trips to Eastern and Southern Africa, we are pleased to call Londolozi our 'African home!'

Lucie and I are retired and have turned our energies to photography and videography, of which wildlife is by far the favorite subject.  We have been to Africa every 2-3 years over the last 35 years.  We have been to several camps in each of South Africa, Botswana, Kenya, Tanzania, Namibia, Uganda and Rwanda but Londolozi and Tiger Canyon are our go-to favorite places.  We are unabashedly predator-centric and aviary-sated.  And we are so thankful that the Varty family built this community-driven concept and has taught us all the meaning of "ubuntu".
First visited Londolozi in June 2011.  My profile picture up close with the Nkuwa female during our 2023 visit. We returned again in 2025.  Can't wait to come back again!

Garrett has always had an incredible love for the wilderness and found his way to Londolozi straight after University. After spending time as a Londolozi Camp Manager, the incredible stories of daily sightings from his ranger counterparts and guests alike pushed him to become a Londolozi Guide, where he enjoyed 3 years in the field sharing Londolozi with thousands of guests. After a brief sabbatical travelling through Southern Africa and working in Tanzania, Garrett returned to the Londolozi Family as Sales Manager sharing Londolozi with as many people as possible.

Nick grew up in Johannesburg with a deep love for the outdoors. After finishing high school, he spent a formative gap year in the Zimbabwean bushveld — an experience that cemented his passion for wildlife and conservation. Although he went on to study and build a career in corporate real estate, the pull of the wilderness never faded. Now an experienced member of the Londolozi guiding team, Nick finds the greatest joy in tracking leopards and immersing himself in the intricate world of birding. He has developed a strong passion for wildlife photography, always looking to capture authentic moments in the wild.
Passionate about wildlife conservation and Big Cats!   Travel, family, reading, hiking, skiing, safaris!

I am a published author and wildlife and travel writer, specializing is African safaris.  I have always had a deep affinity with all living creatures, even while growing up in urban Amsterdam. Going on safari has enhanced that innate connection into a lifelong passion.

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: Dominant since 2019. Once skittish Kruger-born giant now rules vast territory, transforming from elusive presence to formidable force.
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
Named after ‘Maxim’s Lookout’ in Mala Mala, an area along the western bank of the Sand River.

Heritage & Lineage
Believed to have originated from Kruger National Park, first viewed in January 2019. His background before arriving at Londolozi remains largely unknown, though his initial skittish behaviour suggests minimal early exposure to vehicles.

Territory
Commands an extensive and expanding territory:

Initially held eastern sections from Mala Mala to Maxabene River
Expanded significantly westward by 2022-2024
Currently controls vast area from western boundary to eastern territories
Primarily focused along the Sand River system
Successfully pushed Senegal Bush Male westward

Physical Characteristics

5:3 spot pattern
The largest male currently viewed at Londolozi
Impressive muscular build
Distinctive golden coat
Notably large tracks, easily identifiable

Presumed Offspring
Successfully sired multiple cubs including:

Stonedrift Female (with Nkoveni Female)
Xinkhova Female (with Nkoveni Female)
Nsuku Male (with Three Rivers Female)
Current cubs of Nkoveni Female
Current cub of Three Rivers Female
Current cub of Ximungwe Female

Behavioural Notes
Shows remarkable transformation in behaviour:

Initially extremely skittish during daylight
More relaxed during nocturnal hours
Gradually habituating to vehicles
Particularly relaxed during mating episodes
Demonstrates fierce territorial defence
Shows increasing confidence in vehicle presence

Historical Significance
Represents an important case study in:

Successful leopard habituation in adulthood
Territory expansion and male dominance

section_profile.lol_basic_profile_content:
Named after ‘Maxim’s Lookout’ in Mala Mala, an area along the western bank of the Sand River.

Heritage & Lineage
Believed to have originated from Kruger National Park, first viewed in January 2019. His background before arriving at Londolozi remains largely unknown, though his initial skittish behaviour suggests minimal early exposure to vehicles.

Territory
Commands an extensive and expanding territory:

Initially held eastern sections from Mala Mala to Maxabene River
Expanded significantly westward by 2022-2024
Currently controls vast area from western boundary to eastern territories
Primarily focused along the Sand River system
Successfully pushed Senegal Bush Male westward

Physical Characteristics

5:3 spot pattern
The largest male currently viewed at Londolozi
Impressive muscular build
Distinctive golden coat
Notably large tracks, easily identifiable

Presumed Offspring

Xinkhova Female (with Nkoveni Female)

Current cubs of Nkoveni Female

users_spotted.user_description: Love nature, watching animals and going on safari. Been lots of times on safari to different African countries. Londolozi is one of my favourite places. I am always looking forward to my next trip to Londolozi!

Bob and I live in the San Francisco Bay Area where we enjoy boating, hiking, photography and travel. After many trips to Eastern and Southern Africa, we are pleased to call Londolozi our 'African home!'

I came here for the 1st time with my husband in Feb 2010, 2nd stop on a Vic Falls-Londolozi-Cape Town trip. I'd wanted to come here for years, as my ambition was to see a leopard in the wild. We looked at the cost, thought "ouch!" then - well it is just a one-off! On our 1st game drive  we saw Vomba, so mission achieved. Then the next morning we saw Camp Pan mating with Nottens! Within 24 hours of arriving we were completely smitten, and knew we not only had to come back, but come back the next year. So began a highly expensive addiction, and my trip 3 weeks ago was my 9th consecutive year and I celebrated my 100th game drive!

Growing up in the small coastal town of Mtunzini, Matt's childhood was shaped by endless hours spent exploring the forests, beaches and wetlands that sparked a lifelong passion for wildlife. After completing a BSc degree, he worked in construction and landscaping before the opportunity to join Londolozi changed the course of his career. Today, as a ranger and wildlife photographer, he has the privilege of spending every day immersed in the wilderness that first inspired him as a child.

For the past 35 years I've been amazed and inspired by wildlife from all corners of the world. Following a career in the City of London I now dedicate my time to wildlife photographer and commitment to wildlife conservation. When not travelling I volunteer for Conservation Organisations based in London. Social Media - www.janeaddey.co.uk & @addeyphotos.

I am a lifelong animal lover, especially cats!  I got to fulfill my dream of going on an African safari for my 52nd birthday (it was supposed to be for my 50th but Covid interfered!).  I fell in LOVE with Londolozi, the people, and the country.  I am counting the days until I can return!!

Nick grew up in Johannesburg with a deep love for the outdoors. After finishing high school, he spent a formative gap year in the Zimbabwean bushveld — an experience that cemented his passion for wildlife and conservation. Although he went on to study and build a career in corporate real estate, the pull of the wilderness never faded. Now an experienced member of the Londolozi guiding team, Nick finds the greatest joy in tracking leopards and immersing himself in the intricate world of birding. He has developed a strong passion for wildlife photography, always looking to capture authentic moments in the wild.

After a few years of working in the world of economic consulting, Kate’s love of adventure, wilderness and sense of curiosity led her to move away from the city and join the Londolozi guiding team.  It was amidst her years of studying politics, philosophy and economics that her love of exploring and understanding different wilderness areas in South Africa compounded through trips with friends and family. Kate has been fortunate to travel to many different corners of the world but she’ll argue that nothing quite beats being surrounded by nature watching an African sunrise or sunset, especially at Londolozi!

Wildlife Photography Enthusiast
@wildcattraveler on IG

Passionate Londolozi Guests! Avid wildlife photographers. Supporters and advocates for the Good Work Foundation through the All Heart Fund in the USA. Restaurateurs and wine & spirits retailers in Sarasota, Florida at Michael’s On East (www.bestfood.com)

Born in New York and settled down in Hong Kong for the past 20 years after living in London and Tokyo.  I "found" Londolozi in 2009 and have been a regular visitor since.  Over that time I have gained a passion for the bush and the photographic opportunities it provides.  Thanks to the tutelage of the Londolozi rangers and Creative hub I am getting my photography to an acceptable level.

Lucie and I are retired and have turned our energies to photography and videography, of which wildlife is by far the favorite subject.  We have been to Africa every 2-3 years over the last 35 years.  We have been to several camps in each of South Africa, Botswana, Kenya, Tanzania, Namibia, Uganda and Rwanda but Londolozi and Tiger Canyon are our go-to favorite places.  We are unabashedly predator-centric and aviary-sated.  And we are so thankful that the Varty family built this community-driven concept and has taught us all the meaning of "ubuntu".

I am a published author and wildlife and travel writer, specializing is African safaris.  I have always had a deep affinity with all living creatures, even while growing up in urban Amsterdam. Going on safari has enhanced that innate connection into a lifelong passion.

Keagan has always had a connection with wildlife, having been lucky enough to visit Londolozi as a child. After growing up in Johannesburg, he attended boarding school in the KwaZulu Natal Midlands where weekends were spent exploring the reserve and appreciating his surroundings. Keagan further went on to study Engineering at the University of Cape Town, during which each holiday was spent with either family or friends in the Lowveld, solidifying his dream of becoming a ranger. Having joined the Londolozi team, he is now fulfilling his childhood dream of living and working in the African bush.

I am a published writer of three non fiction books, including My Life With Leopards, the Graham Cooke Story, which was set at Londolozi in the early 1990s. I am a seasoned safari traveller, contributing publications of safari lodges and destinations to various magazines and a keen safari photographer.
South African living in Canada for the past +25 years, lover of the African bush!
If I’m not running, I’m hanging with Jo Ann loving retired life and planning our next trip!

acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
Born in a litter of two, but the female sibling was killed by the Tortoise Pan Male at approx. 8 months old.

As a young male, he was pushed further north by the encroaching Senegal Bush Male and Maxims Male.
As a young nomadic male, he has passed through Sparta a number of times during the winter of 2021.

Now he has settled for the time being in the north-eastern corner of Marthly and possibly looking to expand further north.

acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
Named after the iconic ‘Plaque Rock’ along the banks of the Sand River, a place of high significance to the Varty family, it bears three plaques in remembrance of Charles Boyd Varty, Maidie Varty and Howard Mackie.

Heritage & Lineage

Born in March 2018 to the Nkoveni Female, the Plaque Rock Female represented a significant milestone as her mother’s first successfully raised offspring. Her birth marked a new chapter in the prestigious Sunsetbend lineage, connecting her through her grandmother, the Mashaba Female, to one of Londolozi’s most celebrated leopard dynasties. Raised in the productive areas around the Sand River, she grew up remarkably relaxed around vehicles, a trait inherited from both her mother and grandmother.

Territory

Her territory acquisition tells a story of careful maternal planning. As she approached independence, her mother, the Nkoveni Female, began a gradual shift eastward, effectively ceding prime river territory to her daughter. The Plaque Rock Female established herself in an ideal location that included the Sand River’s eastern sections near Londolozi camps, creating a perfect base for both hunting and future denning sites. This territory offered everything a female leopard could desire – access to water, abundant prey, and numerous secure locations for raising cubs. The complex network of drainage lines and granite boulder clusters would later prove crucial in her own attempts at motherhood.

Physical Characteristics

Like her mother, she carried the 2:2 spot pattern that would later be shared by her sister, the Xinkhova Female.
Distinctive pink nose

Reproductive History

The Plaque Rock Female’s story as a mother reflects both the harsh realities and profound determination of leopard motherhood. Though she never successfully raised cubs to independence, each attempt revealed her growing experience and maternal instincts:

First Litter (2022): Cubs were lost before they could be viewed
Second Litter (2022): Briefly seen before disappearing in the challenging summer months
Third Litter (2023-2024): Her most successful attempt, giving birth to three cubs which she moved between multiple den sites, showing remarkable maternal care before their tragic loss
Final Litter (2024): Had just revealed a single cub to the world before her untimely death

Behavioural Notes

Her character was marked by a playful spirit that never quite faded even as she matured into a formidable hunter. She showed particular skill in hunting kudu calves and impala, regularly utilizing the riverine vegetation for cover. Her comfort around vehicles allowed for intimate observations of her behaviour, from playful tree-climbing sessions to tender moments with her cubs. Perhaps most remarkably, she maintained an unusual tolerance of her mother’s presence, often allowing relatively close proximity without the typical aggression shown between territorial females.

Final Chapter

The Plaque Rock Female’s life came to a tragic end in June 2024, during an encounter with the Ntsevu Pride and Ndzhenga Males in the Sand River on Mala Mala. At just six years old, her passing marked the end of a short but impactful presence in Londolozi’s leopard population. The vacancy left in her territory opened the possibility for her sister, the Xinkhova Female, to establish herself in this prime location, potentially continuing the family’s legacy along the Sand River.

Historical Significance

Though her time was cut short, the Plaque Rock Female’s legacy lives on through the stories of those who witnessed her journey. She demonstrated the successful inheritance of territory from mother to daughter, showed remarkable resilience in the face of reproductive challenges, and maintained the prestigious Sunsetbend lineage’s presence along the Sand River. Her life, though tragically brief, embodied the complex dynamics of leopard society at Londolozi, from territorial relationships to the challenges of motherhood in this unforgiving environment.

users_spotted.user_description: Passionate about wildlife conservation and Big Cats!   Travel, family, reading, hiking, skiing, safaris!

Bob and I live in the San Francisco Bay Area where we enjoy boating, hiking, photography and travel. After many trips to Eastern and Southern Africa, we are pleased to call Londolozi our 'African home!'

I came here for the 1st time with my husband in Feb 2010, 2nd stop on a Vic Falls-Londolozi-Cape Town trip. I'd wanted to come here for years, as my ambition was to see a leopard in the wild. We looked at the cost, thought "ouch!" then - well it is just a one-off! On our 1st game drive  we saw Vomba, so mission achieved. Then the next morning we saw Camp Pan mating with Nottens! Within 24 hours of arriving we were completely smitten, and knew we not only had to come back, but come back the next year. So began a highly expensive addiction, and my trip 3 weeks ago was my 9th consecutive year and I celebrated my 100th game drive!

California native, travel junkie, animal lover...... have traveled to Africa over a dozen times to fulfill my passion for observing animals in their natural environment. Londolozi has become my favorite place to stay, with almost yearly visits since 2019.

Garrett has always had an incredible love for the wilderness and found his way to Londolozi straight after University. After spending time as a Londolozi Camp Manager, the incredible stories of daily sightings from his ranger counterparts and guests alike pushed him to become a Londolozi Guide, where he enjoyed 3 years in the field sharing Londolozi with thousands of guests. After a brief sabbatical travelling through Southern Africa and working in Tanzania, Garrett returned to the Londolozi Family as Sales Manager sharing Londolozi with as many people as possible.

Born in New York and settled down in Hong Kong for the past 20 years after living in London and Tokyo.  I "found" Londolozi in 2009 and have been a regular visitor since.  Over that time I have gained a passion for the bush and the photographic opportunities it provides.  Thanks to the tutelage of the Londolozi rangers and Creative hub I am getting my photography to an acceptable level.

Lucie and I are retired and have turned our energies to photography and videography, of which wildlife is by far the favorite subject.  We have been to Africa every 2-3 years over the last 35 years.  We have been to several camps in each of South Africa, Botswana, Kenya, Tanzania, Namibia, Uganda and Rwanda but Londolozi and Tiger Canyon are our go-to favorite places.  We are unabashedly predator-centric and aviary-sated.  And we are so thankful that the Varty family built this community-driven concept and has taught us all the meaning of "ubuntu".

I am passionate about travel, photography, Africa(its people and wildlife), my family, especially my grandchildren! Going to Africa for the first time in 2010 changed my life and made me want to do wildlife expeditions! Since then I have traveled to all the continents mostly focusing on photographing wildlife! Londolozi has become one of my favorite places of all and I look forward to returning as many more times as possible! It has stolen my heart and I am humbled by the beauty of all the amazing creatures I have seen there.

Growing up in the small coastal town of Mtunzini, Matt's childhood was shaped by endless hours spent exploring the forests, beaches and wetlands that sparked a lifelong passion for wildlife. After completing a BSc degree, he worked in construction and landscaping before the opportunity to join Londolozi changed the course of his career. Today, as a ranger and wildlife photographer, he has the privilege of spending every day immersed in the wilderness that first inspired him as a child.

Tristan is a Zimbabwean born journalist. He grew up moving farms in his home country and moved to South Africa to attend Rhodes University. With a passion for wildlife, it was a natural progression that he gravitated to Londolozi. He worked in the creative team bringing content to our online audience.

Megan grew up at Londolozi, where her love for nature blossomed. With a degree in Visual Studies and Social Media Marketing, her journey came full circle when she joined the dynamic Londolozi Creative Hub, where her love for nature and visuals finds its perfect home. 

Guided by an unwavering love for photography, videography, and the captivating realm of visuals, Megan hopes to impart a unique and vibrant essence to each of the creative projects she takes on.

After a few years of working in the world of economic consulting, Kate’s love of adventure, wilderness and sense of curiosity led her to move away from the city and join the Londolozi guiding team.  It was amidst her years of studying politics, philosophy and economics that her love of exploring and understanding different wilderness areas in South Africa compounded through trips with friends and family. Kate has been fortunate to travel to many different corners of the world but she’ll argue that nothing quite beats being surrounded by nature watching an African sunrise or sunset, especially at Londolozi!

Coming to Africa has kick-started a life of wildlife based travel for me. My first adventure was to Kenya, Tanzania and Rwanda. That trip would become one of the things that define who I am. I was bitten hard with the Africa travel bug as they say. The rest is so called history (still in the making of course), and over the years I have come to know South Africa as a second home.

Nick grew up in Johannesburg with a deep love for the outdoors. After finishing high school, he spent a formative gap year in the Zimbabwean bushveld — an experience that cemented his passion for wildlife and conservation. Although he went on to study and build a career in corporate real estate, the pull of the wilderness never faded. Now an experienced member of the Londolozi guiding team, Nick finds the greatest joy in tracking leopards and immersing himself in the intricate world of birding. He has developed a strong passion for wildlife photography, always looking to capture authentic moments in the wild.
First visited Londolozi in June 2011.  My profile picture up close with the Nkuwa female during our 2023 visit. We returned again in 2025.  Can't wait to come back again!

Love nature, watching animals and going on safari. Been lots of times on safari to different African countries. Londolozi is one of my favourite places. I am always looking forward to my next trip to Londolozi!

Passionate Londolozi Guests! Avid wildlife photographers. Supporters and advocates for the Good Work Foundation through the All Heart Fund in the USA. Restaurateurs and wine & spirits retailers in Sarasota, Florida at Michael’s On East (www.bestfood.com)

I live in Canada. My first visit was June 2023 and I stayed at Tree Camp for 1 week. 
I returned in June 2024 for another week. June 2025 I have reserved 10 days at Tree Camp. Londolozi has changed me. I am on a non-stop thrill during visits. The animals, the food, the service, nothing is too much to ask for during your stay. The Healing House services are spectacular! Londolozi is a truly magical place. It makes one feel alive! That is me with the amazing John Varty in my profile photo.

Keagan has always had a connection with wildlife, having been lucky enough to visit Londolozi as a child. After growing up in Johannesburg, he attended boarding school in the KwaZulu Natal Midlands where weekends were spent exploring the reserve and appreciating his surroundings. Keagan further went on to study Engineering at the University of Cape Town, during which each holiday was spent with either family or friends in the Lowveld, solidifying his dream of becoming a ranger. Having joined the Londolozi team, he is now fulfilling his childhood dream of living and working in the African bush.

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: A stunning female found in the north. Successfully raised the Thumbela Female while establishing dominance in NW Marthly.
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
Named after Xinzele road in northwestern Marthly, ‘xinzele’ meaning honeybadger in Shangaan.

Heritage & Lineage
Born in early 2017 to the Ingrid Dam Female and the Anderson Male. Her almost identical spot pattern to her mother’s makes her easily recognizable as part of this lineage, though she is notably smaller in size.

Territory
Has firmly established herself in northwestern Marthly, particularly around:

Ximpalapala Koppie area
Leadwood forest
Manyelethi River system
Rocky outcrops and boulder-strewn hillsides
Areas near the northern boundary

Physical Characteristics

4:4 spot pattern (nearly identical to her mother’s)
Smaller frame than her mother
Particularly adept at navigating rocky terrain

Reproductive History
Has shown increasing success in her reproductive efforts:

Successful Offspring:

March/April 2022: Thumbela Female (sibling lost at approximately 2 months)

Previous Attempts:

September 2021: First litter denned at Our Father’s Crossing (lost to nomadic male)
April 2022: Two cubs (one survived – Thumbela Female)
December 2024: Believed to be denning on Ximpalapala Koppie

Current Status
Successfully established as a territorial female in northwestern Marthly, where she has raised the Thumbela Female to independence. Known for utilizing the dramatic landscape of rocky outcrops and riverine systems for denning and hunting.

Behavioural Notes
Shows remarkable comfort in the challenging terrain of northwestern Marthly, particularly adept at utilizing rocky outcrops and the Manyelethi River system. Her choice of den sites demonstrates excellent maternal instincts, often selecting areas that balance accessibility with security. Despite the challenges of raising cubs near the reserve’s boundary, she has successfully adapted her movements to maintain territory while protecting her offspring.

Historical Significance
Represents an important presence in Londolozi’s northern territories, maintaining regular leopard viewing in an area that can be challenging to monitor. Her success in raising the Thumbela Female, particularly given the challenging landscape and proximity to the boundary, demonstrates her capabilities as a mother and territorial female. Her presence has helped maintain consistent leopard activity in the scenic but less frequently traversed northern sections of the reserve.

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: The only surviving cub of the Nanga female, currently territorial northern Marthly. Currently denning north of boundary
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
Named after the Makomsava road where she was frequently seen in her early independence

Heritage & Lineage

Born in September 2016 to the Nanga Female and sired by the Anderson Male, she represents the continuing legacy of the Saseka Female lineage. Born in a litter of two, though her sibling disappeared at approximately five months of age.

Territory

Initially established in her mother’s former territory along the Manyelethi River system, particularly around the Leadwood forest. Her territory has shifted significantly over time, expanding westward towards Ximpalapala koppie in late 2019. Currently, she maintains a territory primarily north of Londolozi’s boundary, though recently showing increasing presence back on the reserve.

Physical Characteristics

2:2 spot pattern
Facial features characteristic of the Saseka lineage

Reproductive History

Has faced significant challenges in her reproductive efforts:
Attempts:

Mid 2020: Two cubs denned at Marthly Pools (litter lost)
October 2021: Two cubs north of boundary (Young Female reached independence)
June 2022: Two cubs born north of the boundary (litter lost)
November 2024: Currently believed to be denning with two cubs north of the boundary

Current Status

Currently raising what’s believed to be a litter of two cubs, denned north of Londolozi’s boundary. Shows increasing presence back on Londolozi property, suggesting possible territory expansion or shift.

Behavioural Notes

Demonstrated remarkable adaptability in her territorial movements, particularly in response to pressure from other females. Her early establishment in the Leadwood forest area showed excellent strategic thinking in terms of hunting territory. The loss of several litters hasn’t diminished her reproductive efforts, showing the persistence characteristic of successful female leopards.

Historical Significance

Represents an interesting case study in territorial flexibility among Londolozi’s leopards. Her mother’s complete ceding of territory to her was unusual, and her subsequent movements northward and recent returns to Londolozi demonstrate the dynamic nature of leopard territories. While facing challenges in raising cubs to independence, her recent success with one female offspring suggests growing maturity and experience as a mother.

users_spotted.user_description: Passionate about wildlife.

Our first visit was in 2011, we returned in 2014, then again in 2017, and again in 2018.  It is favorite place to be.  We plan on coming 2020 for my 70th birthday (3/2/50) and our 50th wedding anniversary (9/5/70)
We recently visited with our daughter's family, including 8 yr old granddaughter.  She is still talking about all the wonderful things that she saw on Safari.  We were worried that it might be a little gory for her, but she reacted with vigor to the most gruesome of events.  We plan a return visit in 2020 - that will be our 5th trip to visit this incredible place where the guides, trackers, and all the staff make this such a memorable experience for all that visit.

I came here for the 1st time with my husband in Feb 2010, 2nd stop on a Vic Falls-Londolozi-Cape Town trip. I'd wanted to come here for years, as my ambition was to see a leopard in the wild. We looked at the cost, thought "ouch!" then - well it is just a one-off! On our 1st game drive  we saw Vomba, so mission achieved. Then the next morning we saw Camp Pan mating with Nottens! Within 24 hours of arriving we were completely smitten, and knew we not only had to come back, but come back the next year. So began a highly expensive addiction, and my trip 3 weeks ago was my 9th consecutive year and I celebrated my 100th game drive!

Bob and I live in the San Francisco Bay Area where we enjoy boating, hiking, photography and travel. After many trips to Eastern and Southern Africa, we are pleased to call Londolozi our 'African home!'

Born in New York and settled down in Hong Kong for the past 20 years after living in London and Tokyo.  I "found" Londolozi in 2009 and have been a regular visitor since.  Over that time I have gained a passion for the bush and the photographic opportunities it provides.  Thanks to the tutelage of the Londolozi rangers and Creative hub I am getting my photography to an acceptable level.
Passionate about wildlife conservation and Big Cats!   Travel, family, reading, hiking, skiing, safaris!
I love big cats (animals as well), cricket, and food.

Africa enthusiast; lover of all things Africa, photography, safari, and conservation. My lifelong dream of visiting Africa came true in June 2023, second trip in 2025, and third in September 2026. Londolozi is a dream destination.

I am a published author and wildlife and travel writer, specializing is African safaris.  I have always had a deep affinity with all living creatures, even while growing up in urban Amsterdam. Going on safari has enhanced that innate connection into a lifelong passion.

Love nature, watching animals and going on safari. Been lots of times on safari to different African countries. Londolozi is one of my favourite places. I am always looking forward to my next trip to Londolozi!
Self proclaimed Leopardographer.

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: A daughter of the Nhlanguleni female, born into a litter of two, both of which survived to independence.
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
In early 2018 the Nhlanguleni female gave birth to a litter of two females.
Kept well hidden at various dens along the Mhangeni drainage during their formative months, as well as in the Sand River itself, both these cubs nevertheless grew up relatively relaxed around the Land Rovers.

Both females were raised to independence; the first time an intact litter had been successfully raised since the litter their mother was part of 7 years prior.

Upon reaching independence, the sisters were regularly encountered in close proximity to one another, sometimes even feeding off the same kills.

Towards late 2019 they began splitting up, with one female (renamed the Nkuwa female) spending the majority of her time further west in her mother’s territory, and the Finfoot female (so named because of the number of times she was encountered near Finfoot Crossing) spending the majority of her time in the eastern sector of her mother’s territory, much closer to the Londolozi camps.

During 2020, this female was seen along the fenceline in southern Sabi Sabi nearing the Paul Kruger Gate. Seeking out a territory further afield.

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: Raised as an intact litter, first in 7 years, who has now made her own history by raising two males to independence as an intact litter.
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
Named after the Shangaan word for Sycamore Fig trees which dot her territory along the Sand River

Heritage & Lineage

Born in March 2018 to the Nhlanguleni Female and sired by the Anderson Male, she carries the prestigious Sunsetbend lineage. She was born in a historical litter – with her sister the Finfoot Female, they were the first intact litter to reach independence since their mother’s own generation in 2012.

Territory

Maintains territory in northwestern Londolozi, primarily in western Sparta south of the Sand River, extending north along the Marthly/Othawa boundary. Her territory significantly overlaps with her mother’s, though she has established dominance in the western portions. The area is characterized by dense vegetation along the riverbanks and prominent Sycamore Fig trees.

Physical Characteristics

3:3 spot pattern
Distinctive bright pink nose
Facial features characteristic of the Sunsetbend lineage

Reproductive History

Has shown increasing success in her reproductive efforts:

Successful Offspring:

February 2023: Two male cubs (2:2 and 3:3 spot patterns) successfully raised to independence

Previous Attempts:

The first litter lost at a few months old
Currently seen mating with Ntomi Male and Thamba Male, suggesting potential pregnancy

Current Status

At six years old, she has proven herself as a capable mother after successfully raising two male cubs to independence – a rare achievement at Londolozi. Currently seeking to reproduce again, showing mating behaviour with the Ntomi and Thamba Males.

Behavioural Notes

Demonstrates similar secretive denning behaviour to her mother, often keeping cubs well hidden during their early months. Shows exceptional hunting abilities, particularly important during the demanding period of raising two male cubs. Her success in raising both male cubs to independence, despite the increased nutritional demands, speaks to her hunting prowess and maternal capability.

Historical Significance

The Nkuwa Female represents a significant success story in the continuation of the Sunsetbend lineage. Her achievement in raising two male cubs to independence is particularly noteworthy, as it’s relatively rare for both cubs in a litter to survive, especially males. Her overlapping territory with her mother, the Nhlanguleni Female, provides an interesting study in mother-daughter dynamics among Londolozi’s leopards.

Today, as a ranger and wildlife photographer, he has the privilege of spending every day immersed in the wilderness that first inspired him as a child.

I came here for the 1st time with my husband in Feb 2010, 2nd stop on a Vic Falls-Londolozi-Cape Town trip. I'd wanted to come here for years, as my ambition was to see a leopard in the wild. acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: Dominant from 2019-2024, transformed from cautious visitor to powerful territorial force. Mastered central Londolozi until his final days.
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
Named after an area in Mala Mala known as ‘Senegal Bush’ after a Senegalia senegal tree.

Heritage & Lineage

First viewed as a young male in 2016, after a short stint in the north he moved eastwards. Here he received his name and grew into a large dominant male.

Territory Evolution

His territory establishment followed several distinct phases:

Initial Phase (2016): Brief appearances in northern Londolozi around Mahlahla Dam
Eastern Phase (2017-2019): Established in eastern Marthly and Mala Mala
Expansion Phase (2019): Pushed westward, displacing the ageing Inyathini Male
Prime Period (2020-2023): Dominated central Londolozi from Mala Mala to central Sparta
Final Phase (2023-2024): Gradually shifted northwestward under pressure from Maxims Male

Physical Characteristics

3:3 spot pattern
Distinctive deeply set eyes with a dark eyeliner that gave an intense stare
Tattered ears from territorial conflicts
Notable scars accumulated through years of territorial defence

Behavioural Notes
The Senegal Bush Male’s story is one of strategic territory acquisition and maintenance. Initially spotted making brief forays into Londolozi, he showed remarkable patience in establishing himself, choosing his moments carefully before making decisive moves to claim territory. His hunting prowess was particularly notable, showing exceptional skill with warthog hunting, often successfully ambushing them at their burrows.

His territorial strategy was methodical and effective, using drainage lines and river systems to navigate his vast domain. He demonstrated remarkable tolerance of certain young males, particularly those likely to be his offspring, allowing them to feed from his kills – behaviour that proved crucial in establishing his genetic legacy in the area.

Perhaps most remarkably, he maintained complex relationships with several females across his territory, successfully mating with the Nhlanguleni, Nkuwa, and Three Rivers females among others. His success in protecting these females’ territories and allowing his offspring to flourish demonstrated an impressive understanding of prime real estate.

Final Chapter

Last seen in June 2024, the Senegal Bush Male’s disappearance marked the end of a significant era in Londolozi’s leopard dynamics. Though his fate remains uncertain, his legacy continues through multiple offspring, including the Ntomi Male, who shows signs of following in his father’s footsteps.

Historical Significance

His impact on Londolozi’s leopard population extends far beyond his territorial reign:

Successfully established and maintained prime territory through strategic expansion
Contributed significantly to genetic diversity through multiple successful offspring
Demonstrated exceptional parental tolerance, allowing likely offspring to share kills
Showed remarkable adaptability in territory defence and expansion
Left a lasting legacy through multiple offspring who continue to shape Londolozi’s leopard dynamics

The Senegal Bush Male’s story embodies the complex dynamics of male leopard society, from initial establishment through territorial dominance to eventual succession. His influence continues through his offspring, who now shape the next chapter of Londolozi’s leopard population.

acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
Named after the productive Piccadilly Triangle area in Mala Mala

Heritage & Lineage

Born in December 2013 to the Xidulu Female, the Piccadilly Female represents another branch of the prestigious Sunset bend lineage, evidenced by her distinctive golden coat. She was born in a litter of two females, both reaching independence – a notable achievement. Her sister, the Sibuye Female, established territory further north and east in Mala Mala.

Territory

Her territory has evolved significantly over time. Initially spending much time beyond Londolozi’s borders, she began exploiting opportunities created when the Nkoveni Female shifted east, establishing a presence along the southern bank of the Sand River and occasionally north towards the Manyelethi. Recently, she’s been seen more frequently just south of the Sand River, east of the Londolozi Camps – territory previously held by the late Plaque Rock Female. This area is currently contested, with the Xinkhova Female also showing interest in establishing herself there.

Physical Characteristics

Distinctive 3:3 spot pattern
Pink nose
Golden coat characteristic of the Sunset bend lineage

Reproductive History

The Piccadilly Female has shown increasing success in her reproductive efforts:

Successful Offspring:

April 2020: Ngungwe Female (viewable on Marthly)
Mid 2023: Matumi Male (currently within mother’s territory)

Notable Attempts:

Mid 2019: One cub (litter lost)
April 2020: Ngungwe Female
January 2023: Two cubs denned near Stwise (litter lost)
Mid 2023: Matumi Male

Current Status
Currently maintaining territory while raising the Matumi Male. Her movements between Londolozi and Mala Mala demonstrate the fluid nature of leopard territories, particularly in border areas. She faces potential territorial pressure from the Xinkhova Female in areas previously controlled by the Plaque Rock Female.

Behavioural Notes

Despite not being frequently viewed on Londolozi historically, she has shown remarkable adaptability in utilizing territorial opportunities. Her success in raising cubs to independence suggests she’s found a balance between the different reserves she frequents. Like many leopards of the Sunset Bend lineage, she’s proven to be an attentive mother, successfully raising offspring despite the challenges of a territory spanning multiple reserves.

Historical Significance

The Piccadilly Female represents an important extension of the Sunset Bend lineage, successfully establishing herself across reserve boundaries. Through her daughter, the Ngungwe Female, she’s contributed to the continuation of this prestigious bloodline, while her current success with the Matumi Male demonstrates her ongoing contribution to the leopard population. Her territorial movements provide valuable insights into how leopards adapt to changing dynamics and opportunities in neighbouring reserves.

acf.lol_territory_desc:
The Piccadilly female is usually encountered close to the Sand River or the Manyelethi River, east of the Londolozi camps. Her territory extends from the Manyelethi/Sand RIver confluence, north past Stwise koppies towards the Marthly/Marthly boundary.
The majority of her territory is on Mala Mala.

users_spotted.user_description:
Our first visit was in 2011, we returned in 2014, then again in 2017, and again in 2018.  It is favorite place to be.  We plan on coming 2020 for my 70th birthday (3/2/50) and our 50th wedding anniversary (9/5/70)
We recently visited with our daughter's family, including 8 yr old granddaughter.  She is still talking about all the wonderful things that she saw on Safari.  We were worried that it might be a little gory for her, but she reacted with vigor to the most gruesome of events.  We plan a return visit in 2020 - that will be our 5th trip to visit this incredible place where the guides, trackers, and all the staff make this such a memorable experience for all that visit.

Bob and I live in the San Francisco Bay Area where we enjoy boating, hiking, photography and travel. After many trips to Eastern and Southern Africa, we are pleased to call Londolozi our 'African home!'
I love big cats (animals as well), cricket, and food.

California native, travel junkie, animal lover...... have traveled to Africa over a dozen times to fulfill my passion for observing animals in their natural environment. Londolozi has become my favorite place to stay, with almost yearly visits since 2019.

Garrett has always had an incredible love for the wilderness and found his way to Londolozi straight after University. After spending time as a Londolozi Camp Manager, the incredible stories of daily sightings from his ranger counterparts and guests alike pushed him to become a Londolozi Guide, where he enjoyed 3 years in the field sharing Londolozi with thousands of guests. After a brief sabbatical travelling through Southern Africa and working in Tanzania, Garrett returned to the Londolozi Family as Sales Manager sharing Londolozi with as many people as possible.

Love nature, watching animals and going on safari. Been lots of times on safari to different African countries. Londolozi is one of my favourite places. I am always looking forward to my next trip to Londolozi!

Lucie and I are retired and have turned our energies to photography and videography, of which wildlife is by far the favorite subject.  We have been to Africa every 2-3 years over the last 35 years.  We have been to several camps in each of South Africa, Botswana, Kenya, Tanzania, Namibia, Uganda and Rwanda but Londolozi and Tiger Canyon are our go-to favorite places.  We are unabashedly predator-centric and aviary-sated.  And we are so thankful that the Varty family built this community-driven concept and has taught us all the meaning of "ubuntu".

I am a lifelong animal lover, especially cats!  I got to fulfill my dream of going on an African safari for my 52nd birthday (it was supposed to be for my 50th but Covid interfered!).  I fell in LOVE with Londolozi, the people, and the country.  I am counting the days until I can return!!

Wildlife Photography Enthusiast
@wildcattraveler on IG
Passionate about wildlife conservation and Big Cats!   Travel, family, reading, hiking, skiing, safaris!

I am a published author and wildlife and travel writer, specializing is African safaris.  I have always had a deep affinity with all living creatures, even while growing up in urban Amsterdam. Going on safari has enhanced that innate connection into a lifelong passion.

Born in New York and settled down in Hong Kong for the past 20 years after living in London and Tokyo.  I "found" Londolozi in 2009 and have been a regular visitor since.  Over that time I have gained a passion for the bush and the photographic opportunities it provides.  Thanks to the tutelage of the Londolozi rangers and Creative hub I am getting my photography to an acceptable level.

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: Born 2016 to Ndzanzeni Female, royal descendant of Mother Leopard. Now a dominant force in the north.
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
Named after the waterhole where he was frequently seen during early independence

Heritage & Lineage
Born in winter 2016 to the Ndzanzeni Female, representing the sixth generation descendant of the original Mother Leopard. His birth at the Python Rock den site was discovered by the same tracking team that first found his mother as a cub, creating a poetic connection in Londolozi’s leopard history.

Territory Evolution

Early Phase (2016-2018): Extended dependency around Mad Elephant Pan
Establishment Phase (2018-2019): Concentrated around Tortoise Pan
Northern Phase (2019-2023): Dominant north of Londolozi boundary
Current Phase (2024): Expanding southward into Marthly, potentially filling the vacancy left by Senegal Bush Male

Physical Characteristics

4:3 spot pattern
Large, thickset impressive build
Recent battle scars from territorial disputes
Notably powerful presence

Presumed Offspring
Potential father to multiple cubs in northern territories, though specific offspring is unconfirmed due to his territory being primarily beyond Londolozi’s boundaries.

Behavioural Notes
Shows several distinctive characteristics:

Unusually extended period of dependency with mother (over two years)
Rare father-son tolerance with Inyathini Male
Shared mating rights with father in early years
Strategic territory expansion
Shows growing confidence in Southern expansion
Currently challenging multiple males for northern territory

Historical Significance
Represents important aspects of Londolozi’s leopard dynamics:

A direct descendant of Mother Leopard lineage
Demonstrated unusual male-male tolerance with father
Currently influencing major territorial shifts
Potential to reshape Northern Territory Dynamics

His presence in northern territories and recent southern expansion represents a significant shift in Londolozi’s male leopard dynamics, particularly as he challenges younger males like Ntomi, Hlambela, and Xitsalala for dominance.

users_spotted.user_description: Jemma grew up on a farm in the Midlands Meander in Kwa-Zulu Natal and studied at the University of Cape Town. With little bush experience but with many hours of au pairing, teaching English and forming a love for travel, Jemma found herself working at Londolozi as the Cubs Den Manager in January 2018. A few months later she started working for the Londolozi Creative Hub in Digital Marketing, the person behind the scenes of Londolozi's Blog and social media - and she hasn't looked back since...

Richie is Londolozi's Director of Technology and Sustainability and the founder of the Londolozi blog. Over the past decade he has built Londolozi's online ecosystem into a platform for advocacy of the restoration and rewilding of the natural world. Today he applies that same thinking to the land itself, helping lead the Save the Sand initiative to restore the Sand River catchment that gives Londolozi its lifeblood. His work lives at the meeting point of ancient wisdom, modern technology and nature. You'll find him in the LCH at Londolozi. Come say hi on your next visit.

Passionate Londolozi Guests! Avid wildlife photographers. Supporters and advocates for the Good Work Foundation through the All Heart Fund in the USA. Restaurateurs and wine & spirits retailers in Sarasota, Florida at Michael’s On East (www.bestfood.com)

California native, travel junkie, animal lover...... have traveled to Africa over a dozen times to fulfill my passion for observing animals in their natural environment. Londolozi has become my favorite place to stay, with almost yearly visits since 2019.

Bob and I live in the San Francisco Bay Area where we enjoy boating, hiking, photography and travel. After many trips to Eastern and Southern Africa, we are pleased to call Londolozi our 'African home!'

I came here for the 1st time with my husband in Feb 2010, 2nd stop on a Vic Falls-Londolozi-Cape Town trip. I'd wanted to come here for years, as my ambition was to see a leopard in the wild. We looked at the cost, thought "ouch!" then - well it is just a one-off! On our 1st game drive  we saw Vomba, so mission achieved. Then the next morning we saw Camp Pan mating with Nottens! Within 24 hours of arriving we were completely smitten, and knew we not only had to come back, but come back the next year. So began a highly expensive addiction, and my trip 3 weeks ago was my 9th consecutive year and I celebrated my 100th game drive!

Our first visit was in 2011, we returned in 2014, then again in 2017, and again in 2018.  It is favorite place to be.  We plan on coming 2020 for my 70th birthday (3/2/50) and our 50th wedding anniversary (9/5/70)

We plan a return visit in 2020 - that will be our 5th trip to visit this incredible place where the guides, trackers, and all the staff make this such a memorable experience for all that visit.

Born in New York and settled down in Hong Kong for the past 20 years after living in London and Tokyo.  I "found" Londolozi in 2009 and have been a regular visitor since.  Over that time I have gained a passion for the bush and the photographic opportunities it provides.  Thanks to the tutelage of the Londolozi rangers and Creative hub I am getting my photography to an acceptable level.
Alan and I have been ambassadors for many years, this is our favorite place on earth ?

Bronwyn is 4th generation custodian of Londolozi Game Reserve, a mother, Master life coach and also one of its most longstanding employees, having grown up on the floors of the kitchen and in the gardens of the lodge.  Bronwyn’s official title is that of Londolozi’s Creative Director and as such she has spearheaded the reinvention of the Londolozi brand from 2007 until present day. In 2018, Bronwyn led the creation of the Londolozi Healing House, establishing one of the safari industry’s most innovative wellness offerings.  By weaving healing, mindfulness, and nature-based transformation into the guest experience, she helped reinvent the concept of wilderness wellness in the safari space.
Hopelessly addicted and devoted to leopards.

Love nature, watching animals and going on safari. Been lots of times on safari to different African countries. Londolozi is one of my favourite places. I am always looking forward to my next trip to Londolozi!

As a young boy growing up on an agricultural farm in Zimbabwe, Sean spent every opportunity entertaining himself outdoors, camping in the local nature reserve and learning about all facets of the natural world.  

After completing a Bachelor of Science degree in Environmental Science in Cape Town, Sean was free to follow his nature ambitions and return to his bush-loving childhood dreams, which led him to Londolozi.

Going into semi-retirement on the guiding front in 2020 saw Sean settle into a far more permanent role in the LCH, focusing his efforts on producing media content for the Londolozi online space.

Garrett has always had an incredible love for the wilderness and found his way to Londolozi straight after University. After spending time as a Londolozi Camp Manager, the incredible stories of daily sightings from his ranger counterparts and guests alike pushed him to become a Londolozi Guide, where he enjoyed 3 years in the field sharing Londolozi with thousands of guests. After a brief sabbatical travelling through Southern Africa and working in Tanzania, Garrett returned to the Londolozi Family as Sales Manager sharing Londolozi with as many people as possible.

Nick was a ranger at Londolozi from 2018 - 2022. He always had a love for nature. Growing up in Johannesburg, the annual family trip to the bush (particularly the Kruger Lowveld region of South Africa) became an escape from city life. When he and his brother weren't physically in the bush, they would pretend they were by watching wildlife documentaries and making animal tracks in the garden at home. After high school, Nick spent a year teaching sport in England and then returned to South Africa to study Engineering at Stellenbosch University. It was in the mountains of Stellenbosch where Nick further cultivated his passion for nature.
Passionate about wildlife conservation and Big Cats!   Travel, family, reading, hiking, skiing, safaris!

Robbie developed a passion for the African bush from many visits to his family’s small holding in a greater conservancy just outside Johannesburg. Living in the big city his whole life, he always found refuge in the outdoors and has grown to appreciate the slower pace of life and connectivity with nature that comes with spending time in the bush. After completing his studies in Finance and Accounting at university in Cape Town he leapt at the opportunity to follow his dream by partaking in Londolozi’s 2020 ranger training programme. His dream of sharing his passion for the African bush with others is being lived and will continue to evolve as he furthers his career as a guide at Londolozi.
Self proclaimed Leopardographer.

Megan grew up at Londolozi, where her love for nature blossomed. With a degree in Visual Studies and Social Media Marketing, her journey came full circle when she joined the dynamic Londolozi Creative Hub, where her love for nature and visuals finds its perfect home. 

Guided by an unwavering love for photography, videography, and the captivating realm of visuals, Megan hopes to impart a unique and vibrant essence to each of the creative projects she takes on.
