Passionate Londolozi Guests! Avid wildlife photographers. Supporters and advocates for the Good Work Foundation through the All Heart Fund in the USA. Restaurateurs and wine & spirits retailers in Sarasota, Florida at Michael’s On East (www.bestfood.com)

I arrived at Londolozi on 1 st December 1998. I was a trainee ranger and I was green behind the ears. Londolozi became my family and my home. I left in 2005 and returned later that year to get married down in the Sand River at Londolozi. I have been very fotunate to return with my wife every year since then and I have a son who is mad about tracking and anti-poaching thanks to the many hours he has spent wit me in the bush.
Following my passion for wildlife and photography

Born in New York and settled down in Hong Kong for the past 20 years after living in London and Tokyo.  I "found" Londolozi in 2009 and have been a regular visitor since.  Over that time I have gained a passion for the bush and the photographic opportunities it provides.  Thanks to the tutelage of the Londolozi rangers and Creative hub I am getting my photography to an acceptable level.
Talley Smith's father. Resident of Bermuda. Huge fan of Londolozi and Africa generally. Keen amateur photographer.
Serial Londo New Year visitor with Nicki and our sons Harry and Toby. Still tracking the Anderson male leopard.
Alan and I have been ambassadors for many years, this is our favorite place on earth ?

I came here for the 1st time with my husband in Feb 2010, 2nd stop on a Vic Falls-Londolozi-Cape Town trip. I'd wanted to come here for years, as my ambition was to see a leopard in the wild. We looked at the cost, thought "ouch!" then - well it is just a one-off! On our 1st game drive  we saw Vomba, so mission achieved. Then the next morning we saw Camp Pan mating with Nottens! Within 24 hours of arriving we were completely smitten, and knew we not only had to come back, but come back the next year. So began a highly expensive addiction, and my trip 3 weeks ago was my 9th consecutive year and I celebrated my 100th game drive!

Our first visit was in 2011, we returned in 2014, then again in 2017, and again in 2018.  It is favorite place to be.  We plan on coming 2020 for my 70th birthday (3/2/50) and our 50th wedding anniversary (9/5/70)
We recently visited with our daughter's family, including 8 yr old granddaughter.  She is still talking about all the wonderful things that she saw on Safari.  We were worried that it might be a little gory for her, but she reacted with vigor to the most gruesome of events.  We plan a return visit in 2020 - that will be our 5th trip to visit this incredible place where the guides, trackers, and all the staff make this such a memorable experience for all that visit.

Being surrounded by wilderness from a young age, you experience it in all of its essence. Matt was privileged enough to grow up in the Lowveld and its surroundings, sparking a great love for nature and all it has to offer, be it the sunsets, vast landscapes or amazing wildlife. As a young boy, his favourite trips were always going to the bush with family, spending time with only the best that Africa has to offer.

Matt discovered a passion that went hand-in-hand with his love for wildlife, Photography, and this is how he found his path leading to Londolozi from 2016 to 2020.
Love love love Londolozi and our visit!!

Jemma grew up on a farm in the Midlands Meander in Kwa-Zulu Natal and studied at the University of Cape Town. With little bush experience but with many hours of au pairing, teaching English and forming a love for travel, Jemma found herself working at Londolozi as the Cubs Den Manager in January 2018. A few months later she started working for the Londolozi Creative Hub in Digital Marketing, the person behind the scenes of Londolozi's Blog and social media - and she hasn't looked back since...
I love animals! A big intrest of mine is to play golf. I love to travel.

Bronwyn is 4th generation custodian of Londolozi Game Reserve, a mother, Master life coach and also one of its most longstanding employees, having grown up on the floors of the kitchen and in the gardens of the lodge.  Bronwyn’s official title is that of Londolozi’s Creative Director and as such she has spearheaded the reinvention of the Londolozi brand from 2007 until present day. In 2018, Bronwyn led the creation of the Londolozi Healing House, establishing one of the safari industry’s most innovative wellness offerings.  By weaving healing, mindfulness, and nature-based transformation into the guest experience, she helped reinvent the concept of wilderness wellness in the safari space.
Hopelessly addicted and devoted to leopards.

As a young boy growing up on an agricultural farm in Zimbabwe, Sean spent every opportunity entertaining himself outdoors, camping in the local nature reserve and learning about all facets of the natural world.  

After completing a Bachelor of Science degree in Environmental Science in Cape Town, Sean was free to follow his nature ambitions and return to his bush-loving childhood dreams, which led him to Londolozi.

Going into semi-retirement on the guiding front in 2020 saw Sean settle into a far more permanent role in the LCH, focusing his efforts on producing media content for the Londolozi online space.

Garrett has always had an incredible love for the wilderness and found his way to Londolozi straight after University. After spending time as a Londolozi Camp Manager, the incredible stories of daily sightings from his ranger counterparts and guests alike pushed him to become a Londolozi Guide, where he enjoyed 3 years in the field sharing Londolozi with thousands of guests. After a brief sabbatical travelling through Southern Africa and working in Tanzania, Garrett returned to the Londolozi Family as Sales Manager sharing Londolozi with as many people as possible.

Nick was a ranger at Londolozi from 2018 - 2022. He always had a love for nature. Growing up in Johannesburg, the annual family trip to the bush (particularly the Kruger Lowveld region of South Africa) became an escape from city life. When he and his brother weren't physically in the bush, they would pretend they were by watching wildlife documentaries and making animal tracks in the garden at home. After high school, Nick spent a year teaching sport in England and then returned to South Africa to study Engineering at Stellenbosch University. It was in the mountains of Stellenbosch where Nick further cultivated his passion for nature.

Robbie developed a passion for the African bush from many visits to his family’s small holding in a greater conservancy just outside Johannesburg. Living in the big city his whole life, he always found refuge in the outdoors and has grown to appreciate the slower pace of life and connectivity with nature that comes with spending time in the bush. After completing his studies in Finance and Accounting at university in Cape Town he leapt at the opportunity to follow his dream by partaking in Londolozi’s 2020 ranger training programme. His dream of sharing his passion for the African bush with others is being lived and will continue to evolve as he furthers his career as a guide at Londolozi.

Growing up in the small coastal town of Mtunzini, Matt's childhood was shaped by endless hours spent exploring the forests, beaches and wetlands that sparked a lifelong passion for wildlife. After completing a BSc degree, he worked in construction and landscaping before the opportunity to join Londolozi changed the course of his career. Today, as a ranger and wildlife photographer, he has the privilege of spending every day immersed in the wilderness that first inspired him as a child.

Keagan has always had a connection with wildlife, having been lucky enough to visit Londolozi as a child. After growing up in Johannesburg, he attended boarding school in the KwaZulu Natal Midlands where weekends were spent exploring the reserve and appreciating his surroundings. Keagan further went on to study Engineering at the University of Cape Town, during which each holiday was spent with either family or friends in the Lowveld, solidifying his dream of becoming a ranger. Having joined the Londolozi team, he is now fulfilling his childhood dream of living and working in the African bush.

California native, travel junkie, animal lover...... have traveled to Africa over a dozen times to fulfill my passion for observing animals in their natural environment. Londolozi has become my favorite place to stay, with almost yearly visits since 2019.

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: This rangy male was an enigma, arriving on Londolozi in the mid to latter parts of 2014 and staying mainly in the western areas.
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
This rangy male was rather an enigma, having arrived on Londolozi in the mid- to latter parts of 2014 and staying mainly in the western areas of the reserve, around the Sparta/Ravenscourt break and Mhangeni Donga. Sightings of a relatively unrelaxed male in the block south of Ximpalapala koppie from around the same time were also believed to be him.

His skittish nature led us to suspect that he originated in the Kruger Park and grew up not being used to vehicles approaching him. First reports of this male were in the north of the Sabi Sands as a sub-adult in 2012.

Since 2014 this male has expanded his territory massively, being found from beyond the Maxabene River in the south to the upper reaches of the Manyelethi River in the north, operating mainly in the western portions of Sparta. His territory is roughly the same size as the Camp Pan male’s once was, despite the 4:4 male being a significantly smaller animal.

He was believed to be the father of the Mashaba young female and the February 2016 litter of the Nkoveni female. He was also seen in the company of the Nhlanguleni female and her cubs, and although she was seen mating with the Nyelethi male in the west in 2015, at least the 4:4 male believed himself to be the litter’s father.

Sightings of this leopard were irregular at best, as he was reticent to patrol along roads, preferring to stay in drainage lines and thickets. When females in the area have kills hoisted, it was not uncommon to find the male feeding on the kill the next morning, having smelt it out during the night.

In most sightings this leopard is nervous of more than two vehicles, but sometimes he relaxes tremendously for unknown reasons. We hope he relaxes more as sightings become more frequent.
acf.lol_territory_desc: This leopard has a large territory that encompasses Sparta, predominantly north of the Maxabene all the way to central Marthly. Because this area is so large, he moves constantly and covers big distances in order to scent mark and patrol the area, thereby protecting it from potential male contenders.
acf.lol_status_deceased_desc: Mauled by Ntsevu Pride, died of wounds.

Richie is Londolozi's Director of Technology and Sustainability and the founder of the Londolozi blog. Over the past decade he has built Londolozi's online ecosystem into a platform for advocacy of the restoration and rewilding of the natural world. Today he applies that same thinking to the land itself, helping lead the Save the Sand initiative to restore the Sand River catchment that gives Londolozi its lifeblood. His work lives at the meeting point of ancient wisdom, modern technology and nature. You'll find him in the LCH at Londolozi. Come say hi on your next visit.

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: Born to the Nyelethi female in 2009, this male was one of three cubs that all survived to independence.
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
Born to the Nyelethi female in 2009, this male was one of three cubs that all survived to independence. His sister is the Nanga female and his brother the Nyelethi 2:3 male, who dispersed northwards, while the 4:3 brother moved south and west.

Initially spending time around the Londolozi camps, tolerated to a degree by the Marthly male (believed to be his father), he eventually dispersed westwards, establishing territory in Singita and Othawa.

This male rose in notoriety when he killed the Ravenscourt female in June 2013 when she was trying to protect her cub (now the Ravenscourt male, seen in southern Singita). He has established himself in the western sections of Singita and Othawa, but does have quite a significant territorial overlap with the Kaxane male in the southern reaches of the Singita property.
acf.lol_territory_desc: Since independence this male has established himself in western Singita and Castleton.

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: The brother of the Tu-Tones male from the same litter, the Makhotini male has had a far more successful life.
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
The brother of the Tu-Tones male from the same litter, the Makhotini male has had a far more successful life.  Dispersing at around three years of age, as is normal for young male leopards, he moved into the south western grasslands of Londolozi, an area not renowned for its leopard population, but by virtue of that fact, not hotly competed for.

Slowly this leopard expanded his territory further to the south and west, eventually venturing far beyond Londolozi’s borders to control a substantial portion of Sabi Sabi, as well as the far south-eastern corner of Singita. He has mated with a number of females in the area and sired cubs with the Little Bush female. It is likely that he fathered the Tatowa female’s first litter as well.

General game numbers differ in much of his territory, and the Makhotini male has adapted by hunting a larger variety of prey than other leopards. He has been seen hunting buffalo calves out of large herds on a number of occasions, and reedbuck and aardvark are some of the more unusual prey species that he has been recorded catching.

lol_id_markings.lol_id_markings_marking: Triangular spot pattern on right cheek

acf.lol_territory_desc: This leopard has established a large territory which extends from south west Dudley over much of Sabi Sabi. One of the reasons his territory is so large is that the open grasslands which dominate the area are not as flush with general game, and therefore not as desirable as hunting habitat. Fewer females inhabit the area and so the Makhotini male is forced to roam far to access mating opportunities.

Being surrounded by wilderness from a young age, you experience it in all of its essence. Matt was privileged enough to grow up in the Lowveld and its surroundings, sparking a great love for nature and all it has to offer, be it the sunsets, vast landscapes or amazing wildlife. As a young boy, his favourite trips were always going to the bush with family, spending time with only the best that Africa has to offer.

Matt discovered a passion that went hand-in-hand with his love for wildlife, Photography, and this is how he found his path leading to Londolozi from 2016 to 2020.
Alan and I have been ambassadors for many years, this is our favorite place on earth ?

Bob and I live in the San Francisco Bay Area where we enjoy boating, hiking, photography and travel. After many trips to Eastern and Southern Africa, we are pleased to call Londolozi our 'African home!'

Garrett has always had an incredible love for the wilderness and found his way to Londolozi straight after University. After spending time as a Londolozi Camp Manager, the incredible stories of daily sightings from his ranger counterparts and guests alike pushed him to become a Londolozi Guide, where he enjoyed 3 years in the field sharing Londolozi with thousands of guests. After a brief sabbatical travelling through Southern Africa and working in Tanzania, Garrett returned to the Londolozi Family as Sales Manager sharing Londolozi with as many people as possible.

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: He was born to the Kapen female in 2005, and upon independence moved south the lower Sabi Sand.
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
A male not often viewed on Londolozi, the Kaxane male (Kaxane means ‘far’ in Shangaan) is seen mainly in Singita and the western sectors of the reserve.  He was born to the Kapen female of Mala Mala in 2005,  and upon independence moved south into Sabi Sabi. He then began pushing north and westwards, establishing territory on the Castleton and Savannah properties towards the end of 2009.

This male has very distinctive rich green eyes and a conspicuous notch in his right ear.
acf.lol_territory_desc: The Kaxane male is occasionally viewed near Londolozi's western boundary. He holds a large and desirable territory in central Castleton and onto Ravenscourt.

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: Directly descended from the original mother leopard and therefore part of the royal lineage of Londolozi.
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
Directly descended from the original mother leopard and therefore part of the royal lineage of Londolozi, the Piva male was born to the Piva female beyond our southern borders. Born in 2010 in a litter of two, his sibling was killed by the Tugwaan male leopard later that year, but the Piva male survived to independence, moving into the southern reaches of Londolozi during his nomadic years and occasionally being seen during 2012 and 2013.

In 2014 he began establishing himself properly in the south east, forcing out the old Camp Pan male and taking over a territory that runs from the north eastern corner of Londolozi almost to the Tugwaan riverbed in the south.

He is easily recognized by the distinctive oval of spots on his forehead.
acf.lol_territory_desc: A male that has claimed a fairly large territory in eastern Sparta and eastern Dudley, focusing much of his time and hunting around the Maxabene drainage line. It seems this leopard even has favourite trees for hoisting carcasses in and has been found in a few Jackalberry's and Schotia's repeatedly.

When I was 25, I spent 15 months in South Africa, in a small town called Harrismith well known to those who drive from Johannesburg to Durban as it is a classic pit stop to refuel. It is then that I first heard about Londolozi when I bought the book "the leopards of Londolozi" and promised myself that 1 day I could fulfill my dream of visiting. The Londolozi Photo Studio

Amanda is the Head of Marketing at Londolozi & has been in the marketing & creative industry for 16 years & the health and wellness industry for 10 years. She holds a Bachelor’s degree in Psychology and Journalism from The University of Cape Town & an Honours degree in Brand Management. She's a Life Coach, an Enneagram Practitioner & Londolozi's photographer in residence. Her passion for the creative world, wilderness & wellness has led to a unique role within the Londolozi Family. She spearheaded the creation of the Photographic Studio & brings specialty retreat offerings to life at Londolozi. Amanda ensures that marketing always has deep experience at its roots.

Passionate Londolozi Guests! Avid wildlife photographers. Supporters and advocates for the Good Work Foundation through the All Heart Fund in the USA. Restaurateurs and wine & spirits retailers in Sarasota, Florida at Michael’s On East (www.bestfood.com)

Mike Nicki Harry and Toby, we try to visit Londo once a year. We think of it as our second home and are privileged to have seen the most amazing sights, encountered wonderful animals and learned so much about the bush from some amazing guides and trackers with such knowledge.

James had hardly touched a camera when he came to Londolozi, but his writing skills that complemented his Honours degree in Zoology meant that he was quickly snapped up by the Londolozi blog team. 

An environment rich in photographers helped him develop the photographic skills he needed to start capturing some great images, and 2015 saw him make the move from stills photography into film as well.

James was a member of the Londolozi family from 2010 - 2021.

Keen hobbies:  wild life and nature photography, target shooting, learning to fly fish;

Passionate about wildlife.

I arrived at Londolozi on 1 st December 1998. I was a trainee ranger and I was green behind the ears. Londolozi became my family and my home. I left in 2005 and returned later that year to get married down in the Sand River at Londolozi. I have been very fotunate to return with my wife every year since then and I have a son who is mad about tracking and anti-poaching thanks to the many hours he has spent wit me in the bush.

Work with innovative technology. Based in UK. Have lived in Africa and the Middle East. Passionate about travel, wildlife and photography. Keeping a log of all leopard sightings during trips to Londolozi over last few years!
Talley Smith's father. Resident of Bermuda. Huge fan of Londolozi and Africa generally. Keen amateur photographer.
An Zambian by birth, I am a passionate amateur wildlife photographer, a lover of all things in the African bush and a huge fan of Londolozi and all it offers!

Richie is Londolozi's Director of Technology and Sustainability and the founder of the Londolozi blog. Over the past decade he has built Londolozi's online ecosystem into a platform for advocacy of the restoration and rewilding of the natural world. Today he applies that same thinking to the land itself, helping lead the Save the Sand initiative to restore the Sand River catchment that gives Londolozi its lifeblood. His work lives at the meeting point of ancient wisdom, modern technology and nature. You'll find him in the LCH at Londolozi. Come say hi on your next visit.

Born in New York and settled down in Hong Kong for the past 20 years after living in London and Tokyo.  I "found" Londolozi in 2009 and have been a regular visitor since.  Over that time I have gained a passion for the bush and the photographic opportunities it provides.  Thanks to the tutelage of the Londolozi rangers and Creative hub I am getting my photography to an acceptable level.

Originally from New York USA currently living in the Sunshine state of Florida in the Tampa Bay area. My first trip to Africa was in 2009 when I visited  Botswana and Zambia. My first trip to Sabi Sands South Africa was in 2011. This is where my true addiction began. I stayed at Londolozi Varty camp and fell in love with the people and the animals.  Since then I have been back six more times and returning Sept. 2023 for my 7th . I have written several blogs and enjoy sharing photos and experiences from my trips. Leopards and male lions are my favorite to photograph. At home I have my own little family including my black lion Myra and two wild dogs Max and Jack.
Alan and I have been ambassadors for many years, this is our favorite place on earth ?

Our first visit was in 2011, we returned in 2014, then again in 2017, and again in 2018.  It is favorite place to be.  We plan on coming 2020 for my 70th birthday (3/2/50) and our 50th wedding anniversary (9/5/70)
We recently visited with our daughter's family, including 8 yr old granddaughter.  She is still talking about all the wonderful things that she saw on Safari.  We were worried that it might be a little gory for her, but she reacted with vigor to the most gruesome of events.  We plan a return visit in 2020 - that will be our 5th trip to visit this incredible place where the guides, trackers, and all the staff make this such a memorable experience for all that visit.

Lucie and I are retired and have turned our energies to photography and videography, of which wildlife is by far the favorite subject.  We have been to Africa every 2-3 years over the last 35 years.  We have been to several camps in each of South Africa, Botswana, Kenya, Tanzania, Namibia, Uganda and Rwanda but Londolozi and Tiger Canyon are our go-to favorite places.  We are unabashedly predator-centric and aviary-sated.  And we are so thankful that the Varty family built this community-driven concept and has taught us all the meaning of "ubuntu".

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: Born in June of 2000 to the Mhangeni female, the Mhangeni male moved south to eventually to establish his territory.
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
Born in  June of 2000 to the Mhangeni female, the Mhangeni male moved south to eventually establish territory in the far southern reaches of Londolozi, with the bulk of his territory lying beyond our borders.

Known in the south as the Sand River male, he sired a number of cubs with females in that area, with one of them, the Piva male, eventually moving back into Londolozi to establish territory in 2014.

In later life he lost the use of his right eye to unknown causes; some speculate it was in a territorial fight, others suggest a spitting cobra, which in itself would be a cruel twist of irony as this was exactly what happened to his mother.

He became nomadic again in late 2013 and the last recorded sightings of him are from the winter of 2014.
acf.lol_territory_desc: A leopard that held territory in southern Dudley, but mainly further south of that; prime habitat for the movement of medium sized antelope, consistent water sources as well as a high density of females.

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: This female was a small leopard with a shorter than average tail. She was territorial around the western reaches of Londolozi ’s Sand River.
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
This female was a small leopard with a shorter than average tail. She was territorial around the western reaches of Londolozi ’s Sand River frontage, but as most of her territory lay north of the river, sightings of her only became consistent after the purchase of the Marthly property in 1999.

She raised a number of cubs to independence, the most notable of which are the Ximpalapala female, who although skittish is still seen in her mother’s old territory, and the Tugwaan male, who dispersed into the south east. These two were born in the same litter in 2001

The last sighting of the short tailed female was in 2003, when she was seen in poor condition with a missing ear and cuts all over her. She was not seen after that and it is presumed that she died of her wounds.

lol_family_litters.lol_family_litters_desc: Male and female cub. Both survived.
Female killed by lions at seven months. Male survived, reappeared in August 2003 at Gert's Pan before dispersing.

acf.lol_territory_desc: Deep gully systems, a small portion of the Sand River, portions of open clearing and thick mixed woodland provided this female with a diverse and optimal territory in western Marthly.

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: This leopard was the first cub of the Nottens female, and therefore inherited the royal blood of the original Mother Leopard.
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
This leopard was the first cub of the Nottens female, and therefore inherited the royal blood of the original Mother Leopard. She established territory in the far south east of Londolozi, getting her name from Piva Pan, a small waterhole where she spent much of her time when first independent.

She wasn’t viewed often on Londolozi, spending the majority of her time beyond our southern boundary, but would occasionally venture back north, especially when raising litters as the area around Piva Pan itself offers numerous densites in the form of rocky clusters.

One of her notable litters, born in early 2010, included a young male who grew up to become the Piva male, dominant over the south eastern regions of Londolozi. His sister was killed around the age of 8 months by the Tugwaan male but the male survived to independence.

In early 2016 the Piva female was seen in very poor condition near Kirkman’s Camp in the southern reaches of the Sabi Sands. It is suspected that in her old age (over 17 years) she was pushed out of her territory by a younger, stronger leopard (possibly Hlarulini female from the south) and was forced into a nomadic lifestyle.
acf.lol_territory_desc: Although rarely seen on Londolozi, this leopard's territory fell into eastern Sparta and eastern Dudley. She raised a few litters around a waterhole called Piva Pan from which she got her name. This area has dense drainage lines and rocky bands making it fairly inaccessible and ideal for hiding small cubs.

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: The Campbell Koppies female was born to the Sunset Bend female in September 1999 in an uncommon litter of three.
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
The Campbell Koppies female was born to the Sunset Bend female in September 1999 in a litter of three, and was officially independent when her mother birthed another litter of three in October 2001 and became more aggressive towards her.

She established territory to the north and east of Londolozi, and had only two surviving offspring; the Ostrich Koppies female who is territorial to the east of our boundary was born in 2004 and the Maliliwane female who died in early 2016 was born in  in 2007. Other litters were almost certainly born (one in early 2004 almost) but none of these cubs survived to independence. One would have thought that a leopard with such an abundance of good den sites in her territory (the Campbell Koppies themselves) would have had better success in raising cubs, but it was not to be.

The Campbell Koppies female was last seen in mid 2013, and would have been just shy of 14 years old at the time of her death.
acf.lol_territory_desc: This leopard's territory lay beyond our borders, and although her progeny were viewed on Londolozi, the Campbell Koppies female stayed east of Londolozi

lol_territory_maps.lol_territory_maps_desc: The map is a complete approximation of her territory.

users_spotted.user_description: Richie is Londolozi's Director of Technology and Sustainability and the founder of the Londolozi blog. Over the past decade he has built Londolozi's online ecosystem into a platform for advocacy of the restoration and rewilding of the natural world. Today he applies that same thinking to the land itself, helping lead the Save the Sand initiative to restore the Sand River catchment that gives Londolozi its lifeblood. His work lives at the meeting point of ancient wisdom, modern technology and nature. You'll find him in the LCH at Londolozi. Come say hi on your next visit.

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: The Little Bush female is a rare visitor to Londolozi as most of her territory lies beyond our southern borders.
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
The Little Bush female is a rare visitor to Londolozi as most of her territory lies beyond our southern borders. She is occasionally encountered in the deep south west around Makhotini and Vertical Dams, although the long grass of the area is not conducive to easy leopard finding.

Notable sightings of her include August 2014, when she was viewed with a cub in the enormous sycamore fig tree near Makhotini dam, and then in June 2015 when she was found in company with the Warthog Wallow female (also from beyond our southern borders), both of them trailing the Makhotini male, who was ignoring both females, opting to hunt warthogs instead, one of which he successfully caught.

The last recorded sighting of her on Londolozi soil was in mid-2015, when she was found with her female cub (the Kigelia female) off Handpump Road with a reedbuck kill which the Makhotini male had stolen from.

lol_family_litters.lol_family_litters_desc: Male cub killed by Mhangeni male. Female cub survived.
One cub disappeared at around four months. Female cubs till alive as of June 2016

acf.lol_territory_desc: This female holds a territory in the grasslands of south west Dudley. Within her territory lie a few very large Sycamore figs. Because of the open nature of the terrain, these trees serve as important training spots for her cubs to learn to climb in and noteable sightings include seeing them in the enormous boughs.

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: The Tatowa female was one of a litter of three females born in early 2012 to the Ximpalapala female of the north.
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
This leopard is a bit of an anomaly, as she was born to a female who remains very skittish around vehicles, yet her cubs grew up far more relaxed than her.

The Tatowa female was one of a litter of three females born in early 2012 to the Ximpalapala female of the north. The litter was first confirmed when viewed on top of Ximpalapala koppie, and viewing over the next few months was pretty special, with three young cubs observed almost daily, playing around up on the rocks. As the cubs got to decide their own level of exposure to the vehicles by descending or ascending the koppie as they pleased, it wasn’t long before they were relaxed enough around the Land Rovers to be venturing down to ground level by themselves. Interestingly enough, when their mother returned her influence would turn them skittish again, and viewing tended to be far better when she was not around.

Towards the end of 2012 the Gowrie male claimed the territory of Ximpalapala koppie and the surrounding areas, and we believe he killed two of the cubs in the litter, with the 3:3 young female alone surviving.

After a few forays into the southern reaches of Londolozi she eventually established territory quite far to the south, and as she was viewed in the vicinity of Tatowa Dam on a number of occasions, was given the name Tatowa female.

She was seen heavily pregnant in early 2016 and was believed to be denning somewhere in the deep south of Londolozi, but after she was viewed mating with the Inyathini male with no signs of suckle marks a few weeks later, it was presumed the litter had been lost.
acf.lol_territory_desc: The Tatowa female's territory falls on south and central Dudley. For a female, particularly a young female, she may have a large territory because a significant portion of it falls in open grassland and as a result it is harder for her to hunt or to find suitable den sites. It may also be that there is less competition for this slightly less suitable leopard habitat.

Passionate about wildlife.

Thanks to the tutelage of the Londolozi rangers and Creative hub I am getting my photography to an acceptable level.

I came here for the 1st time with my husband in Feb 2010, 2nd stop on a Vic Falls-Londolozi-Cape Town trip. I'd wanted to come here for years, as my ambition was to see a leopard in the wild. We looked at the cost, thought "ouch!" then - well it is just a one-off! On our 1st game drive  we saw Vomba, so mission achieved. Then the next morning we saw Camp Pan mating with Nottens! Within 24 hours of arriving we were completely smitten, and knew we not only had to come back, but come back the next year. So began a highly expensive addiction, and my trip 3 weeks ago was my 9th consecutive year and I celebrated my 100th game drive!

Lucie and I are retired and have turned our energies to photography and videography, of which wildlife is by far the favorite subject.  We have been to Africa every 2-3 years over the last 35 years.  We have been to several camps in each of South Africa, Botswana, Kenya, Tanzania, Namibia, Uganda and Rwanda but Londolozi and Tiger Canyon are our go-to favorite places.  We are unabashedly predator-centric and aviary-sated.  And we are so thankful that the Varty family built this community-driven concept and has taught us all the meaning of "ubuntu".

Our first visit was in 2011, we returned in 2014, then again in 2017, and again in 2018.  It is favorite place to be.  We plan on coming 2020 for my 70th birthday (3/2/50) and our 50th wedding anniversary (9/5/70)
We recently visited with our daughter's family, including 8 yr old granddaughter.  She is still talking about all the wonderful things that she saw on Safari.  We were worried that it might be a little gory for her, but she reacted with vigor to the most gruesome of events.  We plan a return visit in 2020 - that will be our 5th trip to visit this incredible place where the guides, trackers, and all the staff make this such a memorable experience for all that visit.

Being surrounded by wilderness from a young age, you experience it in all of its essence. Matt was privileged enough to grow up in the Lowveld and its surroundings, sparking a great love for nature and all it has to offer, be it the sunsets, vast landscapes or amazing wildlife. As a young boy, his favourite trips were always going to the bush with family, spending time with only the best that Africa has to offer.

Matt discovered a passion that went hand-in-hand with his love for wildlife, Photography, and this is how he found his path leading to Londolozi from 2016 to 2020.

Nick was a ranger at Londolozi from 2018 - 2022. He always had a love for nature. Growing up in Johannesburg, the annual family trip to the bush (particularly the Kruger Lowveld region of South Africa) became an escape from city life. When he and his brother weren't physically in the bush, they would pretend they were by watching wildlife documentaries and making animal tracks in the garden at home. After high school, Nick spent a year teaching sport in England and then returned to South Africa to study Engineering at Stellenbosch University. It was in the mountains of Stellenbosch where Nick further cultivated his passion for nature.

For the past 35 years I've been amazed and inspired by wildlife from all corners of the world. Following a career in the City of London I now dedicate my time to wildlife photographer and commitment to wildlife conservation. When not travelling I volunteer for Conservation Organisations based in London. Social Media - www.janeaddey.co.uk & @addeyphotos.

Matt was privileged enough to grow up in the Lowveld and its surroundings, sparking a great love for nature and all it has to offer, be it the sunsets, vast landscapes or amazing wildlife. As a young boy, his favourite trips were always going to the bush with family, spending time with only the best that Africa has to offer.

Matt discovered a passion that went hand-in-hand with his love for wildlife, Photography, and this is how he found his path leading to Londolozi from 2016 to 2020.

Richie is Londolozi's Director of Technology and Sustainability and the founder of the Londolozi blog. Over the past decade he has built Londolozi's online ecosystem into a platform for advocacy of the restoration and rewilding of the natural world. Today he applies that same thinking to the land itself, helping lead the Save the Sand initiative to restore the Sand River catchment that gives Londolozi its lifeblood. His work lives at the meeting point of ancient wisdom, modern technology and nature. You'll find him in the LCH at Londolozi. Come say hi on your next visit.

As a young boy growing up on an agricultural farm in Zimbabwe, Sean spent every opportunity entertaining himself outdoors, camping in the local nature reserve and learning about all facets of the natural world.  

After completing a Bachelor of Science degree in Environmental Science in Cape Town, Sean was free to follow his nature ambitions and return to his bush-loving childhood dreams, which led him to Londolozi.

Going into semi-retirement on the guiding front in 2020 saw Sean settle into a far more permanent role in the LCH, focusing his efforts on producing media content for the Londolozi online space.

Garrett has always had an incredible love for the wilderness and found his way to Londolozi straight after University. After spending time as a Londolozi Camp Manager, the incredible stories of daily sightings from his ranger counterparts and guests alike pushed him to become a Londolozi Guide, where he enjoyed 3 years in the field sharing Londolozi with thousands of guests. After a brief sabbatical travelling through Southern Africa and working in Tanzania, Garrett returned to the Londolozi Family as Sales Manager sharing Londolozi with as many people as possible.

Nick was a ranger at Londolozi from 2018 - 2022. He always had a love for nature. Growing up in Johannesburg, the annual family trip to the bush (particularly the Kruger Lowveld region of South Africa) became an escape from city life. When he and his brother weren't physically in the bush, they would pretend they were by watching wildlife documentaries and making animal tracks in the garden at home. After high school, Nick spent a year teaching sport in England and then returned to South Africa to study Engineering at Stellenbosch University. It was in the mountains of Stellenbosch where Nick further cultivated his passion for nature.

For the past 35 years I've been amazed and inspired by wildlife from all corners of the world. Following a career in the City of London I now dedicate my time to wildlife photographer and commitment to wildlife conservation. When not travelling I volunteer for Conservation Organisations based in London. Social Media - www.janeaddey.co.uk & @addeyphotos.

acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
This leopard is the only cub the Tamboti female has so far raised to independence. Her male sibling disappeared at the age of around 4 months, but the Island female survived long enough to begin establishing her own territory at the end of 2015.

She was independent relatively early on, making her first recorded kill at only 8 months old; a young impala lamb near Sunset Bend Clearing.

As of early 2016 we are still unsure exactly where she will settle down, as the areas she is viewed in most often lie sandwiched between the territories of three other females; her mother, the Nkoveni female and the Ndzanzeni female. It is quite possible she will establish territory further east and sighting frequency could decline.
acf.lol_territory_desc: Still expanding her areas of movement and yet to properly establish herself, this female seems to be attempting to settle in eastern Sparta. She is focusing her attention around the Maxabene drainage line, which has proven an ideal area for leopards over the past few decades. This area also has large, substantial trees that serve as ideal vantage points and hoisting sites.

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: A young female who was not often seen during her time on Londolozi, owing to her inhabiting a not-often traversed section of the property.
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
A young female who was not often seen during her time on Londolozi, owing to her inhabiting a not-often traversed section of the property. The far north-east has few roads, and sightings of this female were few and far between.

She was easily recognised by her pink nose and the distinct notch in her left ear.  She was born in 2007 to the Campbell Koppies female, herself a daughter of the legendary Sunset Bend female.  A few of her recorded 5 litters have been viewed briefly, but so far only one cub seems to have survived; a female from the 2014 litter. A further litter was viewed briefly during winter of 2015 but disappeared shortly afterwards.

After not having been seen for a few months, reports from the reserves north of Londolozi indicated that this female was raising a litter of three at the beginning of 2016. Sadly however, her condition was also reported as very poor, and it was theorised that she may have been bitten by a snake.

After more than a month with no sightings on any reserve in the Sabi Sands, it was accepted that she, along with her young litter, had perished.
acf.lol_territory_desc: This female held a territory over eastern Marthly. A lack of roads in this area as well as her movements into our neighbours north and east of our property meant this was a leopard we did not see very regularly. Dense drainage lines and combretum woodlands also meant she often moved through this area unnoticed.
acf.lol_status_deceased_desc: Seen in very poor condition then no further sightings. Possible snakebite.

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: Sister of Tugwaan Male, this secretive female evaded us and very little was known about her. Successfully raised the Totowa Female
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
Named after the Ximpalapala Koppie in the north due to her spending a lot of time around that area.

Heritage & Lineage

Born in 2001 to the Short Tailed Female
Sister to the Tugwaan Male
Bloodline continued through the Tatowa Female
Part of a successful northern leopard lineage

Territory

Initially  grew up in neighboring Othawa property
Expanded eastward into NW Londolozi after Nyelethi Female’s death (2011)
Core territory centred around:

Ximpalapala Koppie
Northwestern sectors
Areas with limited vehicle access

The territory was characterized by rocky outcrops and dense vegetation

Physical Characteristics

4:4 spot pattern
Notably wary demeanor around vehicles
Distinctive furtive movement patterns

Reproductive History
Most notable offspring:

Early 2012: Three cubs (litter including Tatowa Female)

Two cubs lost to Gowrie Male
Tatowa Female successfully reached independence

Successfully raised at least one female to continue the lineage

Behavioural Notes

Remained extremely elusive and skilled at avoiding detection throughout her life
Mastered use of challenging terrain to maintain privacy
Maintained limited habituation despite years of territory overlap with vehicles
Exhibited strategic den site selection in rocky areas
Demonstrated excellent maternal abilities despite skittish nature
Specialized in utilizing areas with minimal vehicle access
Showed slight relaxation around vehicles only in her final years

Historical Significance

Represented successful adaptation to human presence while maintaining wild nature
Demonstrated how unhabituated leopards could thrive alongside the viewed population
Successfully raised the Tatowa Female who became more relaxed than her mother
Provided valuable insights into leopard behaviour in less-viewed areas
Her story highlighted the diversity of leopard personalities at Londolozi
Legacy continued through more relaxed offspring

Her disappearance in 2016 marked the end of an era in northwestern Londolozi, opening territory for the Ingrid Dam Female and her daughter. Through her daughter the Tatowa Female, her genes continued in the population, though manifesting in a more relaxed individual. Her story served as a reminder that even in an area known for viewable leopards, some individuals maintained their secretive nature while still successfully raising the next generation.

lol_family_litters.lol_family_litters_desc: Three cubs. All female. Two presumed killed by Gowrie male.

acf.lol_territory_desc: A leopard named after a rocky outcrop in western Marthly, where she has been encountered in the past. It seems she established a territory to the west of Londolozi and expanded it to include the western section of Marthly upon the death of the Nyelethi female. Due to the inaccessibility of this rocky section, the dense thickets surrounding it and her fairly skittish nature, this is not a leopard we see particularly often but the area does provide her with a multitude of game to hunt, including the rock dwelling Klipspringer.
acf.lol_status_deceased_desc: Cause of death unknown. Not seen in latter half of 2016 so presumed dead.

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: Initially skittish female who transformed into a regular presence. Made history by raising first intact litter since her own generation.
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
Heritage & Lineage

Born in June 2011 to the Tutlwa Female and sired by the Marthly Male, she represents the continuing strength of the Sunsetbend lineage. Part of a litter of two, she and her brother (who later dispersed) were one of the rare examples of both cubs reaching independence successfully.

Territory

Currently maintains territory in northwestern Sparta and southwestern Marthly, spanning from the Londolozi Camps across to Singita. Her territory represents a portion of her mother’s former range, exemplifying the common practice of female leopards ceding territory to their daughters. This region includes significant portions of the Sand River system and its associated drainages.

Physical Characteristics

3:2 spot pattern
Distinctive pink nose with spots in it
Currently notable limp on back left leg

Reproductive History

The Nhlanguleni Female has shown remarkable persistence in her reproductive efforts:

Successful Offspring:

March 2018: Nkuwa Female and Finfoot Female (first intact litter successfully raised since her own generation)

Notable Attempts:

November 2015: Two cubs denned in Sand River (litter lost)
October 2017: One cub denned in Sand River (litter lost)
March 2018: Intact litter raised- Nkuwa Female and Finfoot Female
Mid-late 2019: Two cubs denned in Sand River (litter lost)
January 2020: Two cubs denned at Mhangeni Double Crossing (litter lost)
August 2020: One cub denned in Sand River (litter lost)
March 2022: Two cubs denned in Sand River then Mhangeni Double Crossing (litter lost)
January 2023: One cub seen at Mhangeni Double Crossing (litter lost)
June 2023: Two cubs at Mhangeni Double Crossing (lost to hyenas)
August 2024: Cub moved to Mhangeni Double Crossing (litter lost)

Current Status

Maintains a presence in her territory despite now suffering from a significant limp in her back left leg. Despite this physical challenge, she continues to demonstrate reproductive persistence after numerous setbacks. Her successful raising of the Nkuwa and Finfoot Females remains a significant achievement in recent Londolozi leopard history.

Behavioural Notes

Her journey from a skittish, rarely-seen leopard to a regularly viewed individual is a testament to the patience of Londolozi’s tracking team. Only beginning to relax around vehicles in 2015 at age 4, her transformation can be attributed to the consistent, sensitive viewing practices employed by guides and trackers. Her early years spent in the relatively inaccessible sections of the Sand River shaped her initial wary nature.

Historical Significance

The Nhlanguleni Female’s successful raising of an intact litter (Nkuwa and Finfoot females) marks a significant milestone, being the first time this had been achieved since her own generation. This success has particular importance for the continuation of the Sunsetbend lineage, with her daughter the Nkuwa Female now establishing herself as a territorial female in her own right. Her story demonstrates both the challenges and potential successes in leopard conservation, particularly regarding the habituation process and the importance of genetic continuity in the population.

acf.lol_territory_desc: The Nhlanguleni female holds territory around north-west Sparta. Despite spending a majority of her time in the short grasslands of western Londolozi, she has been consistently shifting her territory further north and east to incorporate parts of the Sand River. This leopard particularly favours hunting and moving in the dense riverine bush making her difficult to find at times; her presence only known by the multitude of alarm calls that follow in her wake.

users_spotted.user_description: Amanda is the Head of Marketing at Londolozi & has been in the marketing & creative industry for 16 years & the health and wellness industry for 10 years. She holds a Bachelor’s degree in Psychology and Journalism from The University of Cape Town & an Honours degree in Brand Management. She's a Life Coach, an Enneagram Practitioner & Londolozi's photographer in residence. Her passion for the creative world, wilderness & wellness has led to a unique role within the Londolozi Family. She spearheaded the creation of the Photographic Studio & brings specialty retreat offerings to life at Londolozi. Amanda ensures that marketing always has deep experience at its roots.

An environment rich in photographers helped him develop the photographic skills he needed to start capturing some great images, and 2015 saw him make the move from stills photography into film as well.

James was a member of the Londolozi family from 2010 - 2021.

When I was 25, I spent 15 months in South Africa, in a small town called Harrismith well known to those who drive from Johannesburg to Durban as it is a classic pit stop to refuel. It is then that I first heard about Londolozi when I bought the book "the leopards of Londolozi" and promised myself that 1 day I could fulfill my dream of visiting. It took me exactly 20 years after I had moved back to France and in April 2017, at last, I brought my wife and 9-year son Antoine to what I now consider to be the nicest place on earth: Londolozi. Richie is Londolozi's Director of Technology and Sustainability and the founder of the Londolozi blog. Over the past decade he has built Londolozi's online ecosystem into a platform for advocacy of the restoration and rewilding of the natural world. Today he applies that same thinking to the land itself, helping lead the Save the Sand initiative to restore the Sand River catchment that gives Londolozi its lifeblood. His work lives at the meeting point of ancient wisdom, modern technology and nature. You'll find him in the LCH at Londolozi. Come say hi on your next visit.

Here at Londolozi in awe.
I fell in love with S. Africa in 2014 and returned again in 2018.  My next visit will be May, 2019.  My husband and I can’t get enough.  His hobby is photography and I am a professional artist.

I came here for the 1st time with my husband in Feb 2010, 2nd stop on a Vic Falls-Londolozi-Cape Town trip. I'd wanted to come here for years, as my ambition was to see a leopard in the wild. We looked at the cost, thought "ouch!" then - well it is just a one-off! On our 1st game drive  we saw Vomba, so mission achieved. Then the next morning we saw Camp Pan mating with Nottens! Within 24 hours of arriving we were completely smitten, and knew we not only had to come back, but come back the next year. So began a highly expensive addiction, and my trip 3 weeks ago was my 9th consecutive year and I celebrated my 100th game drive!

I left a successful corporate career 18 months ago to explore my passion for the bush.  The last year has been incredible having completed my field guide training and travelled extensively to some of Southern Africa's best safari destinations!

Bronwyn is 4th generation custodian of Londolozi Game Reserve, a mother, Master life coach and also one of its most longstanding employees, having grown up on the floors of the kitchen and in the gardens of the lodge. As a young boy growing up on an agricultural farm in Zimbabwe, Sean spent every opportunity entertaining himself outdoors, camping in the local nature reserve and learning about all facets of the natural world.  

After completing a Bachelor of Science degree in Environmental Science in Cape Town, Sean was free to follow his nature ambitions and return to his bush-loving childhood dreams, which led him to Londolozi.

Going into semi-retirement on the guiding front in 2020 saw Sean settle into a far more permanent role in the LCH, focusing his efforts on producing media content for the Londolozi online space.

Garrett has always had an incredible love for the wilderness and found his way to Londolozi straight after University. After spending time as a Londolozi Camp Manager, the incredible stories of daily sightings from his ranger counterparts and guests alike pushed him to become a Londolozi Guide, where he enjoyed 3 years in the field sharing Londolozi with thousands of guests. After a brief sabbatical travelling through Southern Africa and working in Tanzania, Garrett returned to the Londolozi Family as Sales Manager sharing Londolozi with as many people as possible.

Nick was a ranger at Londolozi from 2018 - 2022. He always had a love for nature. Growing up in Johannesburg, the annual family trip to the bush (particularly the Kruger Lowveld region of South Africa) became an escape from city life. When he and his brother weren't physically in the bush, they would pretend they were by watching wildlife documentaries and making animal tracks in the garden at home. After high school, Nick spent a year teaching sport in England and then returned to South Africa to study Engineering at Stellenbosch University. It was in the mountains of Stellenbosch where Nick further cultivated his passion for nature.

California native, travel junkie, animal lover...... have traveled to Africa over a dozen times to fulfill my passion for observing animals in their natural environment. Londolozi has become my favorite place to stay, with almost yearly visits since 2019.

Robbie developed a passion for the African bush from many visits to his family’s small holding in a greater conservancy just outside Johannesburg. Living in the big city his whole life, he always found refuge in the outdoors and has grown to appreciate the slower pace of life and connectivity with nature that comes with spending time in the bush. After completing his studies in Finance and Accounting at university in Cape Town he leapt at the opportunity to follow his dream by partaking in Londolozi’s 2020 ranger training programme. His dream of sharing his passion for the African bush with others is being lived and will continue to evolve as he furthers his career as a guide at Londolozi.

Robyn grew up in Johannesburg and every family holiday was spent exploring the Lowveld or camping around Southern Africa. Her love of nature and conservation propelled her to complete her Masters degree at the University of Edinburgh’s school of Geoscience. Although this gave her a great understanding of world-wide ecological processes, she wanted to develop a better knowledge of smaller elements in the environment closer to home - birds, trees, animals and the landscape in South Africa. This lead her back to the Lowveld and to the place where her love of nature was originally ignited when she was younger.

Growing up in the small coastal town of Mtunzini, Matt's childhood was shaped by endless hours spent exploring the forests, beaches and wetlands that sparked a lifelong passion for wildlife. After completing a BSc degree, he worked in construction and landscaping before the opportunity to join Londolozi changed the course of his career. Today, as a ranger and wildlife photographer, he has the privilege of spending every day immersed in the wilderness that first inspired him as a child.

For the past 35 years I've been amazed and inspired by wildlife from all corners of the world. Following a career in the City of London I now dedicate my time to wildlife photographer and commitment to wildlife conservation. Self proclaimed Leopardographer.

Guided by an unwavering love for photography, videography, and the captivating realm of visuals, Megan hopes to impart a unique and vibrant essence to each of the creative projects she takes on.

After a few years of working in the world of economic consulting, Kate’s love of adventure, wilderness and sense of curiosity led her to move away from the city and join the Londolozi guiding team. Kate has been fortunate to travel to many different corners of the world but she’ll argue that nothing quite beats being surrounded by nature watching an African sunrise or sunset, especially at Londolozi!

Nick grew up in Johannesburg with a deep love for the outdoors. After finishing high school, he spent a formative gap year in the Zimbabwean bushveld — an experience that cemented his passion for wildlife and conservation. Although he went on to study and build a career in corporate real estate, the pull of the wilderness never faded. Now an experienced member of the Londolozi guiding team, Nick finds the greatest joy in tracking leopards and immersing himself in the intricate world of birding. He has developed a strong passion for wildlife photography, always looking to capture authentic moments in the wild.

I am a published author and wildlife and travel writer, specializing is African safaris.  I have always had a deep affinity with all living creatures, even while growing up in urban Amsterdam. Going on safari has enhanced that innate connection into a lifelong passion.

section_profile.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: Initially skittish female who transformed into a regular presence. Made history by raising first intact litter since her own generation.
section_profile.lol_basic_profile_excerpt_alt: Initially skittish she spent a lot of time in the Sand River, now relaxed she makes up the majority of leopard viewing west of camp.
section_profile.lol_basic_profile_content:
Heritage & Lineage

Born in June 2011 to the Tutlwa Female and sired by the Marthly Male, she represents the continuing strength of the Sunsetbend lineage. Part of a litter of two, she and her brother (who later dispersed) were one of the rare examples of both cubs reaching independence successfully.

Territory

Currently maintains territory in northwestern Sparta and southwestern Marthly, spanning from the Londolozi Camps across to Singita. Her territory represents a portion of her mother’s former range, exemplifying the common practice of female leopards ceding territory to their daughters. This region includes significant portions of the Sand River system and its associated drainages.

Physical Characteristics

3:2 spot pattern
Distinctive pink nose with spots in it
Currently notable limp on back left leg

Reproductive History

The Nhlanguleni Female has shown remarkable persistence in her reproductive efforts:

Successful Offspring:

March 2018: Nkuwa Female and Finfoot Female (first intact litter successfully raised since her own generation)

Notable Attempts:

November 2015: Two cubs denned in Sand River (litter lost)
October 2017: One cub denned in Sand River (litter lost)
March 2018: Intact litter raised- Nkuwa Female and Finfoot Female
Mid-late 2019: Two cubs denned in Sand River (litter lost)
January 2020: Two cubs denned at Mhangeni Double Crossing (litter lost)
August 2020: One cub denned in Sand River (litter lost)
March 2022: Two cubs denned in Sand River then Mhangeni Double Crossing (litter lost)
January 2023: One cub seen at Mhangeni Double Crossing (litter lost)
June 2023: Two cubs at Mhangeni Double Crossing (lost to hyenas)
August 2024: Cub moved to Mhangeni Double Crossing (litter lost)

Current Status

Maintains a presence in her territory despite now suffering from a significant limp in her back left leg. Despite this physical challenge, she continues to demonstrate reproductive persistence after numerous setbacks. Her successful raising of the Nkuwa and Finfoot Females remains a significant achievement in recent Londolozi leopard history.

Behavioural Notes

Her journey from a skittish, rarely-seen leopard to a regularly viewed individual is a testament to the patience of Londolozi’s tracking team. Only beginning to relax around vehicles in 2015 at age 4, her transformation can be attributed to the consistent, sensitive viewing practices employed by guides and trackers. Her early years spent in the relatively inaccessible sections of the Sand River shaped her initial wary nature.

Historical Significance

The Nhlanguleni Female’s successful raising of an intact litter (Nkuwa and Finfoot females) marks a significant milestone, being the first time this had been achieved since her own generation. This success has particular importance for the continuation of the Sunsetbend lineage, with her daughter the Nkuwa Female now establishing herself as a territorial female in her own right. Her story demonstrates both the challenges and potential successes in leopard conservation, particularly regarding the habituation process and the importance of genetic continuity in the population.

Cubs only viewed for a few months to the west of camp.
Cubs spent a fair amount of time to the west of Londolozi camps. Cubs were then all of a sudden no longer seen so presumed to not have survived.
Only one cub ever seen and only found by chance while feeding on a carcass during the day at the age of about three and a half months old.
Initially denned in the Sand River, she moved the cubs to a number of different dens int he first two months. Eventually settling back at Mhangeni Double-crossing in April.

section_territory.lol_territory_desc: The Nhlanguleni female holds territory around north-west Sparta. Despite spending a majority of her time in the short grasslands of western Londolozi, she has been consistently shifting her territory further north and east to incorporate parts of the Sand River. This leopard particularly favours hunting and moving in the dense riverine bush making her difficult to find at times; her presence only known by the multitude of alarm calls that follow in her wake.

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: Daughter of Sunset Bend Female, this resilient leopard raised at least 5 cubs to independence before a tragic end defending her final litter
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
Named after the Shangaan word xidulu for termite mound.

Heritage & Lineage

Born October 2001 to the Sunset Bend Female
Inherited distinctive golden coat of the Sunset Bend lineage
Sister to Ravenscourt Female
Successfully continued prestigious bloodline through multiple offspring

Territory

Although her initial territory covered much of eastern Londolozi to our eastern neighbours (where she was called the Kikilezi Female), she subsequently moved steadily north and east and was seldom encountered on Londolozi leading up to her death.
The territory included diverse terrain from dense riverine thickets along Sand River to the wide open clearings dotted with numerous termite mounds.

Physical Characteristics

2:3 spot pattern
Rich golden coat characteristic of Sunset Bend lineage
Athletic build maintained into senior years
Distinctive ageing features in later life, such as tattered ears and sunken eyes.

Reproductive History
Demonstrated remarkable success as a mother, raising at least five cubs to independence:

2013: Piccadilly Female and Sibuye Female
2016: Three Rivers Female, a male sibling also survived and dispersed (cubs approximately 11 months old at the time of her death)

Behavioural Notes

Exceptional mother even in advanced age
Known for fierce defence of territory and cubs
Skilled at utilizing dense riverine vegetation for denning
Notable for aggressive defence of kills against other leopards
Successfully navigated complex territorial dynamics with neighbouring females

Historical Significance

A crucial link in perpetuating the Sunset Bend lineage
Successfully raised cubs in areas with the  highest predator density
Demonstrated exceptional parenting abilities into advanced age
The final act of defending cubs at age 16 exemplified maternal dedication
Her story highlighted the challenges faced by ageing leopards
The legacy continued through multiple surviving offspring
Provided valuable insights into leopard maternal behaviour

Her death in 2017 at the hands of male lions, possibly while defending her cubs, marked the end of a remarkable life that exemplified the resilience and maternal dedication of Londolozi’s leopards. At almost 16 years old, she had successfully navigated one of the most predator-rich environments to raise multiple generations of cubs, contributing significantly to the continuation of the prestigious Sunset Bend lineage.

users_spotted.user_description: Bob and I live in the San Francisco Bay Area where we enjoy boating, hiking, photography and travel. After many trips to Eastern and Southern Africa, we are pleased to call Londolozi our 'African home!'

Amanda is the Head of Marketing at Londolozi & has been in the marketing & creative industry for 16 years & the health and wellness industry for 10 years. She holds a Bachelor’s degree in Psychology and Journalism from The University of Cape Town & an Honours degree in Brand Management. She's a Life Coach, an Enneagram Practitioner & Londolozi's photographer in residence. Her passion for the creative world, wilderness & wellness has led to a unique role within the Londolozi Family. She spearheaded the creation of the Photographic Studio & brings specialty retreat offerings to life at Londolozi. Amanda ensures that marketing always has deep experience at its roots.

When I was 25, I spent 15 months in South Africa, in a small town called Harrismith well known to those who drive from Johannesburg to Durban as it is a classic pit stop to refuel. It is then that I first heard about Londolozi when I bought the book "the leopards of Londolozi" and promised myself that 1 day I could fulfill my dream of visiting. It took me exactly 20 years after I had moved back to France and in April 2017, at last, I brought my wife and 9-year son Antoine to what I now consider to be the nicest place on earth: Londolozi. As I couldn't help myself, we came back this year for another 4 days of pure happiness
The Londolozi Photo Studio

Born in New York and settled down in Hong Kong for the past 20 years after living in London and Tokyo.  I "found" Londolozi in 2009 and have been a regular visitor since.  Over that time I have gained a passion for the bush and the photographic opportunities it provides.  Thanks to the tutelage of the Londolozi rangers and Creative hub I am getting my photography to an acceptable level.

I came here for the 1st time with my husband in Feb 2010, 2nd stop on a Vic Falls-Londolozi-Cape Town trip. I'd wanted to come here for years, as my ambition was to see a leopard in the wild. We looked at the cost, thought "ouch!" then - well it is just a one-off! On our 1st game drive  we saw Vomba, so mission achieved. Then the next morning we saw Camp Pan mating with Nottens! Within 24 hours of arriving we were completely smitten, and knew we not only had to come back, but come back the next year. So began a highly expensive addiction, and my trip 3 weeks ago was my 9th consecutive year and I celebrated my 100th game drive!

Our first visit was in 2011, we returned in 2014, then again in 2017, and again in 2018.  It is favorite place to be.  We plan on coming 2020 for my 70th birthday (3/2/50) and our 50th wedding anniversary (9/5/70)
We recently visited with our daughter's family, including 8 yr old granddaughter.  She is still talking about all the wonderful things that she saw on Safari.  We were worried that it might be a little gory for her, but she reacted with vigor to the most gruesome of events.  We plan a return visit in 2020 - that will be our 5th trip to visit this incredible place where the guides, trackers, and all the staff make this such a memorable experience for all that visit.
Alan and I have been ambassadors for many years, this is our favorite place on earth ?

As a young boy growing up on an agricultural farm in Zimbabwe, Sean spent every opportunity entertaining himself outdoors, camping in the local nature reserve and learning about all facets of the natural world.  

After completing a Bachelor of Science degree in Environmental Science in Cape Town, Sean was free to follow his nature ambitions and return to his bush-loving childhood dreams, which led him to Londolozi.

Going into semi-retirement on the guiding front in 2020 saw Sean settle into a far more permanent role in the LCH, focusing his efforts on producing media content for the Londolozi online space.

Garrett has always had an incredible love for the wilderness and found his way to Londolozi straight after University. After spending time as a Londolozi Camp Manager, the incredible stories of daily sightings from his ranger counterparts and guests alike pushed him to become a Londolozi Guide, where he enjoyed 3 years in the field sharing Londolozi with thousands of guests. After a brief sabbatical travelling through Southern Africa and working in Tanzania, Garrett returned to the Londolozi Family as Sales Manager sharing Londolozi with as many people as possible.

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: Abandoned at 1 year old, this resilient female transformed from hunting squirrels to survive into one of Londolozi's most successful mothers
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
Named after the prominent dry riverbed flowing through the central parts of Londolozi- the Maxabene River

Heritage & Lineage

Born January 1998 to the Mhangeni Female
Daughter of a female who herself showed remarkable resilience after being blinded by a spitting cobra
Her survival story as a young leopard became legendary at Londolozi
Part of the River Female lineage

Territory

Established domain around the central Maxabene riverbed
Core territory centred in the heart of Londolozi
Notable for maintaining valuable central territory despite her small size
The territory included prime hunting grounds around central drainage systems

Physical Characteristics

2:2 spot pattern
Notably small for a female leopard
Distinctive ageing features in later years
Remarkable agility despite small stature

Reproductive History
Had at least 17 cubs across 9 litters, with four reaching independence:
Successful Offspring:

2002: Female reached independence but believed to have died shortly after on mange in the western sector.
2006: Maxabene 3:3 Male (dispersed southeast)
2008: Tu-tones 3:2 Male and Makhotini 3:3 Male (both reached independence)

Other Attempts:

2001: One cub (presumed drowned)
2002: Two cubs (male killed at 2 months, female died of mange)
2004: Two cubs (both died)
2005: Two cubs (killed by Manyeleti Male and Sparta pride)
2007: Three cubs (one killed by Vomba Young Male, two killed in Sand River)
2007: Two cubs (both killed)
2012: Final cub (lost when mother disappeared)

Behavioural Notes

Demonstrated extraordinary survival instincts from a young age
Known for surviving two weeks alone in a tree by hunting squirrels
The first major kill (impala) at 12.5 months marked a turning point in her life
Exceptional mother despite the small size
Notable for providing for cubs well beyond typical independence age
Worked cooperatively with male leopard during a hunt

Historical Significance

Her early survival story inspired many
Successfully raised multiple male offspring who established territories
Her territory remained crucial to Londolozi’s leopard dynamics
Last seen in October 2012 north of the Sand River while mating with Marthly Male
Her story serves as a testament to the determination and adaptability of leopards
Legacy lives on through her male offspring who established territories of their own

Her disappearance in 2012, following a bold venture north of her territory, while mating with the Marthly Male, marked the end of an era at Londolozi. Her remarkable journey from an abandoned cub to a successful mother, despite her small size, remains one of the most inspiring stories in Londolozi’s leopard history.

acf.lol_territory_desc: With a long, thin territory this female was eventually named after the land she claimed along the Maxabene Riverbed in central Sparta. Guests still speak to this day of the magnificent viewing she provided with her youngsters in this drainage line; playing and hunting amongst its tall, well-established trees.

I am a wildlife, nature, and scenic photographer, living in Castro Valley, California, in the East Bay. Previously, I worked full time for Applied Biosystems and Life Technologies as a senior business analyst. I left this position in 2010 to concentrate on my true passion for nature photography. My Photography Website is https://dreamcatcherimages.net/ You can see my recent images on my Flickr Photostream at https://www.flickr.com/photos/brucefinocchio/ I also post my best images now on Instagram, at https://www.instagram.com/brucefinocchio/

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: Initially calm and graceful, this resilient female overcame partial blindness to continue hunting and raising cubs in western Londolozi.
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
Heritage & Lineage
First encountered in 1991 as an adult leopard, the origins of the Mhangeni Female remain unknown. Though her early lineage is unclear, she established an important bloodline through her daughter, the Maxabene Female, and her son, the Mhangeni Male.
Territory

Originally established in western Londolozi
Gradually pushed further west by her daughter, the Maxabene Female
Maintained territory in western Sparta extending into Castleton
Notable for defending territory despite visual impairment

Physical Characteristics

2:3 spot pattern
Most recognizable feature was her milky right eye (from 2002 cobra encounter)
Distinctive disability made her easily identifiable
Known for calm demeanour around vehicles

Reproductive History
Demonstrated persistence in reproduction despite numerous setbacks:
Successful Offspring:

January 1998: Maxabene Female (female cub reached independence despite early abandonment)
June 2000: Mhangeni Male (reached independence at 2 years)

Other Attempts:

June 1996: Two cubs (killed by spotted hyenas)
January 1997: Two cubs (killed by lions)
January 1998: Male cub killed by lions
June 2000: Female cub died at 6 months

Behavioural Notes

Remarkably calm nature around vehicles despite challenges
Adapted hunting techniques after losing sight in one eye, demonstrated remarkable resilience after cobra encounter.
Known for rarely hoisting kills, which may have contributed to cub losses
Maintained territorial behaviour despite visual impairment
Sometimes abandoned cubs earlier than typical.

Historical Significance

Proved leopards could adapt to significant physical challenges
Contributed to Londolozi’s leopard population through two successful offspring
Demonstrated the challenges of raising cubs in a predator-rich environment
Her story highlights the constant threats faced by leopards
Through the Maxabene Female, her bloodline continued in the area

Her story serves as a testament to the resilience of leopards, showing how they can adapt to severe injuries while continuing to hunt and raise cubs in challenging conditions. Her legacy lives on through her daughter, the Maxabene Female, who went on to establish herself in prime territory.

lol_family_litters.lol_family_litters_desc: Male cub killed by lions at four months. Female survived.
Both cubs killed by spotted hyena
Both cubs killed by lion; male at four months, female at nine months.
Male and female. Female died at six months. Male survived.

acf.lol_territory_desc: This female held territory around western Sparta and into Castleton. These areas are predominantly open grassland and thus lack a huge amount of cover. This serves as a good example of how adaptable these cats are, as the Mhangeni female was very successful huntress. There are a number of Marula trees in this area that would have helped as vantage and hoisting points.
