acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: Born 1984, fierce daughter of Mother Leopard. Her unpredictable nature challenged rangers, legacy lived on through 3:4 Female.
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
Named after the Tugwaan Drainage central in her territory

Heritage & Lineage
Born in April 1984 to the original Mother Leopard, representing an intriguing contrast to her mother’s relaxed nature. Despite her aggressive temperament, she proved to be a crucial link in Londolozi’s most prestigious leopard lineage through her daughter, the 3:4 Female.

Territory
Established territory in and around the Tugwaan riverbed shortly after reaching independence at about one year of age. Her territory would later be inherited by her daughter, the 3:4 Female, maintaining the family’s presence in this significant area.

Physical Characteristics

2:3 spot pattern
Notably aggressive posture around vehicles
Commanding presence that demanded respect

Reproductive History
Most notable offspring:

1992: Gave birth to the legendary 3:4 Female
Known as an excellent mother despite her fierce nature
High success rate in raising cubs

Behavioural Notes
Famous for her unpredictable and often aggressive nature:

Completely relaxed at night but notoriously aggressive during the day
Would charge vehicles and people on foot without warning
Required special vehicle positioning techniques for safe viewing
Never fully habituated despite 16 years of viewing
Demonstrated remarkable contrast between daytime and nighttime behaviour
Required elaborate safety protocols for tracking on foot

Historical Significance
The Tugwaan Female represents a fascinating chapter in Londolozi’s leopard history:

Proved that even direct descendants of habituated leopards can maintain wild tendencies
Demonstrated the individual nature of leopard personalities
Successfully raised the 3:4 Female who would become one of Londolozi’s most photographed leopards
Became legendary among rangers and trackers for her unpredictable nature
Her reputation lives on in ranger stories and analogies
Served as a constant reminder of leopards’ true wild nature despite habituation

Her legacy extends beyond her fearsome reputation through her daughter, the 3:4 Female, who showed that an aggressive mother could produce a remarkably relaxed offspring, challenging assumptions about inherited behaviour in leopards.

Fate unknown. Cubs were very shy and few records exist.

acf.lol_territory_desc: Her territory fell around southern Sparta/northern Dudley with the core around the Tugwaan drainage line. This area of Londolozi is dense with vegetation, especially around the drainage line where it remains fairly green year round. This made tracking this notoriously aggressive leopard even more hair raising because she was typically only spotted at very close quarters.

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: The original viewable leopard of Londolozi, if not Africa. In 1979 this leopard appeared as if by magic, allowing vehicles to view her.
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
She did not announce herself. She simply stayed.

In 1979, on a morning that looked like every other morning in the Sabi Sand, a young female leopard was found in the drainage lines south of the Londolozi camps. She was watchful and uncertain — but she did not run. That single choice, made by a wild animal on no particular morning, changed the course of Londolozi’s history more completely than anything that came before or after it.

John Varty and tracker Elmon Mhlongo spent the next twelve years of their lives following her. They adjusted their hours to match hers, sleeping through the heat of the day to be with her at night. They documented her hunts, her cubs, her territorial movements. In doing so, they captured moments no camera had ever been permitted to see, including the first filmed mating sequence of wild leopards ever recorded. That footage became Silent Hunter, the documentary that brought Londolozi to the attention of the world.

She had a 2:2 spot pattern and a temperament that became legendary. Over the course of her life, she raised nine litters, from which twelve cubs reached independence, a breeding record that remains unmatched at Londolozi. Through her daughters and their daughters, she founded a dynasty that now reaches eight generations. Her descendants include the 3:4 Female, the Dudley Riverbank Female, and the Ndzanzeni Female.

She died in 1991 at approximately sixteen years of age. The exact circumstances were never determined. She had, by then, done something that no one had believed possible: she had demonstrated that trust between a wild leopard and a human being was not only possible, but repeatable. Her cubs were habituated to vehicles. Their cubs were habituated. And so it continued, generation by generation, until the leopard-viewing that Londolozi is known for today became simply the way things were.

There is nothing at Londolozi that marks where she walked or what she left behind. There doesn’t need to be. Her legacy is not something you can point to, it is something you feel the moment a leopard holds your gaze from a branch above the road and does not look away. That feeling, repeated across five decades and thousands of people, is what she began. Every morning that a tracker follows fresh prints in the sand of the Maxabene, it continues. Every afternoon that a leopard holds a visitor’s gaze without looking away, it continues still.
acf.lol_territory_desc: The Mother Leopard held territory around central Sparta for the duration of her life. The Maxabene drainage line, where this female was first seen, lay at the heart of the territory and provided her with ideal hunting opportunities on its heavily vegetated banks, whilst the tangled root systems provided den sites in which to raise her cubs. Today this still area remains as heavily contested territory for both male and female leopards.

users_spotted.user_description: I arrived at Londolozi on 1 st December 1998. I was a trainee ranger and I was green behind the ears. Londolozi became my family and my home. I left in 2005 and returned later that year to get married down in the Sand River at Londolozi. I have been very fotunate to return with my wife every year since then and I have a son who is mad about tracking and anti-poaching thanks to the many hours he has spent wit me in the bush.

Our first visit was in 2011, we returned in 2014, then again in 2017, and again in 2018.  It is favorite place to be.  We plan on coming 2020 for my 70th birthday (3/2/50) and our 50th wedding anniversary (9/5/70)
We recently visited with our daughter's family, including 8 yr old granddaughter.  She is still talking about all the wonderful things that she saw on Safari.  We were worried that it might be a little gory for her, but she reacted with vigor to the most gruesome of events.  We plan a return visit in 2020 - that will be our 5th trip to visit this incredible place where the guides, trackers, and all the staff make this such a memorable experience for all that visit.

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: The Gowrie male first appeared in the Sabi Sands around 2011. Judging by his size, he is estimated to have been born around 2005/6.
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
The Gowrie male first appeared in the Sabi Sands around 2011, and was reportedly quite skittish. This makes it likely that he was born in the Kruger Park and grew up unused to vehicles. His dispersal into the private game reserve system as a young male meant he soon began being viewed regularly and began to relax around vehicles as a result. Judging by his size when he was first viewed, he is estimated to have been born around 2005/2006, although it is impossible to say for sure.

As he moved into the northern parts of Londolozi in 2012, he began putting pressure on the dominant and much older Marthly male, who was forced to retreat slowly, conceding territory all the time and eventually being forced south of the Sand River altogether. The Gowrie male’s arrival was ill-timed as far as the local female population was concerned, as the Tutlwa and Ximpalapala females were raising litters at the time, both of which were believed to have been killed by the Gowrie male.

The Gowrie male subsequently became dominant over the whole of Marthly, even being seen on the Southern bank of the river on a few occasions. Then, in mid-2015, sightings of him suddenly dried up. No tracks moved through the Manyelethi River and his territorial call was heard no more.

Eventually it was accepted that he was dead, through causes unknown. A part of a leopard’s lower jaw was found in the Manyelethi riverbed near Marthly Pools, but as the displaced Marthly male had been seen in the area only a few months previously, it remains unclear who the jaw belonged to.

lol_id_markings.lol_id_markings_marking: Orange eyes, scar next to single spot on his left cheek

acf.lol_territory_desc: This male established himself as the dominant male in the north of Londolozi on the section known as Marthly. He would move between the northern bank of the Sand River, with its profileration of game, through the rocky sections of central Marthly and through the seasonal Manyelethi River to our northern boundary. His territory had many females falling within it; a major drawing factor for a dominant male leopard.

Bob and I live in the San Francisco Bay Area where we enjoy boating, hiking, photography and travel. After many trips to Eastern and Southern Africa, we are pleased to call Londolozi our 'African home!'
Talley Smith's father. Resident of Bermuda. Huge fan of Londolozi and Africa generally. Keen amateur photographer.
An Zambian by birth, I am a passionate amateur wildlife photographer, a lover of all things in the African bush and a huge fan of Londolozi and all it offers!

Richie is Londolozi's Director of Technology and Sustainability and the founder of the Londolozi blog. Over the past decade he has built Londolozi's online ecosystem into a platform for advocacy of the restoration and rewilding of the natural world. Today he applies that same thinking to the land itself, helping lead the Save the Sand initiative to restore the Sand River catchment that gives Londolozi its lifeblood. His work lives at the meeting point of ancient wisdom, modern technology and nature. You'll find him in the LCH at Londolozi. Come say hi on your next visit.

I came here for the 1st time with my husband in Feb 2010, 2nd stop on a Vic Falls-Londolozi-Cape Town trip. I'd wanted to come here for years, as my ambition was to see a leopard in the wild. Within 24 hours of arriving we were completely smitten, and knew we not only had to come back, but come back the next year. So began a highly expensive addiction, and my trip 3 weeks ago was my 9th consecutive year and I celebrated my 100th game drive!

We plan a return visit in 2020 - that will be our 5th trip to visit this incredible place where the guides, trackers, and all the staff make this such a memorable experience for all that visit.
Alan and I have been ambassadors for many years, this is our favorite place on earth ?

Garrett has always had an incredible love for the wilderness and found his way to Londolozi straight after University. After spending time as a Londolozi Camp Manager, the incredible stories of daily sightings from his ranger counterparts and guests alike pushed him to become a Londolozi Guide, where he enjoyed 3 years in the field sharing Londolozi with thousands of guests. After a brief sabbatical travelling through Southern Africa and working in Tanzania, Garrett returned to the Londolozi Family as Sales Manager sharing Londolozi with as many people as possible.

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: Incredibly, the 5:5 male was adopted as a cub by his grandmother, the 3:4 female, and raised by her to adulthood.
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
The story of this leopard has become the stuff of legend. Feeding off a kill with his mother as a cub, the 5:5 young male was somehow adopted by the 3:4 female after she brought her cub to feed on the same kill. Unbelievably, this old leopard took it upon herself to raise this cub of her daughter, and it was solely thanks to her efforts that he survived to independence. A further twist in the tale was that when the 3:4 female was old and becoming infirm, the 5:5 male was seen sharing kills with her on multiple occasions. Male leopards are not known for sharing kills with females, but the fact that this male repeatedly did so with the 3:4 female suggests some very strong tie not previously documented in leopards in the wild.

Upon approaching full size, the 5:5 male began encroaching into the Camp Pan male’s territory around the Londolozi camps, and for a while looked set to establish himself and topple the older male, but the disappearance of the Emsagwen 4:6 male in the east left a territory vacant, and the 5:5 male simply headed there instead. He has remained there to this day, despite losing the use of his left eye, possibly in a fight with another leopard.

As of mid 2015 the 5:5 male has started being seen in a number of spots far outside his usual territory, suggesting that he is under pressure from other another male(s) or has already been ousted.

He is believed to have killed the October 2015 litter of the Tamboti female.
acf.lol_territory_desc: A male that claimed territory fairly easily in eastern Marthly upon the disappearance of the Emsagwen male. We continue to see this male occasionally around the eastern portion of Londolozi, both north and south of the Sand River.
acf.lol_status_deceased_desc: Mauled by Tsalala pride in Manyelethi River. Died of his wounds.

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: This male moved in from the north of the reserve in 2010, and was instantly recognisable by his unique tuft of fur at the back of his neck.
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
This unmistakeable male began being viewed more regularly from 2010 onwards, pushing in from the north of the reserve and forcing the dominant Camp Pan male out. His characteristic mane and notched right ear were easily recognisable. Almost immediately upon his encroachment into the territories of the females along the river, they all began falling pregnant, providing further evidence to support the theory that the ageing Camp Pan male may have become infertile in his old age.

The Marthly male quickly established himself as the dominant male along the Sand River towards the end of 2011, and the Camp Pan male was forced further south.

Towards the end of 2012 the slightly younger Gowrie male began encroaching from the north, forcing the Marthly male to consolidate his territory along an east-west line through the centre of the Marthly property. Venturing as far south as the Maxabene river, the territory was still large enough to allow for adequate mating access to females.

By mid-2014 however, the Marthly male was hardly ever viewed north bank of the Sand River, yet he continued to be be active between the Maxabene and Londolozi Camps.

Caught between the newly arrived Piva and Inyathini males in the south and the 4:4 male to the west, the Marthly male was eventually forced out of his territory altogether, and was nomadic as of the beginning of 2015.

Forced to keep a low profile, avoiding other big males in the area, his condition steadily deteriorated and he was viewed for the last time on Londolozi in winter of 2015, very undernourished and with a number of injuries.

It is assumed that he died shortly after, as after one or two sightings on other properties, he was not seen again.

acf.lol_territory_desc: This male found himself sandwiched between a number of other dominant males throughout his life but managed to hold territory in Marthly, along the Sand River and later northern Sparta. In his later years, he spent a great deal of time south of the Sand River and north of Main Road where there are a number of prominent termite mounds. He would use these as vantage points as well as easy spots to sit and stake out warthog burrows.

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: A beautiful male with a distinctive “V” shape on his forehead, the Tugwaan male was dominant for many years over a huge territory.
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
A beautiful male with a distinctive “V” shape on his forehead, the Tugwaan male was dominant for many years over a huge territory that stretched from beyond the Sand River in the east almost to the western boundary of the Sabi Sand.

Born to the Short-tailed female in Marthly in 2001 in the same litter as the Ximpalapala female, he began moving south and east, establishing himself during the latter part of 2004 in the eastern sections of Londolozi.

From there his territorial shift was southwards, possibly due to pressure from the bigger Camp Pan male.

The Tugwaan male in his prime held territory centred along the Tugwaan riverbed, which is where he got his name, but he was encountered as north of the Maxabene and even beyond Londolozi’s southern borders.

In later life he suffered from the knock-on effect of an influx of males from the north. The Marthly male pushed south, which in turn forced the Camp Pan male south, which led the the Tugwaan male being displaced to the south and east of Londolozi and rarely seen.

At the time of writing the Tugwaan male is 15 years old and in the twilight of his life. Although it is difficult to assign paternity to cubs, as females will mate with multiple males, it is almost certain that the Tugwaan male sired the Ndzanzeni female, and has done his part to incorporate his genes in the royal lineage of Londolozi.
acf.lol_territory_desc: Males typically have a much larger territory than females but the Tugwaan male had a particularly large one that stretched almost the width of the Sabi Sands, incorporating many habitat types. With the movement of other dominant males in his later years, his territory was shifted to south-east Dudley and south of that towards the Sabie River, still prime habitat for leopard.

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: Born to the Vomba Female, this elusive leopard dominant in the north would often go weeks without being seen.
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
Heritage & Lineage

Born March 2006 to the Vomba Female
Sired by Camp Pan Male
Part of the prestigious Sunset Bend lineage
Sister to the Mashaba Female from separate litters
Carried forward the distinctive golden coat of her lineage

Territory

Established territory north of Sand River
The core area centred around Manyelethi River
Territory included:

Dense riverine vegetation
Rolling savannah crests
Multiple drainage systems
Strategic denning sites in rocky outcrops

Notable for utilizing challenging terrain that limited vehicle access

Physical Characteristics

4:3 spot pattern
Rich golden coat characteristic of Sunset Bend lineage
Known for graceful movement through difficult terrain
Distinctive notch in left ear

Reproductive History
Had at least seven litters with a minimum of 13 cubs:

2010: Single cub (did not survive)
2011: Two cubs (Nhlanguleni Female + male reached independence)
2013: Two cubs (both lost)
2014: Three cubs (killed by Marthly Male)
2015: Single cub (fate unknown)
2016: Suspected final litter when killed by Tsalala Pride

Most notable success:

Nhlanguleni Female (2011) who established territory and continued lineage

Behavioural Notes

Extremely elusive despite territory proximity to the lodge
Masterful at utilizing dense vegetation for concealment
Known for raising particularly skittish cubs
Excellent use of terrain features for denning and hunting
Skilled hunter of bushbuck and nyala in riverine habitat
Demonstrated remarkable aggression in territorial defence
Notable for squatting behaviour to see over tall grass

Historical Significance

Demonstrated successful adaptation to challenging terrain
An important link in Sunset Bend lineage through Nhlanguleni Female
Provided insights into leopard behaviour in difficult terrain
Showed the  importance of den site selection in cub survival
Death while defending cubs exemplified maternal dedication
Her story highlighted the challenges of raising cubs in a predator-rich environment

Her death in 2016, likely defending her cubs from the Tsalala Pride, marked the end of a remarkable life that exemplified both the challenges and adaptations required of leopards in Londolozi’s northern territories. Through her daughter the Nhlanguleni Female, her legacy and genes continue to influence the leopard population.

lol_family_litters.lol_family_litters_desc: Denned near Mhangeni Double Crossing. Cub lost at around 3-4 months
Very skittish cubs as kept in Sand River with limited vehicle viewing.
Drowned in flooding of Manyelethi River, aged approx. 12 days
Denned off Marthly pools. Killed by nomadic Marthly male.
One cub viewed briefly in Sand River opp. Granite Camp
Litter never seen. Lost in May 2016.
Killed by Gowrie male in 2014, aged just under one year. Male cub consumed by Gowrie male.

acf.lol_territory_desc: This leopard has set up territory in the Sand river and into southern Marthly, north of the camps. During the summer months she can be seen hunting in the tall grasslands just north of the river, shifting towards the Sand or Manyelethi Rivers at drier times in the year.
acf.lol_status_deceased_desc: Attacked by Tsalala Pride in Sand River opposite Granite Camp. Not seen again.

Rich golden coat characteristic of Sunset Bend lineage
Known for graceful movement through difficult terrain
Distinctive notch in left ear

Reproductive History
Had at least seven litters with a minimum of 13 cubs:

2010: Single cub (did not survive)
2011: Two cubs (Nhlanguleni Female + male reached independence)
2013: Two cubs (both lost)
2014: Three cubs (killed by Marthly Male)
2015: Single cub (fate unknown)
2016: Suspected final litter when killed by Tsalala Pride

Most notable success:

Nhlanguleni Female (2011) who established territory and continued lineage

Behavioural Notes

Extremely elusive despite territory proximity to the lodge
Masterful at utilizing dense vegetation for concealment
Known for raising particularly skittish cubs
Excellent use of terrain features for denning and hunting
Skilled hunter of bushbuck and nyala in riverine habitat
Demonstrated remarkable aggression in territorial defence
Notable for squatting behaviour to see over tall grass

Historical Significance

Demonstrated successful adaptation to challenging terrain
An important link in Sunset Bend lineage through Nhlanguleni Female
Provided insights into leopard behaviour in difficult terrain
Showed the  importance of den site selection in cub survival
Death while defending cubs exemplified maternal dedication
Her story highlighted the challenges of raising cubs in a predator-rich environment

Her death in 2016, likely defending her cubs from the Tsalala Pride, marked the end of a remarkable life that exemplified both the challenges and adaptations required of leopards in Londolozi’s northern territories. Through her daughter the Nhlanguleni Female, her legacy and genes continue to influence the leopard population.

Very skittish cubs as kept in Sand River with limited vehicle viewing.
Drowned in flooding of Manyelethi River, aged approx. 12 days
Denned off Marthly pools. Killed by nomadic Marthly male.
One cub viewed briefly in Sand River opp. Granite Camp
Litter never seen. Lost in May 2016.
Killed by Gowrie male in 2014, aged just under one year. Male cub consumed by Gowrie male.

section_territory.lol_territory_desc: This leopard has set up territory in the Sand river and into southern Marthly, north of the camps. During the summer months she can be seen hunting in the tall grasslands just north of the river, shifting towards the Sand or Manyelethi Rivers at drier times in the year.

users_spotted.user_description: Richie is Londolozi's Director of Technology and Sustainability and the founder of the Londolozi blog. Over the past decade he has built Londolozi's online ecosystem into a platform for advocacy of the restoration and rewilding of the natural world. Today he applies that same thinking to the land itself, helping lead the Save the Sand initiative to restore the Sand River catchment that gives Londolozi its lifeblood. Bob and I live in the San Francisco Bay Area where we enjoy boating, hiking, photography and travel. After many trips to Eastern and Southern Africa, we are pleased to call Londolozi our 'African home!'

An environment rich in photographers helped him develop the photographic skills he needed to start capturing some great images, and 2015 saw him make the move from stills photography into film as well.

James was a member of the Londolozi family from 2010 - 2021.

Originally from New York USA currently living in the Sunshine state of Florida in the Tampa Bay area. My first trip to Africa was in 2009 when I visited  Botswana and Zambia. My first trip to Sabi Sands South Africa was in 2011. This is where my true addiction began. I stayed at Londolozi Varty camp and fell in love with the people and the animals.  Since then I have been back six more times and returning Sept. 2023 for my 7th . I have written several blogs and enjoy sharing photos and experiences from my trips. Leopards and male lions are my favorite to photograph. At home I have my own little family including my black lion Myra and two wild dogs Max and Jack.

I came here for the 1st time with my husband in Feb 2010, 2nd stop on a Vic Falls-Londolozi-Cape Town trip. I'd wanted to come here for years, as my ambition was to see a leopard in the wild. We looked at the cost, thought "ouch!" then - well it is just a one-off! On our 1st game drive  we saw Vomba, so mission achieved. Then the next morning we saw Camp Pan mating with Nottens! Within 24 hours of arriving we were completely smitten, and knew we not only had to come back, but come back the next year. So began a highly expensive addiction, and my trip 3 weeks ago was my 9th consecutive year and I celebrated my 100th game drive!

Lucie and I are retired and have turned our energies to photography and videography, of which wildlife is by far the favorite subject.  We have been to Africa every 2-3 years over the last 35 years.  We have been to several camps in each of South Africa, Botswana, Kenya, Tanzania, Namibia, Uganda and Rwanda but Londolozi and Tiger Canyon are our go-to favorite places.  We are unabashedly predator-centric and aviary-sated.  And we are so thankful that the Varty family built this community-driven concept and has taught us all the meaning of "ubuntu".

Being surrounded by wilderness from a young age, you experience it in all of its essence. Matt was privileged enough to grow up in the Lowveld and its surroundings, sparking a great love for nature and all it has to offer, be it the sunsets, vast landscapes or amazing wildlife. As a young boy, his favourite trips were always going to the bush with family, spending time with only the best that Africa has to offer.

Matt discovered a passion that went hand-in-hand with his love for wildlife, Photography, and this is how he found his path leading to Londolozi from 2016 to 2020.

Our first visit was in 2011, we returned in 2014, then again in 2017, and again in 2018.  It is favorite place to be.  We plan on coming 2020 for my 70th birthday (3/2/50) and our 50th wedding anniversary (9/5/70)
We recently visited with our daughter's family, including 8 yr old granddaughter.  She is still talking about all the wonderful things that she saw on Safari.  We were worried that it might be a little gory for her, but she reacted with vigor to the most gruesome of events.  We plan a return visit in 2020 - that will be our 5th trip to visit this incredible place where the guides, trackers, and all the staff make this such a memorable experience for all that visit.
Alan and I have been ambassadors for many years, this is our favorite place on earth ?

Garrett has always had an incredible love for the wilderness and found his way to Londolozi straight after University. After spending time as a Londolozi Camp Manager, the incredible stories of daily sightings from his ranger counterparts and guests alike pushed him to become a Londolozi Guide, where he enjoyed 3 years in the field sharing Londolozi with thousands of guests. After a brief sabbatical travelling through Southern Africa and working in Tanzania, Garrett returned to the Londolozi Family as Sales Manager sharing Londolozi with as many people as possible.

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: Powerful descendant of Saseka Female, a skilled huntress defied odds by raising intact litter of three cubs to independence in Londolozi.
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
Heritage & Lineage

Born in 2003 to the Saseka Female
Carried forward the impressive hunting abilities of her bloodline
Notable for her notched left ear
Established a significant presence in northern territories

Territory

Initially inhabited her mother’s territory north of Londolozi boundary
Established control over western and southern portions of mother’s range in 2008
Core territory centered around western bank of Manyelethi River
Known for utilizing dense riverine vegetation
Territory particularly rich in prey species

Physical Characteristics

4:4 spot pattern
Notched left ear
Large, powerful build

Reproductive History
Successful Offspring:

March 2008: Two females (one killed by Newington Male, Mbilo Female killed by Majingilane males in 2010)
July 2009: Three cubs (rare intact litter of three reached independence):

Nanga Female (3:3)
Nyelethi Male (4:3)
Nyelethi Young Male (3:2)

 

Behavioural Notes

Exceptional hunter known for devastating efficiency
Remarkable mother who successfully raised three cubs simultaneously
Utilized dense riverine vegetation for denning and hunting
Demonstrated excellent maternal care, particularly evident in raising triple litter

Historical Significance

Successfully raised one of the few recorded intact litters of three cubs
Demonstrated exceptional maternal abilities despite challenging conditions
Her territory selection and hunting prowess enabled the successful raising of multiple cubs
The legacy continues through descendants, particularly through the Nanga Female
Provided valuable insights into maternal behaviour through extensive documentation
Her successful triple litter challenged the conventional understanding of leopard cub survival rates

Her disappearance in 2011 marked the end of an era in northern Londolozi, but her legacy lives on through her offspring, particularly her daughter the Nanga Female who went on to establish territory in similar areas.
acf.lol_territory_desc: In her later years, this female established her territory around western and central Marthly, focusing her time around the Manyelethi River. With pools of water, dense vegetation, rocky sections, overhanging roots, a plethora of visiting game and a soft sand in which to hunt silently, many leopards have made this part of Londolozi their home and will continue to do so in the future.

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: Distinguished by her striking golden coat, this exceptional mother established a dynasty that would come to dominate Londolozi's Sand River
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
Heritage & Lineage

Born August 1992
Origins remain the subject of discussion (possibly the daughter of Tugwaan Female)
Founder of the prestigious Sunset Bend lineage
Her distinctive golden coat became a hallmark of her descendants

Territory

Established territory in the eastern sector of Londolozi
Core territory centred around Sunset Bend road
Dominated eastern Maxabeni River region
The territory included prime Sand River frontage

Physical Characteristics

2:2 spot pattern
Distinctive rich golden coat that became legendary
Large and powerful build
Deliberate and unhurried in movement

Reproductive History
Demonstrated remarkable success in reproduction with 14 cubs across 6 litters:
Successful Offspring:

December 1997: Vomba Female (3:2)
October 1999: Three cubs (male lost in floods, Xidulu and Ravenscourt females survived)
November 2001: Three cubs (male taken by a crocodile, two females reached independence)
2005: Three cubs (one young male killed by a rival male, one Young Male survived)
2007: Final litter (Tamboti Female remained near mother into adulthood)

Behavioural Notes

Known for relaxed demeanour around vehicles
Exceptional mother who successfully raised multiple females
Demonstrated remarkable hunting abilities
Characterized by deliberate and unhurried movements
Adapted well to vehicle presence while maintaining wild nature
Known for a considered and methodical approach to hunting

Historical Significance

Established one of Londolozi’s most successful leopard dynasties
Her bloodline came to dominate Sand River territories
Golden coat characteristics passed through multiple generations
The legacy lives on through numerous descendants:

Vomba Female
Xidulu Female
Ravenscourt Female
Extended through granddaughters including Tutlwa, Mashaba females

The final days showed her resilience, attempting to steal from lions despite fatal consequences
Contributed significantly to Londolozi’s reputation for leopard viewing
Her lineage continues to influence leopard dynamics along the Sand River

Her death in 2010, following injuries sustained from the Sparta pride while attempting to steal a meal, marked the end of an era but not the end of her influence. Through her daughters and their offspring, the distinctive golden coat and strong territorial presence of the Sunset Bend bloodline continues to define the leopard population of Londolozi’s Sand River region.

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: The Tamboti female inhabited the south-eastern sections of Londolozi, having a large part of her territory along the Maxabene Riverbed.
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
The Tamboti female was another of the Sunset Bend lineage that displayed the beautiful golden coat of her mother.

Born on Londolozi in 2007, she moved east of our boundary after attaining independence, but in 2011 began moving back west and further south, pressurising the older females who were territorial at the time. Initially taking over the eastern areas of the Maxabene female’s territory, she eventually moved south to put pressure onto the Dudley Riverbank female, and came to dominate much of the south eastern section of the reserve, from Tsessebe clearing in the west down to Tshabalala Pan in the south, with the Sand River forming her eastern territorial boundary.

Although female leopards can give birth from the age of three onwards, it took far longer than that for the Tamboti female to reproduce for the first time, and she was almost six years old when she finally had her first litter. Two cubs were born in early 2013, one of which survived and is territorial today.

Two further litters were lost; one born in early 2015 and a second in late 2015, which was killed by the Dudley Riverbank 5:5 male in January of 2016.

The Tamboti female spent a large amount of her timing hunting along the Maxabene riverbed, although sightings of her in the early parts of 2016 were fewer in number than in previous years.

She was viewed with great consistency during the majority of 2017 and early 2018 during which time she was raising a young female, but the Tamboti female disappeared in the winter of 2018 after sustaining injuries in what was a suspected lion attack. The cub survived to independence.

acf.lol_territory_desc: This leopard's territory falls predominantly in eastern Sparta and Dudley, with her using the Maxabene drainage line and Sand River for hunting opportunities and den sites. There is a distinct lack of rocky sections though, which may be one of the reasons she struggles to raise youngsters, and she has been seen using fallen root systems and aardvark holes as den sites instead.

section_profile.lol_basic_profile_excerpt_alt: The Tamboti female inhabited the south-eastern sections of the reserve, having a large part of her territory along the Maxabene Riverbed.
section_profile.lol_basic_profile_content:
The Tamboti female was another of the Sunset Bend lineage that displayed the beautiful golden coat of her mother.

Born on Londolozi in 2007, she moved east of our boundary after attaining independence, but in 2011 began moving back west and further south, pressurising the older females who were territorial at the time. Initially taking over the eastern areas of the Maxabene female’s territory, she eventually moved south to put pressure onto the Dudley Riverbank female, and came to dominate much of the south eastern section of the reserve, from Tsessebe clearing in the west down to Tshabalala Pan in the south, with the Sand River forming her eastern territorial boundary.

Although female leopards can give birth from the age of three onwards, it took far longer than that for the Tamboti female to reproduce for the first time, and she was almost six years old when she finally had her first litter. Two cubs were born in early 2013, one of which survived and is territorial today.

Two further litters were lost; one born in early 2015 and a second in late 2015, which was killed by the Dudley Riverbank 5:5 male in January of 2016.

The Tamboti female spent a large amount of her timing hunting along the Maxabene riverbed, although sightings of her in the early parts of 2016 were fewer in number than in previous years.

She was viewed with great consistency during the majority of 2017 and early 2018 during which time she was raising a young female, but the Tamboti female disappeared in the winter of 2018 after sustaining injuries in what was a suspected lion attack. The cub survived to independence.

acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
Heritage & Lineage

Born in March 2012 to the Dudley Riverbank Female and sired by the Tugwaan Male, the Ndzanzeni Female holds a particularly special place in Londolozi’s leopard dynasty. As the great, great-granddaughter of the original Mother Leopard, she represents one of the few remaining direct descendants of this historic lineage. Her birth as a single cub was actually advantageous – her mother, at almost 14 years old, could focus all her energy on raising this sole offspring, typical of older leopards who rarely successfully raise more than one cub at that age.

Territory

Following in her mother’s footsteps, she initially established herself in the territory that the Dudley Riverbank Female once controlled in the deep south and east of Londolozi. Her current range stretches from the Sand River all the way across to the western grasslands. She has shown remarkable stability in maintaining this territory, remaining in roughly the same area since reaching independence.

Physical Characteristics

Distinctive 4:3 spot pattern
Historically recognizable by her noticeable limp on the back left leg

Reproductive History

The Ndzanzeni Female has demonstrated remarkable persistence in her reproductive efforts:

Successful Offspring:

Tortoise Pan Male (August 2016) – Her greatest success story and currently the only offspring raised to independence

Notable Attempts:

December 2015: Two cubs (only seen once at around 2 months before loss)
August 2016: Two cubs at Python Rocks (female cub lost, male survived – Tortoise Pan Male)
Mid 2020: Two cubs (litter lost at about 8 months)
Late 2021: Two cubs (male and female, lost at nine months old)
May 2022: Suspected den site (cubs never viewed)
March 2023: Suckle marks observed (den not located)
September 2023: Two cubs in Umkumbe (litter lost)
May 2024: Denned in Sand River then Piva drainage (litter lost)
November 2024: Suspected den site (cubs never viewed)

Current Status

Continues to maintain her territory successfully in the southern regions of Dudley. Her recovery from a severe leg injury that nearly prevented her from walking demonstrates her exceptional resilience. Despite several setbacks with recent litter, she continues to contribute to the population dynamics of the area.

Behavioural Notes

Perhaps her most remarkable achievement was successfully raising the Tortoise Pan Male while suffering from a debilitating injury to her back left leg. During this period, she could barely put weight on the leg, yet managed to hunt and provide for her cub. This display of determination and adaptability speaks to the incredible resilience of these cats.

Historical Significance

The Ndzanzeni Female’s story is one of remarkable success against the odds. Born as a single cub to an ageing mother, discovered by skilled tracker Freddy Ngobeni at Paul’s Crossing, and going on to successfully raise her own cub despite severe injury, she embodies the resilience of Londolozi’s leopards. As one of the few remaining direct descendants of the Mother Leopard lineage, she represents a crucial link to Londolozi’s leopard history, maintaining the legacy through her son, the Tortoise Pan Male.

acf.lol_territory_desc: A leopard who holds territory in south-east Dudley, essentially having adopted her late mother's territory. This area has a range of different habitat types including grassland, riverine and mixed woodland. Whilst trying to raise her first litter she spent the vast majority of her time in the Tugwaan drainage, close to where her mother denned her and thus an area she is very familiar with.

Bronwyn’s official title is that of Londolozi’s Creative Director and as such she has spearheaded the reinvention of the Londolozi brand from 2007 until present day. In 2018, Bronwyn led the creation of the Londolozi Healing House, establishing one of the safari industry’s most innovative wellness offerings.  By weaving healing, mindfulness, and nature-based transformation into the guest experience, she helped reinvent the concept of wilderness wellness in the safari space.

Nick was a ranger at Londolozi from 2018 - 2022. He always had a love for nature. Growing up in Johannesburg, the annual family trip to the bush (particularly the Kruger Lowveld region of South Africa) became an escape from city life. When he and his brother weren't physically in the bush, they would pretend they were by watching wildlife documentaries and making animal tracks in the garden at home. After high school, Nick spent a year teaching sport in England and then returned to South Africa to study Engineering at Stellenbosch University. It was in the mountains of Stellenbosch where Nick further cultivated his passion for nature.

Robbie developed a passion for the African bush from many visits to his family’s small holding in a greater conservancy just outside Johannesburg. Living in the big city his whole life, he always found refuge in the outdoors and has grown to appreciate the slower pace of life and connectivity with nature that comes with spending time in the bush. After completing his studies in Finance and Accounting at university in Cape Town he leapt at the opportunity to follow his dream by partaking in Londolozi’s 2020 ranger training programme. His dream of sharing his passion for the African bush with others is being lived and will continue to evolve as he furthers his career as a guide at Londolozi.

California native, travel junkie, animal lover...... have traveled to Africa over a dozen times to fulfill my passion for observing animals in their natural environment. Londolozi has become my favorite place to stay, with almost yearly visits since 2019.

Robyn grew up in Johannesburg and every family holiday was spent exploring the Lowveld or camping around Southern Africa. Her love of nature and conservation propelled her to complete her Masters degree at the University of Edinburgh’s school of Geoscience. Although this gave her a great understanding of world-wide ecological processes, she wanted to develop a better knowledge of smaller elements in the environment closer to home - birds, trees, animals and the landscape in South Africa. This lead her back to the Lowveld and to the place where her love of nature was originally ignited when she was younger.

Growing up in the small coastal town of Mtunzini, Matt's childhood was shaped by endless hours spent exploring the forests, beaches and wetlands that sparked a lifelong passion for wildlife. After completing a BSc degree, he worked in construction and landscaping before the opportunity to join Londolozi changed the course of his career. Today, as a ranger and wildlife photographer, he has the privilege of spending every day immersed in the wilderness that first inspired him as a child.

After a few years of working in the world of economic consulting, Kate’s love of adventure, wilderness and sense of curiosity led her to move away from the city and join the Londolozi guiding team.  It was amidst her years of studying politics, philosophy and economics that her love of exploring and understanding different wilderness areas in South Africa compounded through trips with friends and family. Kate has been fortunate to travel to many different corners of the world but she’ll argue that nothing quite beats being surrounded by nature watching an African sunrise or sunset, especially at Londolozi!

Keagan has always had a connection with wildlife, having been lucky enough to visit Londolozi as a child. After growing up in Johannesburg, he attended boarding school in the KwaZulu Natal Midlands where weekends were spent exploring the reserve and appreciating his surroundings. Keagan further went on to study Engineering at the University of Cape Town, during which each holiday was spent with either family or friends in the Lowveld, solidifying his dream of becoming a ranger. Having joined the Londolozi team, he is now fulfilling his childhood dream of living and working in the African bush.

Nick grew up in Johannesburg with a deep love for the outdoors. After finishing high school, he spent a formative gap year in the Zimbabwean bushveld — an experience that cemented his passion for wildlife and conservation. Although he went on to study and build a career in corporate real estate, the pull of the wilderness never faded. Now an experienced member of the Londolozi guiding team, Nick finds the greatest joy in tracking leopards and immersing himself in the intricate world of birding. He has developed a strong passion for wildlife photography, always looking to capture authentic moments in the wild.

Megan grew up at Londolozi, where her love for nature blossomed. With a degree in Visual Studies and Social Media Marketing, her journey came full circle when she joined the dynamic Londolozi Creative Hub, where her love for nature and visuals finds its perfect home. 

Guided by an unwavering love for photography, videography, and the captivating realm of visuals, Megan hopes to impart a unique and vibrant essence to each of the creative projects she takes on.

Love nature, watching animals and going on safari. Been lots of times on safari to different African countries. Londolozi is one of my favourite places. I am always looking forward to my next trip to Londolozi!

I am a published author and wildlife and travel writer, specializing is African safaris.  I have always had a deep affinity with all living creatures, even while growing up in urban Amsterdam. Going on safari has enhanced that innate connection into a lifelong passion.

Born in March 2012 to the Dudley Riverbank Female and sired by the Tugwaan Male, the Ndzanzeni Female holds a particularly special place in Londolozi’s leopard dynasty. As the great, great-granddaughter of the original Mother Leopard, she represents one of the few remaining direct descendants of this historic lineage. Her birth as a single cub was actually advantageous – her mother, at almost 14 years old, could focus all her energy on raising this sole offspring, typical of older leopards who rarely successfully raise more than one cub at that age.

Territory

Following in her mother’s footsteps, she initially established herself in the territory that the Dudley Riverbank Female once controlled in the deep south and east of Londolozi. Her current range stretches from the Sand River all the way across to the western grasslands. She has shown remarkable stability in maintaining this territory, remaining in roughly the same area since reaching independence.

Physical Characteristics

Distinctive 4:3 spot pattern
Historically recognizable by her noticeable limp on the back left leg

Reproductive History

The Ndzanzeni Female has demonstrated remarkable persistence in her reproductive efforts:

Successful Offspring:

Tortoise Pan Male (August 2016) – Her greatest success story and currently the only offspring raised to independence

Notable Attempts:

December 2015: Two cubs (only seen once at around 2 months before loss)
August 2016: Two cubs at Python Rocks (female cub lost, male survived – Tortoise Pan Male)
Mid 2020: Two cubs (litter lost at about 8 months)
Late 2021: Two cubs (male and female, lost at nine months old)
May 2022: Suspected den site (cubs never viewed)
March 2023: Suckle marks observed (den not located)
September 2023: Two cubs in Umkumbe (litter lost)
May 2024: Denned in Sand River then Piva drainage (litter lost)
November 2024: Suspected den site (cubs never viewed)

Current Status

Continues to maintain her territory successfully in the southern regions of Dudley. Her recovery from a severe leg injury that nearly prevented her from walking demonstrates her exceptional resilience. Despite several setbacks with recent litter, she continues to contribute to the population dynamics of the area.

Behavioural Notes

Perhaps her most remarkable achievement was successfully raising the Tortoise Pan Male while suffering from a debilitating injury to her back left leg. During this period, she could barely put weight on the leg, yet managed to hunt and provide for her cub. This display of determination and adaptability speaks to the incredible resilience of these cats.

Historical Significance

The Ndzanzeni Female’s story is one of remarkable success against the odds. Born as a single cub to an ageing mother, discovered by skilled tracker Freddy Ngobeni at Paul’s Crossing, and going on to successfully raise her own cub despite severe injury, she embodies the resilience of Londolozi’s leopards. As one of the few remaining direct descendants of the Mother Leopard lineage, she represents a crucial link to Londolozi’s leopard history, maintaining the legacy through her son, the Tortoise Pan Male.

users_spotted.user_description: Richie is Londolozi's Director of Technology and Sustainability and the founder of the Londolozi blog. Over the past decade he has built Londolozi's online ecosystem into a platform for advocacy of the restoration and rewilding of the natural world. Today he applies that same thinking to the land itself, helping lead the Save the Sand initiative to restore the Sand River catchment that gives Londolozi its lifeblood. His work lives at the meeting point of ancient wisdom, modern technology and nature. You'll find him in the LCH at Londolozi. Come say hi on your next visit.

James had hardly touched a camera when he came to Londolozi, but his writing skills that complemented his Honours degree in Zoology meant that he was quickly snapped up by the Londolozi blog team. 

An environment rich in photographers helped him develop the photographic skills he needed to start capturing some great images, and 2015 saw him make the move from stills photography into film as well.

James was a member of the Londolozi family from 2010 - 2021.
The Londolozi Photo Studio

Mike Nicki Harry and Toby, we try to visit Londo once a year. We think of it as our second home and are privileged to have seen the most amazing sights, encountered wonderful animals and learned so much about the bush from some amazing guides and trackers with such knowledge.

Amanda is the Head of Marketing at Londolozi & has been in the marketing & creative industry for 16 years & the health and wellness industry for 10 years. She holds a Bachelor’s degree in Psychology and Journalism from The University of Cape Town & an Honours degree in Brand Management. She's a Life Coach, an Enneagram Practitioner & Londolozi's photographer in residence. Her passion for the creative world, wilderness & wellness has led to a unique role within the Londolozi Family. She spearheaded the creation of the Photographic Studio & brings specialty retreat offerings to life at Londolozi. Amanda ensures that marketing always has deep experience at its roots.

Keen hobbies:  wild life and nature photography, target shooting, learning to fly fish;
Favorite places: Londolozi, Grand Teton & Yellowstone National Parks

For the past 35 years I've been amazed and inspired by wildlife from all corners of the world. Following a career in the City of London I now dedicate my time to wildlife photographer and commitment to wildlife conservation. When not travelling I volunteer for Conservation Organisations based in London. Social Media - www.janeaddey.co.uk & @addeyphotos.

Passionate Londolozi Guests! Avid wildlife photographers. Supporters and advocates for the Good Work Foundation through the All Heart Fund in the USA. Restaurateurs and wine & spirits retailers in Sarasota, Florida at Michael’s On East (www.bestfood.com)

I arrived at Londolozi on 1 st December 1998. I was a trainee ranger and I was green behind the ears. Londolozi became my family and my home. I left in 2005 and returned later that year to get married down in the Sand River at Londolozi. I have been very fotunate to return with my wife every year since then and I have a son who is mad about tracking and anti-poaching thanks to the many hours he has spent wit me in the bush.

Born in New York and settled down in Hong Kong for the past 20 years after living in London and Tokyo.  I "found" Londolozi in 2009 and have been a regular visitor since.  Over that time I have gained a passion for the bush and the photographic opportunities it provides.  Thanks to the tutelage of the Londolozi rangers and Creative hub I am getting my photography to an acceptable level.

Bob and I live in the San Francisco Bay Area where we enjoy boating, hiking, photography and travel. After many trips to Eastern and Southern Africa, we are pleased to call Londolozi our 'African home!'
Serial Londo New Year visitor with Nicki and our sons Harry and Toby. Still tracking the Anderson male leopard.

I came here for the 1st time with my husband in Feb 2010, 2nd stop on a Vic Falls-Londolozi-Cape Town trip. I'd wanted to come here for years, as my ambition was to see a leopard in the wild. We looked at the cost, thought "ouch!" then - well it is just a one-off! On our 1st game drive  we saw Vomba, so mission achieved. Then the next morning we saw Camp Pan mating with Nottens! Within 24 hours of arriving we were completely smitten, and knew we not only had to come back, but come back the next year. So began a highly expensive addiction, and my trip 3 weeks ago was my 9th consecutive year and I celebrated my 100th game drive!
Alan and I have been ambassadors for many years, this is our favorite place on earth ?

Lucie and I are retired and have turned our energies to photography and videography, of which wildlife is by far the favorite subject.  We have been to Africa every 2-3 years over the last 35 years.  We have been to several camps in each of South Africa, Botswana, Kenya, Tanzania, Namibia, Uganda and Rwanda but Londolozi and Tiger Canyon are our go-to favorite places.  We are unabashedly predator-centric and aviary-sated.  And we are so thankful that the Varty family built this community-driven concept and has taught us all the meaning of "ubuntu".

Our first visit was in 2011, we returned in 2014, then again in 2017, and again in 2018.  It is favorite place to be.  We plan on coming 2020 for my 70th birthday (3/2/50) and our 50th wedding anniversary (9/5/70)
We recently visited with our daughter's family, including 8 yr old granddaughter.  She is still talking about all the wonderful things that she saw on Safari.  We were worried that it might be a little gory for her, but she reacted with vigor to the most gruesome of events.  We plan a return visit in 2020 - that will be our 5th trip to visit this incredible place where the guides, trackers, and all the staff make this such a memorable experience for all that visit.

Being surrounded by wilderness from a young age, you experience it in all of its essence. Matt was privileged enough to grow up in the Lowveld and its surroundings, sparking a great love for nature and all it has to offer, be it the sunsets, vast landscapes or amazing wildlife. As a young boy, his favourite trips were always going to the bush with family, spending time with only the best that Africa has to offer.

Matt discovered a passion that went hand-in-hand with his love for wildlife, Photography, and this is how he found his path leading to Londolozi from 2016 to 2020.
I fell in love with S. Africa in 2014 and returned again in 2018.  My next visit will be May, 2019.  My husband and I can’t get enough.  His hobby is photography and I am a professional artist.

Bronwyn is 4th generation custodian of Londolozi Game Reserve, a mother, Master life coach and also one of its most longstanding employees, having grown up on the floors of the kitchen and in the gardens of the lodge.  Bronwyn’s official title is that of Londolozi’s Creative Director and as such she has spearheaded the reinvention of the Londolozi brand from 2007 until present day. In 2018, Bronwyn led the creation of the Londolozi Healing House, establishing one of the safari industry’s most innovative wellness offerings.  By weaving healing, mindfulness, and nature-based transformation into the guest experience, she helped reinvent the concept of wilderness wellness in the safari space.

As a young boy growing up on an agricultural farm in Zimbabwe, Sean spent every opportunity entertaining himself outdoors, camping in the local nature reserve and learning about all facets of the natural world.  

After completing a Bachelor of Science degree in Environmental Science in Cape Town, Sean was free to follow his nature ambitions and return to his bush-loving childhood dreams, which led him to Londolozi.

Going into semi-retirement on the guiding front in 2020 saw Sean settle into a far more permanent role in the LCH, focusing his efforts on producing media content for the Londolozi online space.

Garrett has always had an incredible love for the wilderness and found his way to Londolozi straight after University. After spending time as a Londolozi Camp Manager, the incredible stories of daily sightings from his ranger counterparts and guests alike pushed him to become a Londolozi Guide, where he enjoyed 3 years in the field sharing Londolozi with thousands of guests. After a brief sabbatical travelling through Southern Africa and working in Tanzania, Garrett returned to the Londolozi Family as Sales Manager sharing Londolozi with as many people as possible.

Nick was a ranger at Londolozi from 2018 - 2022. He always had a love for nature. Growing up in Johannesburg, the annual family trip to the bush (particularly the Kruger Lowveld region of South Africa) became an escape from city life. When he and his brother weren't physically in the bush, they would pretend they were by watching wildlife documentaries and making animal tracks in the garden at home. After high school, Nick spent a year teaching sport in England and then returned to South Africa to study Engineering at Stellenbosch University. It was in the mountains of Stellenbosch where Nick further cultivated his passion for nature.

Robbie developed a passion for the African bush from many visits to his family’s small holding in a greater conservancy just outside Johannesburg. Living in the big city his whole life, he always found refuge in the outdoors and has grown to appreciate the slower pace of life and connectivity with nature that comes with spending time in the bush. After completing his studies in Finance and Accounting at university in Cape Town he leapt at the opportunity to follow his dream by partaking in Londolozi’s 2020 ranger training programme. His dream of sharing his passion for the African bush with others is being lived and will continue to evolve as he furthers his career as a guide at Londolozi.

California native, travel junkie, animal lover...... have traveled to Africa over a dozen times to fulfill my passion for observing animals in their natural environment. Londolozi has become my favorite place to stay, with almost yearly visits since 2019.

Robyn grew up in Johannesburg and every family holiday was spent exploring the Lowveld or camping around Southern Africa. Her love of nature and conservation propelled her to complete her Masters degree at the University of Edinburgh’s school of Geoscience. Although this gave her a great understanding of world-wide ecological processes, she wanted to develop a better knowledge of smaller elements in the environment closer to home - birds, trees, animals and the landscape in South Africa. This lead her back to the Lowveld and to the place where her love of nature was originally ignited when she was younger.

Growing up in the small coastal town of Mtunzini, Matt's childhood was shaped by endless hours spent exploring the forests, beaches and wetlands that sparked a lifelong passion for wildlife. After completing a BSc degree, he worked in construction and landscaping before the opportunity to join Londolozi changed the course of his career. Today, as a ranger and wildlife photographer, he has the privilege of spending every day immersed in the wilderness that first inspired him as a child.

After a few years of working in the world of economic consulting, Kate’s love of adventure, wilderness and sense of curiosity led her to move away from the city and join the Londolozi guiding team.  It was amidst her years of studying politics, philosophy and economics that her love of exploring and understanding different wilderness areas in South Africa compounded through trips with friends and family. Kate has been fortunate to travel to many different corners of the world but she’ll argue that nothing quite beats being surrounded by nature watching an African sunrise or sunset, especially at Londolozi!

Keagan has always had a connection with wildlife, having been lucky enough to visit Londolozi as a child. After growing up in Johannesburg, he attended boarding school in the KwaZulu Natal Midlands where weekends were spent exploring the reserve and appreciating his surroundings. Keagan further went on to study Engineering at the University of Cape Town, during which each holiday was spent with either family or friends in the Lowveld, solidifying his dream of becoming a ranger. Having joined the Londolozi team, he is now fulfilling his childhood dream of living and working in the African bush.

Nick grew up in Johannesburg with a deep love for the outdoors. After finishing high school, he spent a formative gap year in the Zimbabwean bushveld — an experience that cemented his passion for wildlife and conservation. Although he went on to study and build a career in corporate real estate, the pull of the wilderness never faded. Now an experienced member of the Londolozi guiding team, Nick finds the greatest joy in tracking leopards and immersing himself in the intricate world of birding. He has developed a strong passion for wildlife photography, always looking to capture authentic moments in the wild.

Megan grew up at Londolozi, where her love for nature blossomed. With a degree in Visual Studies and Social Media Marketing, her journey came full circle when she joined the dynamic Londolozi Creative Hub, where her love for nature and visuals finds its perfect home. 

Guided by an unwavering love for photography, videography, and the captivating realm of visuals, Megan hopes to impart a unique and vibrant essence to each of the creative projects she takes on.

Love nature, watching animals and going on safari. Been lots of times on safari to different African countries. Londolozi is one of my favourite places. I am always looking forward to my next trip to Londolozi!

I am a published author and wildlife and travel writer, specializing is African safaris.  I have always had a deep affinity with all living creatures, even while growing up in urban Amsterdam. Going on safari has enhanced that innate connection into a lifelong passion.

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: The King of Londolozi in his day; an enormous male whose offspring still inhabit the reserve.
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
One of the true legends of the Leopards of Londolozi, the Camp Pan male was dominant over a significant portion of the property for a good six years, longer than the average tenure expected of a male leopard in a hotly contested environment like the Sabi Sands.

Born in 2000 to the Tavangumi female, he spent a great deal of time around Singita’s Camp Pan during his formative months, which is where he got his name.

In 2007 he began pushing east into Londolozi and established himself almost overnight, pushing out the dominant Sparta 5:5 male in the process.
His territory was enormous, stretching from the Manyelethi River in the north to beyond the Maxabene River in the South. With the arrival of the Marthly male in 2010, the Camp Pan male was forced to start ceding territory in the north while consolidating territory in the south, but he was slowly but surely forced further and further south and east, eventually getting ousted altogether by the Piva male pushing in from the opposite direction.

The Camp Pan male had an interesting relationship with one of his sons, the Tu-Tones male, with whom he almost shared territory, tolerating his presence and not forcing him out as most males would their sons. The two males would be seen on the same kills and even mating with the same female at the same time.

During his reign the Camp Pan male fathered a number of eminently viewable leopards, including the Tutlwa and Mashaba females, ensuring that his legacy lives on.

He was last seen in the Spring of 2015.

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: Despite her small size, this daughter of the Nyelethi Female established herself as a significant presence in Londolozi's northern reaches.
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
Heritage & Lineage

Born June 2009 to the Nyelethi Female
Part of a rare intact litter of three cubs that reached independence
Carried forward the Saseka Female lineage
Success continued through daughter Makomsava Female

Territory
Primary domain included:

The northern bank of Sand River
Manyelethi River system
Southern Cross Koppies
Central to eastern Marthly
Shifted territory northward over time due to pressure from Tutlwa Female

Physical Characteristics

3:3 spot pattern
Notably small for an adult female
Three spots grouped closely together on the right cheek

Reproductive History
Demonstrated persistence despite numerous setbacks:

2013: Two cubs (one lost at 5 months, male forced to independence at 11 months)
2014: Two cubs (both lost, killed by Tutlwa Female)
2015: Single cub (lost at 4 months, killed by Tutlwa Female)
2016: Litter never seen

Most notable success:

2016: Makomsava Female (reached independence and established territory)

Behavioural Notes

Utilized Manyelethi River drainage lines extensively
Favored Southern Cross Koppies for denning sites
Maintained territory despite being one of the smaller females
Regularly moved between riverine and koppie systems
Showed preference for hunting in drainage line vegetation

Historical Significance

Successfully established territory at a young age following mother’s death
Maintained northern territory despite pressure from larger females
Faced unique challenges from female infanticide by Tutlwa Female
Legacy continues through Makomsava Female’s success
Provided early documentation of female leopard infanticide at Londolozi

Her death in 2019 marked the end of a decade-long presence in the northern territories. Through her daughter the Makomsava Female, her bloodline continues to influence Londolozi’s leopard population.

Originally from New York USA currently living in the Sunshine state of Florida in the Tampa Bay area. My first trip to Africa was in 2009 when I visited  Botswana and Zambia. My first trip to Sabi Sands South Africa was in 2011. This is where my true addiction began. I stayed at Londolozi Varty camp and fell in love with the people and the animals.  Since then I have been back six more times and returning Sept. 2023 for my 7th . I have written several blogs and enjoy sharing photos and experiences from my trips. Leopards and male lions are my favorite to photograph. At home I have my own little family including my black lion Myra and two wild dogs Max and Jack.
Alan and I have been ambassadors for many years, this is our favorite place on earth ?

Lucie and I are retired and have turned our energies to photography and videography, of which wildlife is by far the favorite subject.  We have been to Africa every 2-3 years over the last 35 years.  We have been to several camps in each of South Africa, Botswana, Kenya, Tanzania, Namibia, Uganda and Rwanda but Londolozi and Tiger Canyon are our go-to favorite places.  We are unabashedly predator-centric and aviary-sated.  And we are so thankful that the Varty family built this community-driven concept and has taught us all the meaning of "ubuntu".

Our first visit was in 2011, we returned in 2014, then again in 2017, and again in 2018.  It is favorite place to be.  We plan on coming 2020 for my 70th birthday (3/2/50) and our 50th wedding anniversary (9/5/70)
We recently visited with our daughter's family, including 8 yr old granddaughter.  She is still talking about all the wonderful things that she saw on Safari.  We were worried that it might be a little gory for her, but she reacted with vigor to the most gruesome of events.  We plan a return visit in 2020 - that will be our 5th trip to visit this incredible place where the guides, trackers, and all the staff make this such a memorable experience for all that visit.

Coming to Africa has kick-started a life of wildlife based travel for me. My first adventure was to Kenya, Tanzania and Rwanda. That trip would become one of the things that define who I am. I was bitten hard with the Africa travel bug as they say. The rest is so called history (still in the making of course), and over the years I have come to know South Africa as a second home.

As a young boy growing up on an agricultural farm in Zimbabwe, Sean spent every opportunity entertaining himself outdoors, camping in the local nature reserve and learning about all facets of the natural world.  

After completing a Bachelor of Science degree in Environmental Science in Cape Town, Sean was free to follow his nature ambitions and return to his bush-loving childhood dreams, which led him to Londolozi.

Going into semi-retirement on the guiding front in 2020 saw Sean settle into a far more permanent role in the LCH, focusing his efforts on producing media content for the Londolozi online space.

Garrett has always had an incredible love for the wilderness and found his way to Londolozi straight after University. After spending time as a Londolozi Camp Manager, the incredible stories of daily sightings from his ranger counterparts and guests alike pushed him to become a Londolozi Guide, where he enjoyed 3 years in the field sharing Londolozi with thousands of guests. After a brief sabbatical travelling through Southern Africa and working in Tanzania, Garrett returned to the Londolozi Family as Sales Manager sharing Londolozi with as many people as possible.

Nick was a ranger at Londolozi from 2018 - 2022. He always had a love for nature. Growing up in Johannesburg, the annual family trip to the bush (particularly the Kruger Lowveld region of South Africa) became an escape from city life. When he and his brother weren't physically in the bush, they would pretend they were by watching wildlife documentaries and making animal tracks in the garden at home. After high school, Nick spent a year teaching sport in England and then returned to South Africa to study Engineering at Stellenbosch University. It was in the mountains of Stellenbosch where Nick further cultivated his passion for nature.

Megan grew up at Londolozi, where her love for nature blossomed. With a degree in Visual Studies and Social Media Marketing, her journey came full circle when she joined the dynamic Londolozi Creative Hub, where her love for nature and visuals finds its perfect home. 

Guided by an unwavering love for photography, videography, and the captivating realm of visuals, Megan hopes to impart a unique and vibrant essence to each of the creative projects she takes on.

section_profile.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: Despite her small size, this daughter of the Nyelethi Female established herself as a significant presence in Londolozi's northern reaches.
section_profile.lol_basic_profile_excerpt_alt: The Nanga female was born to the Nyelethi 4:4 female in 2009 as part of a litter of three.
section_profile.lol_basic_profile_content:
Heritage & Lineage

Born June 2009 to the Nyelethi Female
Part of a rare intact litter of three cubs that reached independence
Carried forward the Saseka Female lineage
Success continued through daughter Makomsava Female

Territory
Primary domain included:

The northern bank of Sand River
Manyelethi River system
Southern Cross Koppies
Central to eastern Marthly
Shifted territory northward over time due to pressure from Tutlwa Female

Physical Characteristics

3:3 spot pattern
Notably small for an adult female
Three spots grouped closely together on the right cheek

Reproductive History
Demonstrated persistence despite numerous setbacks:

2013: Two cubs (one lost at 5 months, male forced to independence at 11 months)
2014: Two cubs (both lost, killed by Tutlwa Female)
2015: Single cub (lost at 4 months, killed by Tutlwa Female)
2016: Litter never seen

Most notable success:

2016: Makomsava Female (reached independence and established territory)

Behavioural Notes

Utilized Manyelethi River drainage lines extensively
Favored Southern Cross Koppies for denning sites
Maintained territory despite being one of the smaller females
Regularly moved between riverine and koppie systems
Showed preference for hunting in drainage line vegetation

Historical Significance

Successfully established territory at a young age following mother’s death
Maintained northern territory despite pressure from larger females
Faced unique challenges from female infanticide by Tutlwa Female
Legacy continues through Makomsava Female’s success
Provided early documentation of female leopard infanticide at Londolozi

Her death in 2019 marked the end of a decade-long presence in the northern territories. Through her daughter the Makomsava Female, her bloodline continues to influence Londolozi’s leopard population.

lol_family_litters.lol_family_litters_desc: 1 cub believed killed by Tsalala pride. Other cub Nanga young male, believed to have moved north of Londolozi.
Cubs likely killed by territorially dominant Tutlwa 4:3 Female
One disappeared early on. Second cub killed by Tutlwa female, aged 4 months.
One cub survived.

acf.lol_basic_profile_excerpt: Born 1998 to 3:4 Female. Extended Mother Leopard's legacy through successful offspring before being displaced in her final years.
acf.lol_basic_profile_content:
Named after the Dudley Riverbank area as the regions she frequented

Heritage & Lineage
Born in September 1998 to the legendary 3:4 Female and younger sister to the Nottens Female, representing the fourth generation of the Mother Leopard’s lineage. Her successful raising of offspring, particularly the Ndzanzeni Female, ensured the continuation of this prestigious bloodline.

Territory
Her territory evolved significantly throughout her life:

Initially established southeast of her mother’s range
Expanded westward after 3:4’s death
Eventually held territory from Sand River to central Londolozi
In later years, forced into nomadic existence by the Tamboti Female
Frequently utilized the Tugwaan riverbed and Mad Elephant Donga

Physical Characteristics

3:3 spot pattern
Pale coat characteristic of the Mother Leopard lineage
Notable aging features in later life include tattered ears and a gaunt appearance

Reproductive History
Notable offspring include:

December 2002: Two cubs (fate unknown)
December 2004: Two cubs (fate unknown)
December 2005: Two cubs (fate unknown)
October 2006: DRB 5:5 Male and DRB 4:3 Male
July 2009: DRB 3:3 Young Male and one sibling
March 2012: Ndzanzeni Female (last and most significant offspring)

Behavioural Notes
Demonstrated remarkable adaptability throughout her life, particularly in her final years when forced into a nomadic existence. Showed excellent maternal instincts, successfully denning cubs in well-chosen locations like the Mad Elephant Donga drainage system. In her final months, adapted her hunting strategy to focus on smaller prey as age took its toll.
Historical Significance

A crucial link in Mother Leopard’s lineage
Successfully raised multiple offspring to independence
Through the Ndzanzeni Female, ensured the continuation of the Original Mother Leopard bloodline
Her displacement in later years provided valuable insights into ageing leopard behaviour
Demonstrated remarkable resilience, living to 17 years despite territorial pressures
Final months documented the natural progression of ageing in wild leopards

Her story particularly resonates through her final years, when despite being displaced from her territory, she demonstrated the incredible adaptability of leopards, surviving through modified hunting strategies and behavioral adjustments until age finally caught up with her.

1 cub, Ndzanzeni 4:3 female, now independent
